item.title: Lift Each Other Up: A Field Guide for Engineering Teams
item.description: A talk I gave my team to welcome new joiners: ask with context, own the next step, verify what you share, and leave a clearer path for the next person.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

  1. Ask with context. Share the goal and where you’re stuck.
  2. Own the next step. Claim it, or make the handoff explicit.
  3. Verify what you share. Bring your own judgement to AI output and code.
  4. Leave a clearer path. Improve the doc, test or explanation for the next person.

A bunch of new folks joined my team recently, so I put together a short talk for them. Well, for them and for everyone who has been around long enough to still ask “which repo was that in?” 🙃

The point wasn’t onboarding trivia. Nobody is expected to arrive knowing every tool, permission check, repository or historical decision. The point was a handful of habits that make working together easier, habits we can practise on each other. This post is that talk, minus the slides. The examples are made up, but I bet you’ve seen every one of them.

Fresh eyes are useful

If setup feels confusing to a new joiner, that’s not a them problem. That’s feedback.

  • If you’re new: ask early. Show where you got stuck. Your question might save the next person an hour.
  • If you’ve been here a while: explain the why. Pair when words stop helping. Put the answer where the next joiner can find it.

Because nobody learns the auth flow by osmosis.

Pause here: It’s day 3. Setup is stuck. The doc says “just run it”. The terminal disagrees.

What would you send in the team channel? And what would a helpful reply look like?

Hello, with the useful bit attached

I’ve written about this before, and I’ll keep repeating it till the heat death of the universe. Compare:

❌ “Hey, got a minute?”

The other person has to reply before they even know what you need. That’s an extra round trip, and if they’re in another time zone, an extra day.

✅ “Hey! The Jira tool returns a 403 locally. Setup completed. I’ve put the error and request ID in the thread. Could someone help me trace the access check?”

A hello and the question fit in the same message. It’s fine to be warm and chatty, we’re only cutting out the round trip that helps nobody. nohello.net says it better than me.

A help request people can answer

You don’t need a template, but a help request that covers these four things is one people can actually pick up:

A partial investigation is enough. Say where you’re stuck. If you couldn’t find an error or a request ID, say that too. Asking for help shouldn’t turn into homework.

And if you’re the one replying: a 403 doesn’t prove any particular cause. Help find the failing check first. (Also, never paste credentials into a help request. Ever.)

Our broken windows wear TODOs

The broken windows idea comes from Wilson and Kelling (1982). Its use in policing is controversial, so I’m only borrowing it as a metaphor: visible neglect sends a signal, and small bits of neglect start to look normal. In a codebase they look like this:

  • The flaky test: the third retry is now the test strategy.
  • The tool description: accurate last year, confusing today.
  • The setup doc: one missing step. Every. New. Joiner.
  • The “temporary” workaround: celebrating its second birthday. 🎂
  • The unowned TODO: waiting for its forever home.
  • The missing test: “We’ll add it after this PR.”

Make a small repair, or leave a clear owner and a follow-up. Keep it proportionate though: a small cleanup is helpful, a surprise rewrite in an unrelated PR is a nightmare to review. And a new joiner who points out a gap is already helping.

Visibility needs an owner

Pause here: Main is red. Six people have seen it.

Who owns the next move? What’s the first message you’d send?

A seventh pair of eyes does not count as a handoff.

This is the bystander trap: everyone sees it, everyone assumes someone else has it. Darley and Latané’s 1968 study called it diffusion of responsibility. You don’t need to know the root cause before you claim a bounded investigation. Pick whichever one is true:

  • You can investigate: “I’m checking it. I’ll update in 15 minutes.”
  • You’re at capacity: “I can’t take this. Can someone pick it up?”
  • You’re handing over: “Here’s what I checked, and the next useful step.”

Owning it can mean coordinating and asking for help. It doesn’t mean doing every task yourself, and being new doesn’t mean you’re expected to fix an unfamiliar failure alone.

No meat proxy

AI can help. You still own the answer.

❌ “The AI says it’s probably auth.”

The reader still has to go find the evidence. You’ve just forwarded a guess with extra steps.

✅ “I checked the trace. This access check returns the 403. I haven’t confirmed why yet. Can we pair on that step?”

Be clear about what you verified and what you still don’t know. No Meat Proxy puts it nicely: read, understand and verify AI output before you pass it on to people or submit it as work. Using AI is welcome, the responsibility just stays with you. For code, that means you can explain the change and the tests you ran.

A PR should spare us a treasure hunt

Give the reviewer a starting point:

  • What changed: “Handle an error case in tool execution.”
  • Why it matters: “The client needs to see when the operation fails.”
  • What you checked: “Added a regression test and ran the affected suite.”
  • Where you need eyes: “Please check the error mapping and compatibility.”

Link the issue, and flag the decision you want the reviewer to look at. If you couldn’t run a check, say so. And if you’re new, a perfectly good review request is “can you check my understanding of how this works today?”

The engineer’s dilemma

This one is loosely inspired by the prisoner’s dilemma. It’s an analogy, not a payoff model:

Skipping a review can save me time today. If we all skip it, everyone inherits the risk. 🔥

“Help” here means reviewing, sharing context and making docs usable. Sometimes you genuinely can’t help because you’re at capacity, and that’s fine. The point is to make it visible and find a handoff that works, not to label teammates as cooperative or selfish.

We’ll work together again tomorrow

In Axelrod’s tournaments in 1980, the strategy that won was Tit for Tat: cooperate first, then mirror what the other player did last. It won those tournaments, under that setup, so I don’t read it as a universal law. But the shape of it fits a team that works together every single day:

  • Help first: offer context before someone has to chase it.
  • Be clear: say what you can take on, and when.
  • Speak up kindly: challenge the risky change, and explain why.
  • Reset quickly: fix the mistake, keep the trust.

Reciprocity, with room for mistakes. (And no, “mirror the other player” doesn’t mean retaliating against your colleagues. 😅)

Feedback someone can use

In a PR:

“Could we add a test for a missing cloudId? I think this path returns before we validate it.”

Name the concern. Explain the reason. Leave room to be wrong, and actually check the path before you make the claim.

After pairing:

“That setup step was missing. I’ve added it to the doc. Thanks for spotting it.”

Make the answer reusable so it isn’t trapped in a private chat, and credit the person who asked as well as the person who answered. A question that improves the docs is a contribution.

One thing this week

What can we make easier for the next teammate?

Pick one small repair this week: a setup step, a flaky test, a tool description, a missing explanation. And thank the person who helps you make it. 🙌

New joiners can contribute just by naming the step that confused them. They shouldn’t have to fix the whole onboarding experience on their own. That part’s on the rest of us.

Fin.

item.title: I'm moving all my writing here
item.description: Fifteen years of posts, spread across eight platforms, now live in one archive on my own domain. Here's what changed and where to follow along.
item.content:encoded:
From now on I’m writing in one place, and this is it. If you’ve been reading me on Medium, DEV, LinkedIn or X, new posts will only show up here, on jatinkrmalik.com.

How it ended up scattered

I started in 2011 with a gadget news blog in college. Then came a Blogger log of me learning JavaScript, BitSnapper for reviews and Raspberry Pi projects, a short-lived GitHub Pages blog, and later Medium, LinkedIn and X threads. Every time I moved, the old stuff stayed behind, and most of it slowly rotted. Some of those blogs are gone now and only survive on the Wayback Machine.

I got tired of that. I’d rather own one archive that I can move, back up and keep alive than keep renting space on eight platforms that change their rules every few years.

What’s here now

Everything I could recover is on this site, around 220 posts going back to 2011. The About page lists where each batch first lived, and every old post says where it was first published. There’s search (press /), tags, and a few series, like the Zion homelab one.

A bunch of it I rebuilt with help from AI agents: moving posts out of dead platforms, fixing broken images, writing the per-post share cards. They did a lot of the grunt work, and I checked what went in.

Where to follow

  • RSS: add jatinkrmalik.com/rss.xml to your feed reader, or follow in one click. This is the best way.
  • X: @jatinkrmalik. I’ll post a link when something new goes up.

That’s it. No newsletter for now.

What happens to the old accounts

They stay up, I’m not deleting anything. But they’re frozen: the old Medium and DEV posts will stay where they are, and the copies here are the ones I’ll keep fixing and updating. If you find a broken link or a missing image in an old post, tell me on X and I’ll fix it here.

See you in the next one. There’s a lot more homelab coming lol.

item.title: Zion, part 3: my custom-built homelab dashboard, on a Fire 7 tablet from 2015
item.description: Why I wrote my own homelab dashboard in stdlib Python, and what it took to keep a 2015 Fire 7 on LineageOS showing it on the wall 24/7.
item.content:encoded:
Zion runs about 40 containers now, and any of them can break without me noticing. I wanted one screen I could glance at from across the room that either says “All good” or tells me exactly what’s wrong. This part is about that screen, and about the 2015 Fire 7 that shows it on my wall, which turned out to be the harder half lol.

Why not Homepage

I started with Homepage like everyone does, but it’s a launcher. It won’t tell me the last scrub was too long ago or that a SMART counter just went up. Grafana means Prometheus plus a pile of dashboards-as-code. Uptime Kuma (which I do run) only knows up or down.

So I wrote my own: about 700 lines of Python using only the standard library, plus plain JS and CSS, with no framework and no build step. The container sits at around 26 MiB of RAM.

A few weeks later I retired Homepage completely. It was two containers and ~120 MB of RAM for a second list of links I had to keep in sync. The bare zion.<mydomain> now redirects to the dash.

Where the data comes from

  • Netdata, every 5 seconds: CPU (total and per thread), RAM, load, temps, network, disk IO and stall time.
  • The Docker API through a read-only socket proxy. It can list containers and that’s it, any POST gets a 403.
  • Health checks against every app’s own local port every 15 seconds. An app only counts as down after two failures in a row.
  • vnStat for daily and monthly bandwidth.
  • A root collector on a systemd timer every 30 seconds, for the stuff a container shouldn’t be allowed to touch: pool status, scrub and snapshot age, SMART, systemd units, Tailscale, pending updates, and both Surfshark tunnels (it hops into each Gluetun container’s network namespace to check them).

The server turns all of that into one verdict plus a list of problems, and the page just polls it every 5 seconds and draws it. All the logic lives on the server so the page stays dumb, which paid off later when it had to run on a tablet with under 1 GB of RAM.

What turns it amber or red

That’s from day two, when Homepage still had a tile. The thresholds live in one config.json as warn and crit pairs: CPU, memory, swap, temps, pool capacity (amber at 85%, red at 90%), scrub and snapshot age, cert expiry, backups older than 26 hours, the off-site upload older than 8 days. On top of those it flags pool errors, SMART, apps failing their checks, failed systemd units and stopped containers. When anything’s wrong the header turns into a solid ochre or red band with the problems listed under it.

SMART needed a trick. The Seagate in the old pool has 1480 CRC errors on its lifetime counter from old cable trouble, and those counters live in the drive firmware, so you can’t reset them. The first version sat on amber forever. Now config.json holds a baseline (what every counter read on Oct 14) and it only alerts when a counter climbs above it.

The VPN check is my favourite. For each tunnel the collector checks that the container is running, the tunnel is up, it can actually reach the internet, and which city it exits from. Then it compares the tunnel’s public IP with my home IP. If they match, the dash goes red with “LEAK: traffic leaves from the home IP”.

Every app tile has a strip of bars, one per 30 minutes over the last 24 hours, so if something was flaky at 3am I can see it even when it’s green now.

Design stuff I didn’t expect to care about

The first version was the classic dark neon homelab look and I had it redone the same day. Now it’s a light “paper” sheet with one blue accent for charts and status colours only for status. No glows, no pulsing dots, and it always fits one screen.

The CPU panel took three tries. Thin lines for all 8 threads were too faint. Then 8 bars next to the big number, which I didn’t like. Then htop style, one 0[|||||| 45%] meter per thread coloured green to amber to red like btop. That one stuck.

During an IO storm, Netdata’s sensor plugin died and the temperature chart started returning 404. The dash fetched all vitals in one request, so that one 404 blanked CPU, memory, network and disk. Now a missing temperature only drops the temperature.

The wall view

The tablet is a 2015 Fire 7 running LineageOS 14.1 (Android 7.1) with 887 MB of RAM 💀 On its 1024x600 screen the full dash had to be read up close, so it got its own page on top of the same data: clock, verdict, big CPU and memory numbers with a level gauge, pool and boot drive in one split tile, network rates with the VPN exit’s flag and city, and every app as an icon. Slow apps get a yellow outline, down ones go red and grey. Numbers turn white, yellow or red on the current value, so a CPU spike shows from across the room. If the data goes stale it says “Zion not answering” in red.

The tablet can’t run Tailscale, so Caddy serves the dash read-only on a LAN-only port, and both the firewall and Caddy allow only the tablet. It’s plain HTTP because Android 7 doesn’t have the current Let’s Encrypt root cert. No HTTPS also means no screen wake lock, so the tablet relies on “Stay awake while charging”. Remember that setting, it comes back.

The tablet rabbit hole

With under a gig of RAM, Android 7 kills the browser (Fennec from F-Droid) whenever it feels like it, and it won’t relaunch it by itself. Fully Kiosk was out because on this ROM it’s stuck on WebView 100 and restart-after-crash is a paid feature.

Version one was Zion babysitting the tablet over ADB (only Zion’s key is accepted). A timer on Zion ran every minute: wake the screen, bring Fennec back, set the backlight from a sunrise/sunset calculation since there’s no light sensor, and tap the page into full screen. A page can’t go full screen without a tap, so the page reports its full screen state with every poll and Zion taps when it’s false.

On Nov 5 I found it stuck on the Developer options screen. The watchdog had been failing silently for two days. The tablet’s adbd had run out of file descriptors and refused every command, while adb get-state still happily said “device”. Turns out every adb connect leaks a socket in this adbd, even when you’re already connected (5 connects took it from 55 to 60 open files). Connecting every minute meant ~1000 sockets in ~17 hours, then the 1024 limit. Fix: only connect when the tablet isn’t already listed, and restart adbd past 500 open files. During that recovery “Stay awake while charging” got reset, so the screen timed out to the PIN lock. The watchdog puts that setting back now too.

Then on Nov 7 Zion did its 4:30am reboot for a kernel update, and the tablet’s adbd answered “offline” until I toggled ADB over network by hand. Later that day Zion’s IP changed while I sorted out a DHCP reservation, and it went “offline” again.

The cause: this adbd serves one host session at a time. While one is open it accepts every other connection and never reads it (hence the leak). When Zion vanishes mid-session, the tablet keeps that session “established” forever because there’s no keepalive, and every new connect gets ignored.

The fix: the tablet watches itself

Every recovery depended on ADB working, so the watchdog moved onto the tablet. It’s a shell script that init starts as root at boot from an .rc file (this ROM is a userdebug build with SELinux permissive, so that’s allowed). Every 30 seconds it keeps “Stay awake while charging” on, wakes the screen, sets day or night brightness, restarts adbd before the leak gets near 1024 files or when one host session has been open 30 minutes (Zion’s real sessions last seconds), and brings Fennec back if it got killed or the page stopped polling Zion. Reopening adds a fresh ?r=<timestamp> to the URL, because otherwise Fennec keeps an old “Unable to connect” page from while Zion was down.

I force-stopped Fennec and the page was polling again in ~40 seconds, and ADB wasn’t involved at all. For the stale session I tested with a 2.5 minute limit by dropping Zion’s packets: got “offline”, the tablet restarted adbd, Zion reconnected.

Zion is just an observer now. It taps the page back into full screen when needed, falls back to the old ADB nudging if the page has been gone 5 minutes, and shows a failed unit on the dash if that fails too.

And then today it ran flat while plugged in, dropping ~4% an hour while “charging”. The charger reads ~4.72 V and can’t keep up with full brightness, Wi-Fi and Fennec around the clock. Day brightness went from 255 to 150 for now. Next up: a 2A adapter with a short cable, battery level on the dash, and turning ADB over network on at boot, because after the cold boot it was off again. This tablet, man.

Built with a lot of AI help

The dashboard and the tablet watchdog were built with a lot of help from Claude and other AI agents. They wrote most of the code, did a lot of the measuring (counting adbd’s open files, timing recoveries) and kept the log in my repo. They got stuff wrong too: the first guess at the socket leak was wrong, and one agent’s “fix” for the offline tablet was to check every 5 minutes instead of every minute, which only made recovery 5x slower. I decided what the screen should show, picked and rejected designs (RIP the CPU bars), tested on the actual tablet on my actual wall, and checked everything that went in.

What’s on your homelab’s wall? And if you’ve kept an ancient Android tablet alive as a kiosk, how did you stop it from killing the browser? There has to be a less cursed way than an init script lol.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Zion, part 2: about 40 containers and nothing exposed to the internet
item.description: The software on my trash-rescued homelab: ZFS, Docker Compose, Tailscale-only access with real HTTPS, a VPN'd download stack, Immich and the boring backup bits.
item.content:encoded:
Part 1 was about pulling an HP Envy out of the garbage room and fighting its PSU. This one is about what actually runs on it. Short version: about 40 containers, real HTTPS on every app, and not a single port open to the internet.

The base

Ubuntu Server 26.04 on the stock 2TB WD Green, ZFS for the pool, Docker Compose for everything else. Every app gets its own folder with a compose file and an .env, and Dockge sits on top so I can poke at stacks from a browser. I ran Proxmox and TrueNAS on my old lab and this time I wanted something simpler, where the whole config is just files I can keep in git.

16 GB of RAM isn’t a lot for ZFS plus about 40 containers, so the ARC is capped at 6 GiB. Before that it ate nearly all the memory during scrubs.

Remote access without opening anything

Rule one: nothing on Zion is reachable from the internet. There are no port forwards on the router and no tunnels. Cockpit, Dockge and File Browser are basically root or full access to my data, and public login pages get hammered all day.

So everything goes over Tailscale, but I still wanted proper URLs instead of a pile of IP:port bookmarks. I got them like this:

  • A wildcard DNS record at Porkbun points *.zion.<mydomain> at Zion’s tailnet address. Anyone can look the names up, but the address only goes somewhere if you’re on my tailnet.
  • Caddy (a custom build with the Porkbun DNS module) gets real Let’s Encrypt certs with the DNS-01 challenge, so it never has to be reachable from outside to prove it owns the name.
  • Authentik does forward-auth SSO in front of almost everything. Its config lives in the repo as blueprints, so adding an app is a provider, an application and a Caddy block that imports the SSO snippet.

A few apps keep their own logins: Immich, Plex and Kavita, plus Nextcloud, which logs in through Authentik with OIDC instead. Their phone apps talk to the server directly and can’t follow an SSO redirect, so forward auth would just break them. Cockpit is a root shell, so it isn’t proxied at all and keeps its own login on its own port.

Underneath all that, every app container binds to localhost. The only things listening on the network are Caddy, Plex, Cockpit, SSH, Samba and AdGuard’s DNS, and ufw keeps those to the tailnet, with LAN exceptions for SSH, Samba, DNS and Plex (so the TV works without Tailscale).

Fun one from the first week: Plex locked me out of its own Server Settings. plex.tv’s Cloudflare returns a 403 when a server advertises an address in Tailscale’s CGNAT range. Making Plex advertise only its plex.zion.<mydomain> HTTPS name fixed it.

What’s running

  • Media: Plex with Quick Sync, Tautulli, Kavita for books and comics, MeTube for YouTube courses, Tdarr
  • Downloads: Sonarr, Radarr, Prowlarr, Bazarr and qBittorrent, all inside a VPN container. Great for Linux ISOs 🐧
  • Photos and files: Immich, Nextcloud, File Browser, Samba
  • Network: AdGuard Home for DNS on the tailnet, and a Surfshark exit node
  • Monitoring: Netdata, Scrutiny for SMART, Uptime Kuma, Dozzle, vnStat, Cockpit, and my own dashboard (that’s part 3)
  • Misc: IT-Tools, a Firefox container, and Hermes

The download stack

qBittorrent, Sonarr, Radarr and Prowlarr all share one Gluetun container’s network, connected to Surfshark over WireGuard. If the tunnel drops, they drop with it. I tested the kill switch the dumb way, by taking the tunnel down inside the container and checking nothing could get out. qBittorrent is also bound to the tunnel interface, with UPnP off.

Downloads and media sit on the same dataset, so imports are hardlinks instead of copies, and qBittorrent stops at 500 GB free so it can’t fill the pool.

Early on, qBittorrent bit me by memory-mapping torrent files, which it does by default. With 4.4 GB mapped the kernel started swapping my other apps out to the slow boot drive. Switching its disk I/O type to POSIX took it from 4.4 GB to 45 MB.

About that VPN and port forwarding

When I posted Zion on r/homelab, someone pointed out that Surfshark doesn’t do port forwarding, which matters for torrents because nobody can connect in to you, so you only get peers that accept incoming connections themselves. Fair point, and thin swarms do stall (it’s not the disks: at 400 Mbit/s the pool was 75 to 88% idle). For now I work around it. Prowlarr only passes along releases with 5 or more seeders, and qBittorrent appends a public “best trackers” list to every new torrent. The proper fix is a VPN that supports port forwarding for the download tunnel only, and that’s next on the list. Surfshark stays for the exit node.

An exit node so my phone runs one VPN

Phones only run one VPN at a time, so I always had to pick between Surfshark and Tailscale. Now a second Gluetun container (its own WireGuard key, a San Jose server) has Tailscale running inside it, advertised as an exit node. My phone only runs Tailscale, and when I want the VPN I pick the exit node, which is one tap.

It was really slow at first, because Gluetun’s catch-all route also grabbed Tailscale’s own replies, so packets to my phone took a scenic trip through San Jose. A couple of routing rules that send tailnet traffic the normal way fixed that.

700 GB out of Google Photos

Immich went in at the end of October. Takeout links only work while you’re signed in to Google, and Google blocks sign-in from headless browsers, so I ran a Firefox container on Zion, signed in there and clicked the links. The zips downloaded straight onto the box: 13 of them, 541 GB. Then immich-go read the zips and Google’s JSON sidecars for dates, places and albums.

My first run, at 8 concurrent tasks during TV time, pinned the boot drive (load 30, IO pressure 95%) and Plex stalled, because its metadata lives on the same disk. So now big jobs on the boot drive run when nobody’s watching. Final count: 81,864 assets in the Takeout, 12,169 duplicates (Google exports album copies next to the year folders), and 68,011 photos plus 1,498 videos in Immich, about 496 GB. One 19 GB video timed out on both passes and had to go up on its own lol. Then Immich’s background jobs (metadata, thumbnails, faces) hammered the disk so hard that Authentik timed out and SSO went down. Putting Immich in the idle IO class fixed it.

It’s on the boot drive because the pool had 711 GB free against that 500 GB floor, and the second pool doesn’t exist yet (that’s the PSU saga from part 1). So it’s one disk with no redundancy, and Google Photos stays the backup. Immich’s database (albums, faces, edits) gets dumped to the pool every night and goes off-site with everything else.

The boring stuff that keeps it alive

  • Sanoid snapshots (24 hourly, 30 daily, 6 monthly) and a monthly scrub. Snapshots also hang on to files you replace, which I learned when upgrading a batch of movies to 1080p pushed the pool to 85% and I had to prune ~93 GB of old snapshots.
  • A nightly backup at 3:30am, split in two. A sanitized copy of the config (compose files, a slice of /etc, the package list, image digests) goes into a git repo, with a guard that refuses to commit if it spots a real secret. It once refused because it thought Immich’s database user name was a password 💀 The real secrets, the Postgres dumps and the app state go to a root-only folder on the pool, which gets snapshotted like everything else.
  • Every Sunday an encrypted archive of the DB dumps, app databases, configs and secrets goes to Google Drive through rclone crypt. Artwork, caches and logs stay out, so 4.9 GB shrinks to ~330 MB, and it keeps the newest 8. rclone only has access to files it created itself.
  • Restore notes live in the repo: reinstall Ubuntu, import the pool (never create it), put back /etc and app state, load the database dumps, start Authentik, then the rest.

Updates install themselves. Unattended upgrades covers all of Ubuntu’s updates plus the Docker and Tailscale repos at 4am, after the backup, and if a kernel or systemd update needs it the box reboots at 4:30. A Docker upgrade restarts every container, so the run skips itself while a long job like the Immich import or the HEVC batch is going, and tries again the next night. Major Ubuntu upgrades stay manual.

Swap is zram now. The 2 GB swap file lived on the slow boot HDD, filled up with idle pages during heavy IO, and paging them back in made Plex stutter. Now it’s 4 GB of compressed RAM.

I also ran a Quick Sync HEVC batch over the 100 biggest movies, as a plain systemd service with Tdarr’s ffmpeg. Before it replaces anything it checks the duration (within 2 seconds), the audio and subtitle streams, that the last 10 seconds decode cleanly, and that the new file is at most 85% of the original. Result: 13 replaced, 87 kept, 16.7 GB freed. I was hoping for ~130 GB, but my library was already pretty lean lol.

Hermes

Hermes is a self-hosted AI agent running in Docker on Zion. It sees the pool read-only and Docker only through a read-only socket proxy, so it can look at the pool and the containers but can’t change either. Its lane is homelab ops, coding help and research.

Built with a lot of AI help

I didn’t hand-write all of this. Most of the Compose files and configs, the backup scripts and a fair bit of the debugging (the exit node routing, the Immich IO fights) were built with a lot of help from Claude and other AI agents. I decided what Zion should do, made the calls and checked everything that went in, but the agents did a lot of the typing.

What’s next

Vaultwarden and Paperless-ngx are next. Both need an admin account, and those I set up myself. I also want to pull in the feed from my doorbell camera somehow, and part 3 is the dashboard and the wall tablet.

What would you add to this stack, or take out? And if you’ve found a VPN with port forwarding that plays nicely with Gluetun, I’m all ears.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Zion, part 1: one man's trash is another man's homelab
item.description: An HP Envy left in my building's garbage room with a 'Free for parts' note is now Zion. Part 1: the rescue, the drives, a 3D printed cage and a stubborn PSU.
item.content:encoded:
In early October I found an HP Envy 750 sitting in my building’s garbage room with a post-it on it saying “Free for parts”. Took it home, blew out a scary amount of dust (the CPU heatsink and the rear fans were the worst), checked the wiring, swapped the dead CMOS battery and it booted straight into BIOS. So yeah, it’s a homelab now. I’m calling it Zion.

Starting from zero, again

I’ve had a few labs before. A couple of Raspberry Pis, an old gaming PC, and a Dell R510 that sounded like a jet engine. My last setup was Proxmox with TrueNAS in a VM. Then I moved to the US and had to start from zero. Apart from drives and a few small parts, this one cost me nothing.

What’s inside

The spec sticker was scratched up but still readable.

  • HP Envy 750-177c on HP’s own IPM17-DD board
  • i7-6700 (Skylake, 4C/8T, 65 W)
  • 16 GB DDR3L, non-ECC
  • Intel HD 530 iGPU
  • The stock WD Green 2TB HDD
  • Gigabit LAN, which was a nice bonus
  • The stock 300W HP power supply
  • A front power button that doesn’t work, so I turn it on by shorting the header pins like a caveman

In the BIOS I turned on power-on after a power cut, and Wake-on-LAN.

Before installing anything I repasted the CPU with Corsair TM30 left over from my last gaming rig.

Quick Sync, and why the GTX 960 stayed in the box

The HD 530 does Quick Sync for H.264 and 8-bit HEVC, which covers Plex, Immich and a batch HEVC re-encode (part 2). 10-bit HEVC and AV1 fall back to the CPU.

I have a spare GTX 960 that would add 10-bit HEVC decode, and I left it out. It would eat the only x16 slot, needs 6-pin power from a 300W OEM supply (if it even has the cable), is stuck on legacy NVIDIA drivers, and adds heat. If I ever need 4K HDR transcoding I’ll revisit it.

Three SATA ports and an M.2 slot that isn’t

This is where you can tell it’s an OEM board. There are 3 usable SATA ports. A fourth spot on the board has no connector soldered on, and the DVD drive was using one of the three.

M.2 is worse. The one M.2 slot is a key A slot with the Wi-Fi card in it. There’s a second M.2 footprint, also with no connector soldered on, and from what I read PCIe-to-M.2 adapters don’t boot on this BIOS anyway. So no SSD. The boot drive is the stock WD Green HDD. It’s slow, but it’s still a lot more durable than booting off a USB stick.

The SATA card saga

That leaves PCIe: the x16 slot (free) and an x1 slot. The x1 got a SATA card. The plan was an ASMedia ASM1064 or ASM1166, and the one hard requirement was no port multiplier. What I ended up with from a Micro Center run was a JMicron JMB585 (5 ports, AHCI, no port multiplier), and it carried the old pool for its first few weeks.

Later I swapped it for a Marvell 88SE9215 (PCIe 2.0 x1, 4 ports, plain AHCI, no port multiplier). The disks came up at 6 Gbps and ZFS, importing by disk ID, didn’t care about the new controller. What did break was the IP. After the swap the router handed Zion a different one, Caddy couldn’t bind to its old address and every site went down at once lol. A DHCP reservation fixed it for good.

The old pool comes back to life

I also had three 2TB drives (2x WD Blue and a Seagate, all SMR) with a RAIDZ1 pool from my old server. It had been sitting in a box since I moved countries. The last scrub on it was January 2023.

At first I could only hook up one of the three, through the DVD drive’s SATA cable, because I had nowhere to plug in power for the others (more on that below). Funnily enough, past me had also named that pool “zion”. With 1 of 3 disks it showed up as UNAVAIL, so I had to wait for a power splitter from AliExpress.

Once all three were in, it imported (with -f, since another system had last used it) and came up ONLINE. ZFS fixed one checksum error on the Seagate during the import. Then I ran a scrub, which took 8 hours 42 minutes on these SMR drives, repaired 4K and finished with zero errors. Everything was still there: 880 GB of movies, 1.8 TB of TV shows, my comics and the YouTube courses folder.

SMART was mostly fine. The Seagate has 1,480 old CRC errors, but the count hasn’t moved since I put in new cables. The two WD Blues are at around 656k and 683k load cycles against a rating of about 300k, because they love to park their heads. They’re fine for media and second copies, but nothing I can’t replace is going on them.

Seven drives, room for four

Counting everything, I have 7 HDDs:

  • The WD Green 2TB boot drive
  • The three 2TB drives from the old pool
  • 2x WD Red Plus 4TB (CMR)
  • A 4TB I shucked out of a WD My Book

The case fits 4. I was about to buy an enclosure and then remembered I own a 3D printer and I can just do things. Below is the first draft, printed in translucent green PETG. Yes, it’s a monstrosity 💀

The early designs were sloppy. When I checked them against the actual drive spec (SFF-8301), the side screw holes were at mid-height, 10 mm from the front. On a real drive they’re 6.35 mm above the PCB face and 28.5 mm from the connector end, so not one hole would have lined up with a drive. The fan plate also sat right over the SATA plugs.

So v2 is a proper parametric design in OpenSCAD. It’s a 3-drive cage (155 x 112.8 x 98.1 mm) that goes where the slim DVD drive is now, with an 80mm fan on the front, an open back for the SATA cables, 12 side screws at the real SFF-8301 positions, and counterbores so standard 6-32 x 1/4” screws bite about 2.8 mm. The ledges are chamfered so it prints without supports.

There’s also a flat tray for one more drive. Between the bottom edge of the motherboard and the case floor there’s a gap of roughly 40 mm, and a 3.5” drive lying flat is 26 mm tall. The tray holds it PCB-down, screwed from below, on rubber feet, zip-tied to the floor vents. It needs at least 36 mm of clearance, so that gets measured first.

v2 isn’t printed yet. The numbers so far come from HP’s specs and photos, not a ruler, and the cage plus fan (about 180 mm) looks longer than the bay is deep (about 125 mm). Before burning 8 to 12 hours of PETG, I’m going to hold a cardboard box cut to 180 x 113 x 98 mm where the cage goes.

One mystery: under the slim DVD drive there’s a black sheet-metal box I assumed was a 2.5” cage. A teardown of the ENVY 750se (same chassis family) says it’s a 4th tool-less 3.5” bay that loads from the front. I haven’t confirmed it on mine. Either way it comes out for the printed cage, and hopefully its screw holes become the cage’s mounting points.

The actual problem: power

Then I hit the real wall, which is the PSU. It’s a Chicony unit made for HP, 300W, with two 12V rails (12A and 16A). It’s fine for 4 drives. The trouble is everything around it:

  • It has a custom HP motherboard power connector, so I can’t just swap in a normal ATX supply.
  • It has exactly one SATA power cable.
  • The DVD drive’s power plug is a slimline one, useless for a 3.5” drive.

I’m already splitting that one cable to run 4 drives (boot plus the 3-disk pool). What I learned about splitters: avoid molded ones (the connector is one solid block of plastic, a known fire risk), and I passed on one listing just because it said “molded connectors”. Get crimped pins or the flat ribbon kind with press-on connectors, like SilverStone’s CP06-E4. Don’t hang more than 2 drives off one PSU plug. And watch the first power-on, because spin-up is when the drives pull the most.

There’s no sane way to hang 3 more drives off that one cable. The cage can hold them but I can’t power them.

Where I’m stuck: the second pool

The old 2TB pool is fine for media and Linux ISOs. I want a second ZFS pool on the three 4TB drives for the stuff that actually matters (all three are CMR: the two Reds, and I checked the shucked one too). Photos are the big one. Immich lives on the single boot drive right now and Google Photos is the only other copy. Because of the PSU, those drives can’t go inside Zion. Options I’ve been looking at:

  1. A 4-bay SATA HDD enclosure with its own power supply, connected to Zion over eSATA. Cheap and everything stays on one box. I’d need an eSATA card or bracket though, and I’m not sure how I feel about ZFS on an external enclosure, especially if it uses a port multiplier.
  2. The Beelink ME Pro N150 on Kickstarter, which I’ve backed for now (with the deposit that upgrades it to the 4-bay chassis). 16 GB RAM (soldered), 5GbE plus 2.5GbE, native ZFS, low power. Zion would stay the compute box and its 2TB pool would become the backup target. But it’s more money, it ships in December, and it’s Kickstarter hardware. The campaign ends December 5, my last chance to cancel for free, so that’s my real deadline.
  3. Something I haven’t thought of. A proper ATX PSU with an adapter for HP’s connector? A used SAS HBA and a DAS?

I’m torn on this. If you were building a pool for data you can’t replace, which way would you go? And if you’ve had this Envy chassis open, is that box under the slim DVD bay a 3.5” bay or a 2.5” cage? Tell me in the comments.

A note on AI help

The OpenSCAD cage and tray, the check against the drive spec, and a lot of the research (SATA cards, splitters, the chassis teardown) were done with a lot of help from Claude and other AI agents. The agents did a lot of the typing. I made the calls and held the screwdriver, and I checked everything that went in.

Next up is the software: about 40 containers, Tailscale-only access and the VPN setup.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Zion, part 0: my homelabs before it, from a Pi stack to a Dell R510
item.description: Before Zion there was a Raspberry Pi stack in Bangalore and a Dell PowerEdge R510 in Delhi. What they ran, what I sold, and what made it to the US.
item.content:encoded:
In May 2026 I tweeted that I was tired of paying Google for storage, month over month, and that I was building my own cloud storage (yet again) that day. Two WD Red Plus 4TB drives were already sitting on my desk.

Someone caught the “yet again” and asked what happened. Fair question. I replied that I had set up a NAS twice before, in my previous life in Bangalore and Delhi: a Raspberry Pi stack in 2019 and a Dell PowerEdge R510 (I said 2022 in that reply, but it actually showed up in August 2020). I had to take both apart and sell them before moving to the USA. I also promised to write it up soon, so here it is, a bit late lol.

The machine that runs my stuff today is Zion, an HP Envy I pulled out of my building’s garbage room, and it has its own series. This post is everything that came before it.

It started with one Raspberry Pi 2

The first homelab I wrote about was a single Raspberry Pi 2 Model B with 1GB of RAM, back in 2015. I wrote a walkthrough of the board and then kept giving it new jobs: a NAS, a LAMP web server and a PirateBox. Before those guides it had already been a Twitter bot, an FTP/HTTP server, a RetroPie box and an ad-blocking DNS, all done quick and dirty.

That same Pi 2 later ran Pi-hole in Bangalore in 2019, powered off my modem’s USB port. A month in, about 24% of the DNS queries on my network were ads and trackers.

2019: the Bangalore Pi stack

One Pi turned into four. One Sunday in Bangalore I put three of them in a clear acrylic stack, the fourth in a finned aluminium case next to it, wired them all to a gigabit switch, and posted a photo that said “Well, this was a productive Sunday!”

Here’s what each Pi did:

  • A Pi 4 in a finned aluminium case ran Plex with a 2TB drive as the NAS, plus OpenVPN and PirateBox
  • A second Pi 4, at the top of the stack, ran NGINX to host my blog
  • A Pi 3 in the middle was the retro gaming setup
  • The old Pi 2 at the bottom was still blocking ads with Pi-hole

That’s the “PiNAS + PiStack” from my tweet. It’s basically the NAS and PirateBox ideas from my old Pi 2 guides, spread across more boards. Years later I finally retired my RetroPie box and moved my emulators to my phone.

“I think I may have a problem”

In March 2021 I tweeted at @Raspberry_Pi: “Folks, I think I may have a problem. :P” The photo had five boards on my desk: three in the acrylic stack, one in a black finned case and one in a layered acrylic case with a tiny fan.

In 2024, when someone asked me why I’d run a Pi cluster instead of a cheap mini PC, the honest answer was that I’ve been collecting Raspberry Pis like Pokemon for the last 10 years. The longer answer:

While a cheap mini PC will give you more bang for your buck, a Raspberry Pi cluster is a great way to dive into distributed computing concepts. It’s a hands-on way to learn about load balancing, fault tolerance, and other cool stuff. Plus, it’s a fun project!

2020: a Dell PowerEdge R510 in Delhi

In August 2020 the Pis got a big brother in Delhi: a Dell PowerEdge R510 (its first month has a post of its own). No rack. It sat on a wooden cabinet with my mechanical keyboard parked on top, a VGA cable and a USB stick hanging out of the front. It sounded like a jet engine.

In June 2022 I updated my “ancient old Dell R510”, all thanks to @KWF and his site updateyodell.net. It’s a lifesaver 🙌

The Lifecycle Controller listed new diagnostics, a new OS drivers pack (6.2.0.11 to 15.04.00) and new firmware for the Broadcom NetXtreme II NICs. The one unticked row is the BIOS, and look at the versions: the one on offer, 1.12.0, is older than the 1.14.0 already on the box. My verdict at the time: “Beautiful. 🤌”

Proxmox, Matrix style

Next up was upgrading to Proxmox 7 🤞

The R510 ran Proxmox VE 6.4, whose support was ending on 31 July 2022. I called the node matrix, and the guests on it were named after Matrix characters: link, lock, switch, dozer, trinity, zion, neo, morpheus, architect, merovingian, smith and oracle, plus two plainly named ones, pentest and miner.

The screenshot is pve6to7, the checklist Proxmox ships for this upgrade. It found no running guests, warned that two storages, zion and zero_one, were enabled but not active, and flagged the old maxfiles backup setting as deprecated in favour of prune-backups. The last line tells you to switch the Debian security repo from buster/updates to bullseye-security in /etc/apt/sources.list.

My last setup before the move was Proxmox with TrueNAS in a VM.

There was already a storage (and a VM) called zion on matrix back in 2022. When I imported my old ZFS pool on the HP Envy this year, it turned out past me had named that pool zion too.

All my machines get quirky hostnames like this. In 2025 the list was anton (MacBook), sauron (PC), celsus (NAS), zion (laptop), neo, morpheus and trinity (the Pis) and zeus (phone). As I said back then, it makes them easy to find on the network!

Selling it all and moving to the US

Then I moved to the US in August 2024. The R510 was taken apart and sold before the move. What did make the trip: the four-Pi stack (“I hope they don’t end up confiscating it. :’)” I tweeted before flying), and three 2TB hard drives (2x WD Blue and a Seagate, all SMR) pulled out of my NAS server.

HomeLab 3.0

Everything stayed in boxes for two months. In November 2024 I finally unpacked it all and tweeted “HomeLab 3.0 // Coming soon™”. On the desk: the Pi stack, the fan-cased Pi, a Pi in a black aluminium case, a small switch, the boxes for a Sense HAT and a Camera V2, a multimeter, the external HDD (the black mini tower, my cold backup) and, of course, a ThinkPad.

Someone asked if the ThinkPad was part of the homelab too. There was only one correct answer:

A couple of days later I booted everything up for the first time in months. I’d carried most of the hardware across without anti-static bags, so I was a bit worried. Thankfully, other than outdated apt packages, everything worked! The four raspberries on the boot screen are one per CPU core, not one per Pi.

I hadn’t worked out my network topology yet, but the plan was Pi-hole for DNS-based ad blocking first, then probably PiVPN with WireGuard, then a Plex server (maybe on a Pi 5 or a mini PC, for that sweet transcoding support). For the three 2TB drives I was torn between a Synology and a custom PC. A week later I was also asking AMD or Intel for a PC rig to experiment with the homelab and game on once in a while.

The itch comes back

In October 2025 a South Korean government data center fire was in the news, with reports that 858TB of government data might be lost for good. I tweeted the 3-2-1 backup rule: three copies of your data, on two different kinds of media, with one copy off-site, ideally more than a few miles away from the other two.

Then came the May 2026 tweet from the top of this post. When someone asked about the RAID level, I said RAID 5, plus another 4TB sitting in an enclosure that I would shuck for the bare drive.

In September I dragged the Pi stack out again, with a box full of cables, for a project I’ll share soon. I was hoping the SD cards weren’t dead yet 🤞 (if you don’t have a box full of cables, are you even an engineer?)

A couple of weeks later I found the HP Envy in the garbage room, and the rest is Zion. As I put it in a reply once Zion was up, I’ve run all kinds of home labs over the years: a couple of Raspberry Pis, a gaming PC, the Dell rack server, and now I’m starting again in a new city.

What I’d tell someone starting

Mostly things I’ve already said on X:

  • If you want the most bang for your buck, buy a cheap mini PC. If you want to learn distributed systems, a Pi cluster is the fun way to do it.
  • Follow the 3-2-1 rule, and keep a cold backup. Mine was an external HDD.
  • Give your machines memorable hostnames. It makes them easy to find on the network.
  • When it goes over your head, Google is your friend ;)

Zion’s story is in part 1, the software and my current backups are in part 2, and the dashboard is in part 3.

What was your first homelab? Tell me in the comments.

item.title: Labelarium: I kept losing one sheet of paper, so I built an app
item.description: My Brother P-touch has 649 symbols indexed on one paper sheet I kept losing. Labelarium is the offline, open-source companion app I built instead, now on Product Hunt and Peerlist.
item.content:encoded:
Labelarium is on Product Hunt today, and on Peerlist this week. It’s free and open source, and it started with a sheet of paper.

Here it is in 30 seconds:

The sheet of paper

I have a Brother P-touch PT-D220 label maker. Its symbols and frames are buried in menus on the device, and the quick way to find one is a single paper sheet with all 649 symbols on it. I kept losing that sheet, and the fallback was going through the PDF manual every time I wanted a good label.

So in September I made a companion app for myself. It’s a PWA, it works completely offline once installed, and it’s open source. I also added the most popular models from Reddit, from DYMO, NIIMBOT, Brady and Phomemo, for ten models in total.

Of course, the first label I printed with it was for the chaat masala dispenser.

Label number one. Priorities.

What it does

It lives at labelarium.com. For the PT-D220, all 649 symbols are indexed across 30 categories. Search “do not enter” and you get the symbol and the exact keys to press on your model.

There’s also a label designer: you type your text, pick a real tape width and colour, and it gives you a step-by-step recipe of key presses that you tick off as you go.

The ten supported models, and the recipe for one label.

Under the hood

It’s plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no dependencies, plus a service worker for offline use, hosted on GitHub Pages. The code is under AGPL-3.0.

Building with agents

Building with agents still feels unreal: hit an annoying problem, use the fix an hour later, then keep making it better.

If you have a label maker that isn’t in Labelarium yet, tell me which one I should add next.
