item.title: Turning a Samsung Foldable into a Retro Handheld: An AI-Agent-Run ES-DE Setup Guide
item.description: 20 systems, one frontend, every one running at full speed. Here’s how an AI agent and I got there, including the parts that broke.
item.content:encoded:
20 systems, one frontend, every one running at full speed. Here’s how an AI agent and I got there, including the parts that broke.

After an AI agent finished fixing my phone’s battery over ADB (that’s an earlier post in this series), I gave it a more fun job.

For years my emulation box was a Raspberry Pi running RetroPie. Phones are now far more powerful than a Pi. My whole dev setup already runs on one, and I have backups of games I own that I wanted to play on mine. So the plan was to retire the Pi and turn my Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (Snapdragon SM8850, Adreno 840) into a proper retro handheld. Everything had to launch from ES-DE, with good box art, sensible settings per console and an FPS counter.

End of an era.

This is the guide. I wrote it so another person, or another AI agent, can repeat it on any reasonably modern Android phone.

A legal note: this guide is about setting up emulators. It doesn’t cover where to get games and doesn’t link to any. It assumes you’re using backups of games and BIOS files you own and dumped from your own hardware. Emulators are legal. Downloading ROMs or BIOS files you don’t own generally isn’t, and the rules on personal backups vary by country. This isn’t legal advice. And please support the developers: ES-DE for Android is a paid app, sold through Patreon and the Samsung Galaxy Store.

Quick summary

20 systems set up and tested through ES-DE:

  • Nintendo: NES, Famicom, Famicom Disk System, SNES, Super Famicom, Game Boy, Game Boy Color, GBA, N64, Virtual Boy
  • Sega: Genesis, Master System, Game Gear, 32X
  • NEC: PC Engine, TurboGrafx-16, SuperGrafx
  • Sony: PS1, PSP
  • Atari: 7800

Every system held full frame rate in testing: 60 FPS, or 50 for the Virtual Boy, which is its native rate.

The stack: ES-DE as the frontend, RetroArch for 18 of the systems, standalone PPSSPP for PSP, GameNative (open source) for PC games, and Better xCloud plus GeForce NOW for cloud gaming.

The biggest gotchas:

  • PPSSPP needs folder access granted through its own Browse button, or every launch from ES-DE fails.
  • N64’s hardware renderers give a black screen on Adreno 8xx GPUs. The software renderer works.
  • ScreenScraper’s free daily quota disappears fast if you scrape every image type.

The stack

  • ES-DE 3.5: the frontend. It holds your game lists, theme and scraped media, and launches the right emulator for each system.
  • RetroArch 1.22: with the right “core” (emulator plugin) for each system: Mesen, Snes9x, Gambatte, mGBA, Genesis Plus GX, PicoDrive, Beetle PCE / SuperGrafx / VB, ProSystem, PCSX ReARMed and Mupen64Plus-Next.
  • PPSSPP 1.20 (standalone): for PSP. It’s sharper and more configurable than the RetroArch core.
  • GameNative (GPL-3.0): Steam, Epic and GOG PC games through Wine and Box64. I chose it over GameHub because it’s open source.
  • Cloud: Better xCloud (Xbox Cloud Gaming), GeForce NOW and PS Remote Play.

Step 1: Take inventory first (read-only)

# Installed emulators and their versions
adb shell pm list packages --user 0 | grep -iE "retroarch|ppsspp|es_de|dolphin|aethersx2|gamenative|egggame|lemuroid"
adb shell dumpsys package <package> | grep -E "versionName|installerPackageName"
# Do they have "All files" access?
adb shell cmd appops get <package> MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE
# Where are the ROMs and BIOS files? (search by extension)
adb shell 'find /sdcard -type f \( -iname "*.iso" -o -iname "*.cso" -o -iname "*.chd" -o -iname "*.pbp" -o -iname "*.cue" -o -iname "*.zip" -o -iname "*.7z" \) 2>/dev/null'

Then check each app’s latest release. Most publish on GitHub (gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/releases), and ES-DE lists its latest version on its own site.

What the inventory turned up:

  • ES-DE was configured but had zero games. It also turned out to keep its settings in /sdcard/ROMs/settings, not /sdcard/ES-DE.
  • My game backups were still compressed, in a folder no emulator would look in.
  • ES-DE’s default PSP emulator wasn’t installed.
  • ES-DE and GameNative were both out of date.

Step 2: Update safely

Before installing any APK from outside the Play Store:

  1. Get it from the official source: GitHub releases, the project’s website or your Patreon download link. Never grab a paid APK from a random mirror. These apps have “All files” access, and a tampered build would inherit it.
  2. Check the signing certificate matches your installed copy. Run apksigner verify --print-certs new.apk, then adb shell pm path <package>, pull the installed APK and compare. If the certificate’s SHA-256 matches, it’s the same developer. Android refuses mismatched updates anyway.
  3. Compare the file’s SHA-256 with the hash GitHub shows for the release asset.
  4. Scan it, for example with Windows Defender: MpCmdRun.exe -Scan -ScanType 3 -File <apk>.
  5. Install for your main profile only with adb install --user 0 -r app.apk.

A heads-up on step 4: apps that bundle Wine, like GameNative, ship Windows test programs, and Defender may flag one with a heuristic ...!ml detection. In my case the already-installed version had the identical flag, the signature matched and the source is public, so I judged it a false positive.

And on step 5: a plain adb install also installs the app into the work profile, Dual Messenger and Secure Folder. I learned that one the hard way.

Step 3: Put ROMs where ES-DE expects them

ES-DE reads /sdcard/ROMs/<system>/, and each folder name has to match ES-DE’s system name:

nes  famicom  fds  snes  sfc  gb  gbc  gba  n64  virtualboy
genesis  mastersystem  gamegear  sega32x
pcengine  tg16  supergrafx  atari7800  psx  psp

Cartridge games: zipped single-ROM files are fine, since RetroArch loads them directly. Put ROM hacks in a subfolder like nes/hacks/, and ES-DE will show it as a folder in the game list.

PSP: if your dumps are compressed, unpack them on a PC first, then confirm each one is a real PSP disc by reading its game ID:

7z e -so "Game.iso" UMD_DATA.BIN | head -c 10      # prints the disc ID, e.g. ULUS-xxxxx

PS1 games split into .bin + .cue: use ES-DE’s “directories interpreted as files” feature so each game shows up as a single entry:

/sdcard/ROMs/psx/Game Name.cue/Game Name.cue
/sdcard/ROMs/psx/Game Name.cue/Game Name.bin

The folder name has to match the .cue file inside it exactly. For multi-disc games, use a Game.m3u/ folder holding the per-disc files plus a Game.m3u that lists them. Single-file .pbp games go straight into psx/.

Bonus: pulling games out of an old RetroPie SD-card image without mounting it

Coming from a Raspberry Pi? My old RetroPie setup lived on an SD-card image on my PC, and I didn’t need to flash or mount it to move my backups over. The agent read the image’s Linux (ext4) partition directly with debugfs in WSL. No mounting, no sudo, no extracting the whole image:

# Partition offset in bytes, from 7-Zip
7z l -slt image.img        # look at the "Offset" of the Linux partition
# List and copy straight out of the image (-c = read-only catalog mode)
debugfs -c -R "ls -l /home/pi/RetroPie/roms" "/mnt/d/image.img?offset=276824064"
debugfs -c -R "rdump /home/pi/RetroPie/roms/n64 /mnt/c/staging" "/mnt/d/image.img?offset=276824064"

Most RetroPie folder names already match ES-DE’s. The one I had to rename was megadrive → genesis.

Step 4: Make ES-DE launch the right emulator

Every system in ES-DE has a default emulator plus alternatives. On Android the defaults were RetroArch cores for nearly everything. I changed two:

  • PSP: the default is RetroArch’s PPSSPP core. I switched to “PPSSPP (Standalone)”.
  • PS1: the default is Beetle PSX, which requires a BIOS. I switched to “PCSX ReARMed”, which has a built-in BIOS fallback and uses a real BIOS when one is present.

You can change these in ES-DE’s menus, or write them straight into the system’s game list while ES-DE is closed:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<alternativeEmulator>
    <label>PPSSPP (Standalone)</label>
</alternativeEmulator>
<gameList>
</gameList>

Save that as /sdcard/ROMs/gamelists/psp/gamelist.xml. The label has to match the option name in ES-DE exactly.

After adding new system folders, run Main menu → Utilities → Rescan ROM directory. Until I did, ES-DE only showed 4 of my 20 systems.

Step 5: Storage permissions (where most launches fail)

ES-DE needs All files access.

RetroArch from retroarch.com targets an older Android version (SDK 28), so it uses the classic storage permission. ES-DE passes it a file path, and that works once the permission is granted.

Standalone PPSSPP is where launches break. ES-DE hands it the game through Android’s file-picker system, as a content:// link, and PPSSPP can only open it if it’s been given access to that folder. Without it, you get this:

Could not load game. IdentifyFile: File doesn't exist: content://com.android.externalstorage.documents/tree/...

The fix, straight from ES-DE’s docs: open PPSSPP → Browse… → go to ROMs → psp → Use this folder → Allow. It has to be PPSSPP’s own Browse button, and you should grant the system folder itself, not the whole ROMs folder.

Step 6: Tune RetroArch for the best quality per watt

Install the cores: Main Menu → Online Updater → Core Downloader. While you’re there, run Update Core Info Files, Update Assets and Update Slang Shaders.

Global settings: edit retroarch.cfg with RetroArch closed, and back it up first. On Android it’s in /sdcard/Android/data/com.retroarch/files/.

video_driver = "vulkan"
fps_show = "true"
sustained_performance_mode = "true"   # steady clocks instead of bursts → less throttling

2D systems: give each core a crisp pixel-art shader. Load shaders_slang/pixel-art-scaling/sharp-bilinear-simple.slangp, then Quick Menu → Shaders → Save Core Preset. That writes /sdcard/RetroArch/config/<Core>/<Core>.slangp, and once one preset exists, an agent can copy it into the other cores’ folders. Scaled-up pixels stay sharp and it costs nothing in performance.

Game Boy: in Gambatte’s options (config/Gambatte/Gambatte.opt), set gambatte_gb_colorization = "auto". Original Game Boy games then get Super Game Boy-style colour.

PS1 (PCSX ReARMed): put a BIOS dumped from your own PlayStation (for example scph5501.bin) in RetroArch’s system/ folder. The log line Loaded BIOS scph5501.bin confirms it’s being used. Then in Core Options, turn on Enhanced Resolution and Enhanced Resolution Speed Hack. That doubles the internal resolution and still holds 60 FPS.

Other BIOS files that helped (again, dumped from your own hardware):

  • disksys.rom: required for Famicom Disk System
  • gba_bios.bin: optional for GBA
  • 7800 BIOS (U).rom: optional for Atari 7800

N64 is the exception. On Snapdragon 8 Elite-class GPUs (Adreno 830/840), Mupen64Plus-Next’s hardware renderers, GLideN64 and ParaLLEl-RDP, gave a black screen while the audio kept playing. It’s a known issue. The workaround is to set the core option mupen64plus-rdp-plugin = "angrylion" (the accurate software renderer) and save a core override with video_driver = "gl" in config/Mupen64Plus-Next/Mupen64Plus-Next.cfg.

That runs at 60 FPS at native resolution. For HD N64, try RetroArch’s nightly builds, where fixes are reportedly landing, or a standalone N64 emulator.

Angrylion to the rescue.

Step 7: PPSSPP settings for a flagship Snapdragon

PPSSPP keeps its settings in private app storage, so you can’t edit them over ADB. Set them in the app under Settings → Graphics:

  • Backend: Vulkan
  • Rendering resolution: 4x PSP (about 1080p). The Adreno 840 handles it easily and it looks sharp on a big screen. Drop to 3x if you want the phone cooler on long sessions.
  • Anisotropic filtering: 16x
  • Texture filtering: Auto Max Quality
  • Texture upscaling: off. It’s redundant at 4x and causes stutter.
  • Post-processing shader: none
  • Frame skipping: off
  • Show FPS counter: on

Always leave PPSSPP through its own Exit menu. Force-stopping it throws away any settings you just changed. That bit me once.

Step 8: Box art and game info

Theme: ES-DE → UI settings → Theme downloader → Art Book Next, with the “List: Metadata & Boxart” variant. You get box art, screenshots, ratings and descriptions laid out like a coffee-table book.

Scraping: ES-DE → Scraper → ScreenScraper.

  • Make a free account. Without one you’re heavily rate-limited.
  • Watch the quota. The free tier allows about 20,000 requests a day, and every image file counts as a request. Scraping a few hundred games with every image type (cover, back cover, 3D box, disc, screenshot, title screen, logo, fan art) used up a whole day’s allowance.
  • For big libraries, scrape lean: box art, screenshots and logos only, with videos and manuals off. Spread it over a few days.

Learn from my mistakes. Scrape lean.

Shortcut: reuse your old metadata. RetroPie and Skraper keep scraped info in a gamelist.xml per system, using the same tags ES-DE reads: name, desc, rating, releasedate, developer, publisher, genre and players. The agent wrote a small script that:

  1. Pulls each system’s old gamelist.xml out of the image.
  2. Lists the actual files on the phone and keeps only entries whose file exists, mapping old .bin paths to the new Game.cue/ folders.
  3. Strips the old image paths, since ES-DE stores media differently.
  4. Writes /sdcard/ROMs/gamelists/<system>/gamelist.xml, keeping any <alternativeEmulator> block already there.

Most games got full descriptions instantly, and nearly every old entry matched a file on the phone. Old Skraper images are usually “mix” images, with the box, a screenshot and the logo merged into one picture. Modern themes look better with separate images, so I’d still scrape those fresh.

Step 9: The test matrix

The agent launched one game per system from ES-DE and checked the FPS counter:

  • NES / Famicom / FDS (Mesen): 60 FPS. FDS works with disksys.rom.
  • SNES / Super Famicom (Snes9x): 60 FPS, sharp-bilinear shader.
  • Game Boy / GBC (Gambatte): 60 FPS, automatic colorization.
  • GBA (mGBA): 60 FPS, real BIOS detected.
  • Genesis / Master System / Game Gear (Genesis Plus GX): 60 FPS.
  • 32X (PicoDrive): 60 FPS.
  • PC Engine / TG-16 (Beetle PCE), SuperGrafx (Beetle SuperGrafx): 60 FPS.
  • Atari 7800 (ProSystem): 60 FPS.
  • Virtual Boy (Beetle VB): 50 FPS, its native rate. RetroArch hung once on quit, and “Close app” recovers it.
  • N64 (Mupen64Plus-Next): 60 FPS, Angrylion only (see Step 6).
  • PS1 (PCSX ReARMed): 60 FPS with the BIOS loaded and enhanced resolution on.
  • PSP (PPSSPP): 60 FPS at 4x.

Step 10: The performance overlay that didn’t work

I wanted a small FPS/CPU/GPU overlay. Samsung’s Game Booster has a “System Monitor”, but its panel never showed up for emulators, because Samsung’s game manager classifies PPSSPP as non-game, even after I added it to Gaming Hub. I settled for the built-in FPS counters in PPSSPP and RetroArch. On an unrooted phone, most third-party overlays can’t read GPU utilization anyway.

Step 11: Clean up

  • Remove duplicate frontends like Lemuroid once RetroArch covers everything. Back up their saves first. Mine had PSP saves and save states, which I copied to Documents/ before uninstalling.
  • Pick one PC-game layer: GameNative (open source) or GameHub (closed source). Don’t keep both.
  • Delete ES-DE’s empty placeholder folders, the 165 or so systems you’ll never use. ES-DE won’t recreate them if CreatePlaceholderSystemDirectories is off.
  • Delete the compressed copies you moved over and the installer APKs once everything’s verified.

Notes for AI agents automating this

  • Emulators draw their own interface, so uiautomator dump sees nothing in PPSSPP, RetroArch or ES-DE. Use screenshots (screencap -p -d <display-id> on foldables) and D-pad key events (KEYCODE_DPAD_*, KEYCODE_ENTER, KEYCODE_BACK).
  • In ES-DE, Android’s Back key can quit the whole app. Use ES-DE’s on-screen B button to go back inside its menus.
  • Never force-stop an emulator mid-configuration. Quit through its own menus so it saves. RetroArch writes retroarch.cfg on quit when config_save_on_exit is true.
  • Only edit gamelist.xml while ES-DE is closed, or for systems it hasn’t loaded yet. It rewrites game lists on exit.
  • Simulated key presses (input keyevent --longpress ...) are fine for smoke-testing button shortcuts, but have the human confirm with the real buttons.
  • Run large copies as a background job, one system at a time, deleting each staging folder afterwards, so you don’t fill up the PC or the phone.
  • Check free space before each big copy. The agent stopped one plan that would have left the phone with less than about 8 GB free.

Final thoughts

The emulation itself was the easy part. A flagship Snapdragon runs everything up to PSP at 1080p at full speed. The hard parts were all plumbing: Android’s storage permissions, every app keeping its settings somewhere different, one GPU bug and scraper quotas.

Having an agent that reads logs, looks up known issues and tests each system one at a time turned what would have been a weekend of fiddling into an afternoon.

Happy retro gaming. And when your favourite classics get official re-releases, buy them.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: I debloated my TCL Google TV over ADB, found Samba TV’s ACR inside a system service, and replaced the home screen with a 33 KB launcher
item.description: Debloating a TCL Google TV over ADB without root: auditing packages, finding Samba TV ACR in a system service, and building a lightweight custom launcher.
item.content:encoded:
Disable, never uninstall. Every number below came from dumpsys on the actual TV.

In October 2026, posts about debloating smart TVs went around X: cleanyourtv, dumbtv, chill-tv-launcher, tv-makeover. I tried the approach on my own TV. I used no root and installed nothing from theinternet, and every change can be reversed with one script. This post covers the whole process: the audit, what the TV was sending home, the parts that didn’t work, and a GPU problem on the MediaTek chip that took a while to track down. It’s the same ADB-first approach I used to fix my phone’s battery.

“Apps only” mode, sponsored banner included.

Quick summary

Before                                           After
-------------------------------------------  -----------------------------------------------  ----------------------------------
Home screen memory (PSS)                     148 MB (launcherx 106 MB + :coreservices 42 MB)  39 MB (custom launcher, 33 KB APK)
Used RAM, whole TV                           2,017 MB                                         1,621 MB
Packages disabled                            0                                                30 (+1 by hand)
Apps uninstalled                             0                                                7
Sponsored hero banner, TCL tv+, promo tiles  yes                                              gone
Launcher median frame time                   n/a                                              12 ms (1% janky)
Root required                                -                                                no
Reversible                                   -                                                restore.ps1, one command

I already had Google TV’s “Apps only” mode switched on before I started, so my “before” screenshot is tamer than the stock experience. Even so, the sponsored hero banner was still there.

The hardware

ro.product.model         = Smart TV Pro
ro.product.device        = G08            (product G08_4K_US)
ro.build.version.release = 14  (SDK 34)
ro.build.fingerprint     = TCL/G08_4K_US/G08:14/UTT2.250416.001/AU14:user/release-keys
ro.hardware              = mt5896
ro.board.platform        = merak
ro.soc.manufacturer      = Mediatek    ro.soc.model = t50
MemTotal                 = 2,451,280 kB
Display                  = 3840x2160 panel, UI rendered at 1920x1080 (wm size override), 60 Hz

175 packages: 155 system, 20 user-installed, 0 disabled.

The SoC matters. On MediaTek TVs, disabling the partner customizer is known to send a system service into a crash loop, so com.tcl.partnercustomizer stayed on the do-not-touch list.

Rules I set before touching anything

  1. pm disable-user --user 0, never pm uninstall. A disabled package comes back with pm enable.
  2. Back up the full package list first (pm list packages -f -U, -d, -e, -s, -3).
  3. Write the restore script and test it before the first change.
  4. Small batches (1 to 7 packages), with a health check after each.
  5. Ask before touching anything I might actually use.

Step 1: Connecting

Developer options → Network debugging, then:

adb connect 192.168.1.71:5555
# accept "Allow USB debugging?" on the TV, tick "Always allow"

Two gotchas came up right away:

  • A phone was also connected over USB, so every command uses adb -s 192.168.1.71:5555.
  • The TV’s 10-minute idle timeout put it into standby halfway through an adb install. Network ADB died (“device offline”), then refused connections until I toggled Network debugging off and on. Fix (and set it back when you’re done, see Step 9):
adb shell settings put system screen_off_timeout 2147483647   # was 600000
adb shell settings put secure sleep_timeout -1                 # was 3539000

Step 2: Audit

adb shell pm list packages -f -U                 # path + uid tells you a lot
adb shell dumpsys package <pkg>                  # services, receivers, permissions
adb shell dumpsys meminfo                         # "Total PSS by process"
adb shell dumpsys activity services <pkg>        # what's actually running

The UID column turned out to matter most. Several TCL packages run as uid 1000 (system): com.tcl.ttvs, com.tcl.interactive, com.tcl.messagebox, com.tcl.esticker and com.tcl.providers.config. They share every system permission, including ACCESS_SURFACE_FLINGER, READ_LOGS, DUMP, PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS, RECORD_AUDIO and location. So a grep for “dangerous” permissions reports the same set for all of them, and it tells you nothing about any one package.

Top memory users at audit time (PSS):

162,450K  system
105,864K  com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx (activities)
 72,697K  com.google.android.gms
 47,184K  com.tcl.ttvs
 44,372K  com.google.android.katniss:interactor
 41,897K  com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx:coreservices
 36,199K  com.google.android.apps.tv.dreamx:smarthome
 26,803K  com.google.android.syncadapters.calendar      <- calendar sync. On a TV.
 23,079K  com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith
 17,403K  com.tcl.usercenter
  9,553K  com.tcl.providers.config:cloud_service

Step 3: What the TV was sending home

No tv.anoki.acr.controller on this TV, but ACR is still there

The well-known TCL ACR package is not installed on this firmware. The ACR lives inside TCL’s core service instead:

$ adb shell dumpsys package com.tcl.ttvs | grep Samba
  com.tcl.ttvs/.ssm.frameserver.SambaVideoService  permission tcl.permission.SambaVideoService

SambaVideoService is a frame server for Samba TV, the automated content recognition (ACR) service that fingerprints what’s on screen. com.tcl.ttvs (“TCSCore”, version 10.56.38_165fdfc_251120_overseaTV, 47 MB resident) also runs these services:

com.tcl.trackdata.service.TrackDataService             event tracking
.oversea.usagest.core.service.UsagestService            app/input usage stats
.bi.core.BIService                                      "business intelligence"
.identifier.core.service.IdentifierService              device identifier
com.tcl.guard.onlinesupport.service.OnlineSupportService (com.tcl.guard, merged in)
com.tcl.messagebox_core.service.MessageService           pushed promos

The same process also runs casting (T-Cast/AllCast), the Alexa bridge, the remote’s soft keyboard, and the TV’s picture/sound menu service. So you can’t disable the whole package without breaking the TV menu.

Disabling only the tracking components fails without root

$ adb shell pm disable --user 0 com.tcl.ttvs/.ssm.frameserver.SambaVideoService
java.lang.SecurityException: Shell cannot change component state for
ComponentInfo{com.tcl.ttvs/com.tcl.ttvs.ssm.frameserver.SambaVideoService} to 2

The shell user can’t change component state for packages it doesn’t own. So the realistic options are:

  1. Turn off the Samba TV / “Viewing Information Services” opt-in in the TV’s privacy settings.
  2. Block it at DNS.
  3. appops, as a gesture: cmd appops set com.tcl.ttvs RUN_ANY_IN_BACKGROUND ignore. It’s accepted, but am get-standby-bucket stays at 5 (exempted) because it’s a system process. Expect little effect.

Telemetry flags in settings global

tcl_diagnostic_status = 1   -> 0
upload_apk_enable     = 1   -> 0     # uploads your installed-app list

Where it connects

dumpsys netstats per-UID detail is empty on this build, but /proc/net/tcp{,6} is readable from the shell and includes the owning UID:

adb shell 'cat /proc/net/tcp6 /proc/net/tcp | awk "NR>1 && \$4==\"01\"{print \$3, \$8}"' | sort | uniq -c

IPv4 addresses appear in little-endian hex: D842A814 decodes to 20.168.66.216. Before the debloat, uid 1000 held a connection to 20.168.66.216:6177. After the debloat, it still held 20.171.160.197:443 and 4.249.25.67:443, all Microsoft Azure ranges. That’s TTVS, and only DNS blocking will stop it.

Step 4: Disabling in verified batches

Every batch ran through the same script. The script clears logcat, disables the batch, waits 20 s for crash loops, then checks:

  • that core TCL/Android services kept the same PIDs (no restarts),)
  • which activity holds the Home intent,
  • the crash buffer,
  • the count of has died / ANR lines.

It then presses Home and takes a screenshot.

for p in "$@"; do adb -s $S shell pm disable-user --user 0 "$p"; done
sleep 20
for p in com.android.systemui com.tcl.tv com.tcl.ttvs com.tcl.systemserver com.tcl.tvinput com.android.tv.settings; do
  printf '%-28s %s\n' $p "$(adb -s $S shell pidof $p)"
done
adb -s $S shell cmd package resolve-activity --brief -a android.intent.action.MAIN -c android.intent.category.HOME
adb -s $S logcat -d -b crash | grep -E "FATAL EXCEPTION|Process: "
Batch        Packages                                                                                                                                                                What they did
-----------  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1 Ads        com.tcl.tv.plus, com.tcl.channelplus, com.tcl.dashboard, com.tcl.exhibit, com.tcl.ocean.instructions                                                                    TCL tv+ (internally com.tcl.waterfall.overseas), ad-supported channels registered as a TV input, promo dashboard, store-demo portal, e-manual tile
2 Telemetry  com.tcl.usercenter, com.tcl.logkit, com.tcl.smartlink.core, com.tcl.messagebox, com.tcl.esticker, com.tcl.tv.tclhome_passive, com.google.android.feedback               TCL account, log uploader, CustomInstallService (silent push-installs), promo inbox, in-store show mode, IoT companion, Google feedback
3 Google     com.google.android.syncadapters.calendar, android.autoinstalls.config.google.gtvpai, YouTube, YouTube Music, com.tcl.smartalexa                                         Calendar sync, Play Auto Install (re-pushes partner apps), apps I don't use
4 Home       com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith, com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx                                                                                           Only after the replacement launcher was working (see below)
5 Ad stack   com.android.adservices.api, com.android.ondevicepersonalization.services, com.android.federatedcompute.services                                                         Android 14 Privacy Sandbox. Disabled one at a time.
6 Extras     com.android.tv.feedbackconsent, com.google.android.partnersetup, com.android.printspooler, com.android.healthconnect.controller, com.google.android.onetimeinitializer  Feedback consent, partner attribution, unused services

No batch produced a single crash. The one process death, after batch 6, was com.tcl.gamebar at oom-importance 905: a cached app reclaimed for memory, unrelated to the change. A reboot after batches 3, 4 and 6 confirmed that state persisted and nothing crash-looped at boot.

Left alone on purpose: com.tcl.partnercustomizer, com.tcl.ttvs, com.tcl.tv, com.tcl.tvinput, com.tcl.systemserver, com.tcl.suspension (Quick panel), com.tcl.autopair (remote pairing), all com.mediatek.*, Dolby, Assistant/katniss (the mic button), AirPlay, Ambient Mode.

Step 5: The Home button

Google TV doesn’t give up the Home button easily. After installing my launcher:

$ adb shell cmd package set-home-activity --user 0 tv.dock.launcher/.HomeActivity
Success
$ adb shell cmd package resolve-activity --brief -a android.intent.action.MAIN -c android.intent.category.HOME
com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx/.home.HomeActivity      <- "Success" changed nothing

Disabling setupwraith alone didn’t change it either. Only disabling launcherx made Home go to my launcher. Check with the role manager, not the Success string:

$ adb shell cmd role get-role-holders android.app.role.HOME
tv.dock.launcher

Then I tested the Home button from inside SmartTube, Plex, the HDMI input app and Settings, not just from the home screen. All four returned to the new launcher.

Order matters: install and verify the new launcher, then disable setupwraith, then launcherx. One reference repo reports a crash loop from the reverse order. They also warn that disabling setupwraith can wipe Wi-Fi networks saved during setup (all 10 of mine survived) and may break Google Cast. I haven’t tested Cast yet.

“Success” is a state of mind.

Step 6: A 33 KB launcher, no Gradle

With an agent doing the typing, writing my own home screen became a small side project, which is the shift I wrote about in The Age of Infinite Software Supply. Plain Java with no AndroidX, built straight from the SDK tools:

aapt2 compile --dir res -o build/res.zip
aapt2 link -o build/unsigned.apk -I android.jar --manifest AndroidManifest.xml \
  --min-sdk-version 28 --target-sdk-version 34 --java build/gen build/res.zip
javac -encoding UTF-8 -source 8 -target 8 -bootclasspath android.jar \
  -classpath build-tools/34.0.0/core-lambda-stubs.jar -d build/classes $(find src build/gen -name '*.java')
d8 --release --min-api 28 --lib android.jar --output build/dex build/classes/**/*.class
(cd build/dex && aapt add ../unsigned.apk classes.dex)
zipalign -f 4 build/unsigned.apk build/aligned.apk
apksigner sign --ks dock.keystore --out dock-launcher.apk build/aligned.apk

Two build errors worth knowing about:

  • cannot find symbol: method metafactory means android.jar has no LambdaMetafactory. Add core-lambda-stubs.jar from build-tools to the classpath, and d8 desugars the lambdas.
  • unmappable character (0x8F) for encoding windows-1252 comes from emoji in source on Windows. Add -encoding UTF-8.

Features:

  • Manifest: HOME + DEFAULT + LEANBACK_LAUNCHER, launchMode="singleTask", <queries> for package visibility rather than QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES.
  • Dock: 8 favourites. Hold OK on any app to move, add or remove it, saved to SharedPreferences.
  • HDMI inputs named by CEC: TvInputManager.getTvInputList(), with CEC child inputs (getParentId() != null) mapped onto their HDMI port. My PS5 shows up as “PlayStation 5 · HDMI 1”. Selecting it fires ACTION_VIEW on TvContract.buildChannelUriForPassthroughInput(id), which the TCL TV app handles directly.
  • Weather from Open-Meteo (no key, no account), geocoded once and cached. The city is set on the TV or over ADB: am start -n tv.dock.launcher/.HomeActivity --es city "Mountain View, California".
  • Status strip: a Wi-Fi/Ethernet icon from NetworkCapabilities transports, the VPN app’s own icon when TRANSPORT_VPN is up (Surfshark here), and free storage from StatFs.
  • Top bar: pills, as on tvOS. The time and date, then the weather, sit on the left. A notifications bell and the status pill sit on the right, and OK on the status pill opens a small controls panel. The status pill now also shows memory and storage as rings. The per-app colour glow is gone: the focus ring on the tile is enough to show what’s selected.
  • Ambient home (Plex): with nothing selected, the backdrop shows the last five Continue Watching titles from my own Plex server at 1080p. Each page follows the tvOS layout in the lower third, just above the dock: a small “Continue watching” or “Up next” label, the show’s logo, the episode or year, rating and genre, a thin progress bar with the time left, and a two-line summary. Page dots are centred above the dock. It moves on every 10 seconds, Left and Right step through it, OK opens Plex, and the list refreshes every time I come back to the home screen.

Inputs at the end of the app grid: HDMI-CEC names (my PS5), with unused ports folded away

Step 7: The GPU problem

The first redesign had a full-screen blurred backdrop (RenderEffect.createBlurEffect) and felt sluggish. dumpsys gfxinfo agreed:

Total frames rendered: 142
Janky frames: 35 (24.65%)
50th percentile: 48ms     <- 60 Hz budget is 16.7 ms
Number Slow issue draw commands: 12

For comparison, the TV’s own Settings app under the same D-pad input script:

Janky frames: 0 (0.00%)   50th percentile: 7ms

So I removed things one at a time, driving the same 12-keypress D-pad sequence each time with input keyevent and resetting gfxinfo between runs:

Variant                                                                  p50    p90    Janky
-----------------------------------------------------------------------  -----  -----  -----
RenderEffect blur backdrop ×2 + gradient scrim + ScrollView fading edge  48 ms  65 ms  24.7%
Blur replaced by a 32×18 bitmap stretched with bilinear filtering        46 ms  61 ms  18.6%
- ScrollView fading edge (it's a saveLayer per frame)                    31 ms  31 ms  2.3%
- translationZ shadow on the focused tile                                31 ms  31 ms  1.2%
- backdrop ImageViews                                                    23 ms  25 ms  1.3%
- rounded clipToOutline on ~30 tiles                                     22 ms  24 ms  1.3%
- root black background and gradient scrim                               6 ms   8 ms   0%
black background only, put back                                          18 ms  18 ms  2.6%
black as window background instead of view background                    18 ms  18 ms  1.3%

On this MediaTek T50 GPU, a single opaque full-screen fill costs about 12 ms a frame, whether it’s a view background or a window background. Shadows and rounded clipping turned out to cost almost nothing. A blurred backdrop plus a dark scrim plus a background is three full-screen fills, which is the whole frame budget gone before any tile is drawn.

Shadows were innocent. The black background was not.

The fix: take the backdrop out of the UI layer

The backdrop moved to a SurfaceView behind the window, with a fixed buffer size of 480×270. The display hardware scales it to full screen, which costs the GPU nothing, and the upscale produces the blur on its own. Cross-fades are drawn with a software Canvas on a HandlerThread, and the scrim gradient is baked in:

view = new SurfaceView(context);
view.getHolder().setFixedSize(480, 270);   // HW scaler upsizes; free blur
private void draw() {                      // runs on the "backdrop" HandlerThread
    Canvas c = holder.lockCanvas();
    float t = step / (float) FADE_STEPS;
    c.drawColor(Color.BLACK);
    if (from != null && t < 1f) { art.setAlpha(Math.round(220 * (1f - t))); c.drawBitmap(from, null, dst, art); }
    if (to != null)             { art.setAlpha(Math.round(220 * t));        c.drawBitmap(to,   null, dst, art); }
    c.drawRect(dst, scrim);                // LinearGradient baked into the same small buffer
    holder.unlockCanvasAndPost(c);
}

The root view has no background at all. The UI layer only draws tiles and text, which measured at 6 ms. Final numbers, with shadows and rounded corners back on:

Total frames rendered: 86
Janky frames: 1 (1.16%)
50th percentile: 12ms
90th percentile: 15ms
TOTAL PSS: ~38-39 MB at rest (24 MB of it decoded app banners)

Final launcher: time, weather, notifications and a status pill (Wi-Fi, VPN, memory, storage, controls) over a Plex “Up next” carousel and the dock

Then the Plex redesign undid some of that. Moving the artwork up to 1080p and drawing each app’s colour glow live pushed median frames from 10 ms to 28 ms. The fix was the same lesson as before: keep full-screen work out of the UI layer. Every backdrop is now a pre-rendered bitmap, so a cross-fade is just two bitmap draws, and the glow went in favour of the focus ring. Frames are back to 11 ms while moving around, and the carousel’s fades take about 5 ms.

Step 8: Making it survive updates

TCL and Google updates re-enable packages and reset the Home app. So there are two scripts:

  • restore.ps1 re-enables every package from the audit-time backup, restores the settings to their recorded values, resets the TTVS appops and sets the stock launcher as Home.
  • reapply.ps1 is idempotent: it fixes only what has drifted, then verifies with cmd role get-role-holders android.app.role.HOME. It disables setupwraith before launcherx, one pm call per package, and waits about 15 s before any reboot so the package state is written to disk.

Step 9: Updates, cleanup, codecs, and why not root

Is anything out of date?

Channel                    Result
-------------------------  ---------------------------------------------------------------
TCL firmware               V8-0012T02-LF1V321.001899 (AU14). TCL server: CHECK_RESULT_NONE
Android security patch     2025-12-05. Only TCL firmware can move it.
Google system update       "Your system is up to date"
Google Play system update  2024-09-01. Nothing newer offered for TV.
Play Store apps            Surfshark 3.36.0 -> 3.37.0, BrowseHere 8.20.060 -> 8.20.066

TCL’s updater lives inside com.tcl.ttvs, which is one more reason not to disable that package. It can’t be started from ADB:

Permission Denial: starting Intent { act=com.tcl.versionUpdateApp.action.updateEntrance ... }
from null (pid=5136, uid=2000) requires com.tcl.permission.START_CHECK_SYSTEMUPDATE

The check has to be run by hand (Settings → System → About → System update → Network Update). Its log shows one more piece of telemetry: every update check uploads the TV’s full list of system modules and their versions to TCL.

versionUpdate: [CommonUtils]getLocalApexList get ApexBean{packageName='com.tcl.tcore', versionCode=653321001}
versionUpdate: [CommonUtils]getLocalApexList get ApexBean{packageName='com.tcl.hera', versionCode=653321001}
...
versionUpdate: [ComponentStateController]current state is CHECK_RESULT_NONE

Two side effects of my own changes turned up here:

  • The Play updates had been pending for five days, even with “Auto-update apps at any time” switched on. Android runs automatic app updates and app optimisation only while the device is idle (dumpsys deviceidle showed mState=ACTIVE). A TV that never sleeps never goes idle. So the never-sleep setting from Step 1 is for ADB sessions only. I set it back to 10 min / 59 min afterwards.
  • Updating Surfshark dropped the VPN silently. The network went from Transports: WIFI|VPN to plain WIFI. Opening the app reconnected it.

Cleanup by usage data, not guesswork

dumpsys usagestats gives last-used time and total time for every app, and dumpsys diskstats gives sizes:

org.xbmc.kodi                  159 MB  never opened
com.hbo.hbonow                  78 MB  last 2026-03-17
com.peacocktv.peacockandroid    22 MB  last 2026-04-05
com.roku.web.trc                19 MB  last 2026-04-05
tv.pluto.android                58 MB  last 2026-05-02
com.sec.android.app.sbrowser   239 MB  last 2026-07-26  (sideloaded, v28.0.0.59 from May 2025)
cm.aptoidetv.pt                115 MB  last 2026-07-17  (sideloaded, v5.1.2 from Nov 2024)
com.netflix.ninja              122 MB  27 seconds of total use
  • Uninstalled (user-installed, so they can come back from Play): Kodi, Max, Pluto TV, Peacock, The Roku Channel.
  • Uninstalled because sideloaded apps never update: Samsung Internet (a browser 17 months out of date) and Aptoide TV (a third-party app store).
  • Disabled (preinstalled): Netflix, Prime Video, BrowseHere.

What the chip decodes

/vendor/etc/media_codecs-mt5896.xml lists hardware decoders for AV1, HEVC, VP9, H.264, MPEG-2, VC-1 and H.266/VVC. It also has every common Dolby Vision profile, including c2.mtk.dvhe.dtb.decoder, which is Profile 7 (UHD Blu-ray content with an enhancement layer). There are secure (DRM) variants of the main ones. You can’t add codecs to that list without root, and on this chip you don’t need to for video.

Audio is the gap. Dolby and DTS aren’t exposed as regular decoders, but the speaker output accepts them as bitstream:

profiles: ENCODING_AC3, ENCODING_E_AC3, ENCODING_E_AC3_JOC, ENCODING_DTS, ENCODING_DTS_HD
mIsDtsVirtualXSupported: true

So in Plex, set Passthrough to Auto even with no soundbar. The TV’s own audio processor decodes Atmos (E-AC3 JOC) and DTS. With Off, Plex converts everything to stereo PCM first. TrueHD isn’t supported at all, so the Plex server converts that track. For players that can’t handle TrueHD or PGS/ASS subtitles, use VLC as the external player.

Why not root (or a newer Android)?

ro.boot.vbmeta.device_state = locked
ro.boot.verifiedbootstate   = green
ro.boot.veritymode          = enforcing
ro.oem_unlock_supported     = (empty)
ro.build.type               = user

There’s no OEM-unlock path, and I know of no public bootrom exploit for this TV SoC. Even with one, unlocking drops Widevine from L1 to L3, so 4K/HDR streaming falls back to SD. There are no custom ROMs, because the panel, picture-processing, CEC and tuner drivers are closed TCL/MediaTek code. Root would mainly let you disable the Samba components inside com.tcl.ttvs. A DNS blocklist gets most of that benefit with no risk.

Step 10: Blocking the tracking at DNS

I haven’t deployed this part yet, but it’s the only way to stop what ADB can’t touch. TCL’s US backend is almost entirely *.api.leiniao.com (Leiniao is TCL’s smart-TV software company), hosted on Microsoft Azure. Every address the TV was seen talking to maps back to it:

Seen on the TV        Hostname                                    Role
20.168.66.216:6177    hwmsg-as1-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com       push channel, always on
20.168.49.140:6178    hwmsg-as6-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com       push channel, always on
20.171.160.197:443    hw-tdp-o / hwupgrade-o / hwlauncher-o ...   updates and launcher (shared IP)
4.249.25.67:443       hwtpc-o.api.leiniao.com                     unclear

The hwmsg-as1 to as6 hosts are one pool, which is why the push address changed between checks. I built the list below from the hostnames compiled into TCL’s own apps (pulled off the TV), the live connections above, Netify’s passive DNS for leiniao.com, and the Perflyst and hkamran80 smart-TV lists. Every hostname resolved on 25 October 2026. It works as a denylist in Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, NextDNS or any router with DNS blocking:

# Tier 1: push channel, log upload, device registration, Samba TV ACR
hwmsg-as1-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com
hwmsg-as2-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com
hwmsg-as3-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com
hwmsg-as4-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com
hwmsg-as5-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com
hwmsg-as6-azure-usa-o.api.leiniao.com
on-hweudc-o.api.leiniao.com
hweudc-o.api.leiniao.com
analysis.leiniao.com
na-newuser-tcl.cedock.com
na-neuser-tcl.cedock.com
api.cid.samba.tv
events.cid.samba.tv
platform.cid.samba.tv
preferences.cid.samba.tv
dpn.cid.samba.tv
fling.cid.samba.tv
alphonso.tv
# Tier 2: ads and TCL content (safe once TCL tv+ and Channel+ are disabled)
cmp-ads.api.leiniao.com
file-hw-ads-o.api.leiniao.com
hwads-o.api.leiniao.com
ffalconnow-us.api.leiniao.com
bmtchannel-o.api.leiniao.com
hwpreins-o.api.leiniao.com
hwapps-o.api.leiniao.com

Don’t block hw-tdp-o.api.leiniao.com or the IP 20.171.160.197: firmware update checks fail (HaGeZi dns-blocklists issue #4347). For the same reason, don’t block all of leiniao.com, and don’t block Azure IP ranges wholesale, because they’re shared with countless unrelated services.

The VPN catch. While a VPN is connected on the TV, its DNS lookups travel inside the tunnel, so a Pi-hole on your network never sees them. Either exclude TCL’s service from the VPN with split tunnelling, or use a filtering DNS the TV queries directly, such as NextDNS set as the TV’s Private DNS with these hostnames on its denylist.

To check it worked, look for system (uid 1000) connections to ports 6177 to 6179 (hex 1821 to 1823):

adb shell 'cat /proc/net/tcp /proc/net/tcp6' | awk 'NR>1 && $4=="01" && $8==1000 {print $3}'

Gotchas, all in one place

  • set-home-activity prints Success even when it changes nothing. Check cmd role get-role-holders android.app.role.HOME.
  • The shell can’t disable individual components (SecurityException), so pm disable on a component needs root.
  • dumpsys netstats per-UID data may be empty, but /proc/net/tcp{,6} carries UIDs and is readable from the shell.
  • uid-1000 TCL packages all share system permissions, so permission greps can’t tell them apart.
  • Network ADB dies in standby. Raise screen_off_timeout before long operations.
  • On weak TV GPUs, measure with dumpsys gfxinfo and compare against a first-party app on the same TV. Full-screen fills are expensive here, but shadows aren’t.
  • exec-out screencap returns an empty file while a live HDMI/TV input is on screen (secure layer). That’s expected, not an error.
  • Git Bash on Windows rewrites /sdcard/... paths passed to adb shell. Set MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1.
  • TCL’s input panel still shows tiles for disabled apps (Google TV Home, TCL tv+, User Guide). They just do nothing.
  • A TV that never sleeps never goes idle, so Play auto-updates and app optimisation stop. Restore the sleep timer after ADB work.
  • Updating a VPN app can drop the VPN without reconnecting. Check Transports: in dumpsys connectivity.

Still open

  • Google Cast with setupwraith disabled is untested. If it reports “Untrusted device”, re-enable setupwraith and keep the custom launcher as Home.
  • DNS blocking for TTVS: the list in Step 10 is built but not deployed yet, so I can’t say yet whether blocking it breaks anything.

Credits

The debloat lists and gotchas from these projects shaped the plan. I read them, but I didn’t run any of their code.

  • cleanyourtv, which has a G08 example config
  • dumbtv
  • chill-tv-launcher
  • tv-makeover
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: I Let an AI Agent Debug My Foldable’s Battery Over ADB. Here’s the Playbook It Followed.
item.description: 60 MB of diagnostics, six weeks of battery history, and a surprise: the “bloat” from restoring my old phone wasn’t the problem.
item.content:encoded:
60 MB of diagnostics, six weeks of battery history, and a surprise: the “bloat” from restoring my old phone wasn’t the problem.

I moved to a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and restored everything from my old S23 Ultra with Smart Switch. Battery life was worse than it should have been. I had a theory: I’d dragged over hundreds of apps I never use, and they were all quietly running in the background.

So I plugged the phone into my PC, turned on USB debugging, and asked an AI coding agent (Claude Code) to pull weeks of battery history over ADB, work out what was actually draining it, and fix it.

My theory was mostly wrong. The real culprits were more interesting. And nearly every fix turned out to be a setting, a permission or a small automation, all of it reversible.

The short version of this whole post.

What follows is the playbook. I wrote it so that you, or your own AI agent, can run it on any Android phone. I’ve marked the Samsung-only parts.

Quick summary

Baseline: about 103% of a full battery used per day. The screen-on drain was 12.9% an hour and the screen-off drain was 2.5% an hour. A healthy phone sitting idle uses somewhere around 0.5 to 1% an hour, so roughly a third of every charge was vanishing while the phone sat in my pocket.

The restored “bloat” was mostly harmless. 222 of my 315 apps hadn’t been opened in three weeks or more, but Android had already parked 202 of them in its “never” or “restricted” standby buckets. Uninstalling them frees storage. It doesn’t buy you battery.

What was actually draining it:

  • A car-key app’s Bluetooth service stuck in a loop, burning about 50 CPU-minutes a day
  • Samsung Health’s snore detection holding the microphone in the middle of the day
  • Five or more system services doing near-constant Bluetooth LE scans
  • A second SIM that was permanently roaming, plus 5G clinging to one bar of signal at home
  • Cloned app profiles (Dual Messenger, Secure Folder, the work profile), each running its own copy of Google Play services
  • About 10 GB of swap in use, courtesy of Samsung’s “RAM Plus”

The fixes: a handful of ADB settings changes, background restrictions, a few Samsung Routines and one Tasker profile.

Not to scale. Emotionally accurate.

Ground rules (for humans and agents)

  1. Read-only first. Collect, analyze, then propose. Nothing changes until the owner says yes.
  2. Snapshot before you touch anything. Write down every original value and keep an undo script.
  3. Ask before deleting anything, and before touching personal features like SIM cards, health tracking or accounts.
  4. Never handle passwords unless the owner explicitly hands them over. Never use shared or leaked credentials from the internet.
  5. Re-measure after two or three days of normal use. Without a re-measure, you’re going on vibes.

Step 1: Connect and collect everything

Turn on Developer options → USB debugging, then connect the phone:

adb devices -l
adb shell getprop ro.product.model
adb shell getprop ro.build.version.release

If more than one device shows up (a smart TV on your network, say), pin every command to the phone’s serial with adb -s <SERIAL>.

Now dump everything that matters for battery into local files. None of these change anything:

adb shell dumpsys batterystats            > batterystats.txt
adb shell dumpsys batterystats --checkin  > batterystats_checkin.txt
adb shell dumpsys usagestats              > usagestats.txt
adb shell dumpsys procstats --hours 72    > procstats.txt
adb shell dumpsys netstats --full --uid   > netstats.txt
adb shell dumpsys alarm                   > alarm.txt
adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler            > jobs.txt
adb shell dumpsys power                   > power.txt
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle              > deviceidle.txt
adb shell dumpsys appops                  > appops.txt
adb shell dumpsys bluetooth_manager       > bt.txt
adb shell dumpsys telephony.registry      > telephony.txt
adb shell dumpsys sdhms                   > sdhms.txt     # Samsung only
adb shell pm list packages -U             > packages.txt  # UID → package map

Tip for agents: run these in parallel and write them to files. Together they come to tens of megabytes, far too much to stream into an agent’s context. Parse them with small scripts instead.

Step 2: Build a baseline from history, not “since last charge”

dumpsys batterystats mostly covers the time since your last charge. If you charged this morning, that’s a few hours of data.

On Samsung, dumpsys sdhms is where the history lives. Its “Daily batterystats” and “Daily Summary” tables keep per-day totals going back weeks, even across OS updates: battery used, screen-on time, screen-off time, and how much drained with the screen on versus off.

From those, work out two rates for each day: screen-on % per hour and screen-off % per hour. My averages:

~103% used per day · 5.4 h screen-on @ 12.9%/h · 13 h screen-off @ 2.5%/h

One trap in batterystats’ “Discharge step durations”: a step with no screen-on or screen-off label means the screen state changed during that step. Don’t count those as screen-off.

Step 3: Find what’s actually draining

3.1 CPU time per day (catches runaway processes)

adb shell ps -A -o TIME,ETIME,USER,NAME

Divide each process’s CPU TIME by how long it’s been running (ETIME) to get CPU-minutes per day. The system server and display services always sit near the top. That’s normal. You’re looking for apps up there.

What I found: a car “phone as a key” app’s Bluetooth service was eating about 50 CPU-minutes a day, more than SystemUI. After a reboot it used under one CPU-minute in four and a half hours. It had been stuck in a loop.

Normalized CPU time finds runaway services fast. A reboot is a fine first fix, as long as you check again afterwards.

3.2 Who’s holding the microphone or wakelocks?

Two places to look. For wakelocks, check “All partial wake locks” in batterystats. A wakelock called AudioIn means something is recording. For recent mic use, adb shell cmd appops get <pkg> RECORD_AUDIO shows the last time an app used the mic and for how long.

To see which of an app’s services is running, use adb shell dumpsys activity services <pkg>.

What I found: Samsung Health’s SnoreService, a foreground service with the mic open, was recording during the day. My guess is that sleep detection misfired.

Samsung Health’s SnoreService, mid-afternoon.

3.3 Bluetooth LE scanning per app

adb shell dumpsys bluetooth_manager   # look for "LE Scanner Map"

This gives you total scan time per app since boot. Here’s what was scanning on my phone, as a share of the time since boot:

  • SmartThings: about 99%
  • Android’s own Bluetooth stack (LE Audio reconnect): about 99%
  • Google Play services: about 85%
  • Samsung’s “continuity” service: about 81%
  • Samsung’s multi-device service: about 59%

3.4 The cellular radio

dumpsys telephony.registry shows signal level per SIM, and dumpsys isub gives you the subscription IDs.

What I found: I was running two SIMs in dual standby. One was an international SIM that was always roaming. The other, my main SIM, was on 5G standalone with one bar at home. Between them, signal was poor or missing about 40% of the time.

Two radios hunting for a weak signal will drain a phone even while it sits idle.

3.5 Background data over 14 days

dumpsys netstats --full --uid keeps per-app history. Parse the UID stats section. set=DEFAULT is background traffic and set=FOREGROUND is foreground. The transports= field tells you the network: {0} is cellular and {1} is Wi-Fi.

What I found: the photo-backup app was re-uploading about 6 GB in the background, 160 MB of it over mobile data. A speed-test app was quietly running its own background tests, about 800 MB worth. And the social apps were each moving hundreds of megabytes while I wasn’t looking at them.

3.6 Alarms and jobs, per user profile

dumpsys alarm has an Alarm Stats section listing wakeups per package since boot. dumpsys jobscheduler lists how long background jobs ran.

Pay attention to the user prefixes. u0 is your main profile, u10 is usually the work profile, u95 is Samsung’s Dual Messenger and u150 is Secure Folder.

What I found: Dual Messenger was running a second full copy of Google Play services, with 3,281 wakeups in nine days. Its cloned WhatsApp ran about 41 minutes of background jobs a day. I’d used it for 31 minutes in two months.

3.7 Memory pressure

adb shell "grep -E 'MemTotal|MemAvailable|SwapTotal|SwapFree' /proc/meminfo"

What I found: 10.6 of 12.6 GB of swap in use, and kswapd burning about 15 CPU-minutes a day. Samsung’s RAM Plus (virtual RAM backed by storage) was set to 8 GB, and four user profiles were running at once.

3.8 Testing the “it’s the bloat” theory

To find unused apps, line up usage stats against standby buckets. dumpsys usagestats has a yearly in-memory section with lastTimeUsed and appLaunchCount for each app. adb shell am get-standby-bucket lists every app’s bucket: 10 is active, 20 working set, 30 frequent, 40 rare, 45 restricted and 50 never.

What I found: 222 of 315 apps were unused, but 202 of them were already in the never or restricted buckets. Android was keeping them asleep without my help.

Debloating frees storage and cuts down on update churn. It isn’t where your battery goes.

3.9 Don’t trust every alert

Samsung’s anomaly detector flagged “abnormal screen-off drain” three times. One of those lined up with an 80-minute drive on Android Auto, where the phone’s screen is off while it navigates and projects to the car. That drain was real, and it was fine.

Check alerts against what you were actually doing at the time.

Step 4: The fixes

Everything here can be undone. Record each original value before you change it.

4.1 Settings over ADB

# Screen timeout: 5 minutes → 1 minute
adb shell settings put system screen_off_timeout 60000
# Location "Bluetooth scanning" and "Wi-Fi scanning" off
adb shell settings put global ble_scan_always_enabled 0
adb shell settings put global wifi_scan_always_enabled 0
# Samsung: Nearby device scanning, and Continue apps on other devices
adb shell settings put system nearby_scanning_enabled 0
adb shell settings put system mcf_continuity 0

4.2 Take “Unrestricted” battery back from apps that don’t need it

adb shell cmd deviceidle whitelist             # list (look for "user," entries)
adb shell cmd deviceidle whitelist -<package>  # remove one

Leave the exemption on things that really need it: a smartwatch companion app, a VPN, or the car-key app if you depend on it.

4.3 Restrict background activity for apps you rarely use

adb shell cmd appops set <package> RUN_ANY_IN_BACKGROUND ignore
adb shell am set-standby-bucket <package> restricted

4.4 Block background mobile data for specific apps

You’ll need the app’s UID, which pm list packages -U gives you:

adb shell cmd netpolicy add restrict-background-blacklist <UID>

I did this for the photo-backup app, which now waits for Wi-Fi, and for the speed-test app.

4.5 Turn off RAM Plus (Samsung, UI only)

Settings → Device care → Memory → RAM Plus → Off. The phone will reboot. My swap went from 12.6 GB to 4 GB, which is just the compressed in-memory swap.

4.6 LTE at home, 5G when out (Samsung Routines)

On home Wi-Fi, your data goes over Wi-Fi and calls go over Wi-Fi calling, so a 5G radio straining at one bar is pure cost. In Modes and Routines, create a routine:

  • If: Wi-Fi network is your home network. Tick “Check network name only” if you have a mesh or several access points.
  • Then: Network mode → LTE.

When the routine ends, it puts the previous mode back on its own.

Two Samsung quirks to know about. First, the Network mode picker labelled every option “Automatic” on my phone. The order is 5G/LTE, LTE, 3G, so verify over ADB rather than trusting the labels. Second, this action only changes your main (default) SIM.

To check what actually got set:

adb shell cmd phone get-allowed-network-types-for-users -s <slot>

4.7 Second SIM: LTE only, permanently

My second SIM exists to receive OTP texts, so 5G does nothing for it. The set command takes a binary bitmask, where bit = 1 << (NETWORK_TYPE - 1), and NR (5G) is bit 19. Read the current mask, clear bit 19, and write it back:

adb shell cmd phone set-allowed-network-types-for-users -s 0 1001101001110000111

That leaves LTE, LTE-CA, HSPA and the 2G/3G types, with no NR. To undo it, write the original mask back. Here that’s the same string with bit 19 set: 11001101001110000111.

You can also switch a physical SIM off entirely from the shell with cmd phone disable-physical-subscription <subId>. Be careful with this one. Texts sent while the SIM is off only get retried until they expire, and bank OTPs often expire within minutes.

4.8 Battery-saving routines (Samsung)

  • Low battery saver: below 25% → Power saving, Standard.
  • Ultra battery saver: below 10% → Power saving, Maximum. This is the old “Ultra power saving” mode: a plain dark home screen with only the apps you pick.
  • Reading apps timeout: while Kindle or Chrome is open → 5-minute screen timeout, to offset the new 1-minute default.
  • Android Auto charge reminder: Android Auto connected, not charging and battery under 50% → a notification read aloud telling you to plug in.

4.9 Pause the work profile outside work hours (Tasker)

Neither Samsung Routines nor Digital Wellbeing could schedule the work profile on my phone. The agent checked both apps’ code for the feature, and it isn’t there. Tasker can do it after a one-time permission grant:

# The permission's protection level must include "development" (true on Android 17 here)
adb shell dumpsys package android | grep -A1 "MODIFY_QUIET_MODE:"
adb shell pm grant net.dinglisch.android.taskerm android.permission.MODIFY_QUIET_MODE

The Tasker profile:

  • Context: Time 09:00 to 17:00, Monday to Friday
  • Enter task: Work Profile → On, user 10
  • Exit task: Work Profile → Off

I tested both directions, and unpausing didn’t ask for a PIN.

One Tasker trap: an exit task only runs when the profile goes from active to inactive. If you create the profile outside its own time window, run the exit task by hand once.

4.10 Clean up storage

Uninstall for the main profile only with adb shell pm uninstall --user 0 <package>. Leave off --user 0 and you can hit other profiles too.

Firmware apps: on One UI 9, apps built into the system image can’t be removed without root (you’ll see only root can delete system app for a particular user). They don’t use your storage anyway.

Find the biggest files:

adb shell 'find /sdcard/ -type f -size +80M -exec stat -c "%s %n" {} + 2>/dev/null' | sort -rn | head

Google Photos → Free up space only removes phone copies of things that are already backed up. Before you run it, make sure backup shows as complete, and that any folder you want to keep on the phone is not set to back up, because otherwise “Free up space” will delete its local copy. That cleared 18 GB for me.

Quality-of-life extras

Good Lock’s Routines+ module adds hardware-button triggers to Samsung’s Routines, and they work reliably on the lock screen. Mine:

  • Hold Volume Down → flashlight
  • Hold Volume Up → my AI assistant app
  • Double-press Volume Up → camera
  • Double-press Volume Down → voice recorder

I tried Tasker’s “Volume Long Press” event first and it was flaky. Android only delivers it while the screen is on and unlocked, and in testing it stopped firing once the screen went off. Routines+ has been reliable.

One more: when my Bluetooth earbuds connect, the phone opens my music app. You don’t need a volume step, because Android already remembers media volume per audio device.

Gotchas that cost the agent time

If you’re an agent following this, read this section first.

  • adb install installs into every profile: the work profile, Dual Messenger and Secure Folder. Use adb install --user 0 -r app.apk.
  • A work-profile policy that caps screen timeout also disables “Stay awake while charging”. Look for mMaximumScreenOffTimeoutFromDeviceAdmin in dumpsys power. To keep the screen on during UI automation, send a harmless key every 30 seconds, and stop the loop before the owner starts gaming or typing:
while true; do adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_SHIFT_LEFT; sleep 30; done
  • Git Bash on Windows rewrites /sdcard/... paths. Use MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 for remote paths and cygpath -w for local ones.
  • Reading the screen: uiautomator dump works for standard Android UI. Apps that draw their own UI, like games and emulators, need screenshots.
  • On foldables, screencap needs a display ID: screencap -p -d <id>. Get the IDs from dumpsys SurfaceFlinger. Folding the phone locks it.
  • The first few keystrokes into a freshly opened search field sometimes get dropped. Re-read the screen and retype.
  • Dialogs move their “Done” button when options change. Re-read the screen before tapping.
  • Background agents run in parallel nicely, but only one should drive the screen at a time.

Step 5: Re-measure

After two or three days of normal use, pull dumpsys sdhms again and compare screen-off % per hour, screen-on % per hour and % used per day against your baseline.

While you’re at it, re-check CPU per day (ps), BLE scan time and background data for anything that’s crept back.

What I learned

  1. “Unused apps drain your battery” is mostly a myth on modern Android. Standby buckets do their job.
  2. The worst drains are things running when they shouldn’t be. A stuck Bluetooth loop, a mic service, constant scanning, weak radios and cloned profiles running duplicate system services.
  3. An agent with ADB access makes a very good battery auditor. It reads everything, normalizes the numbers and asks before it touches anything. It just needs clear guardrails.

If you try this on your own phone, tell me in the comments what your biggest drain turned out to be.

More from this series: I debloated my TCL Google TV over ADB, and I turned this same foldable into a retro handheld.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: From Vocalinux to the Voca family: a Mac port, a phone app and three app stores
item.description: Porting Vocalinux to macOS, moving it all into one Voca org, and pushing VocaPhone through Google Play, the App Store and F-Droid in a single autumn.
item.content:encoded:
In February I wrote about building Vocalinux, and in July about why cross-distro dictation took more than a model. Both posts were about Linux. This one covers what happened once the same idea left Linux: a macOS port, an org for the whole family, a phone app, and my first time going through three app stores at once.

The idea stayed the same throughout. Press a key, talk, and the text shows up where your cursor is, with the audio staying on your machine.

VocaMac: the port I wanted for myself

I was tired of not having reliable offline voice-to-text on my Mac without signing up for something or installing bloatware. So on 5 March I put out VocaMac v0.1.0, an alpha port of Vocalinux to macOS.

Only the idea came over as is. On Linux the default engine is whisper.cpp, while VocaMac uses WhisperKit, which runs the Whisper models on the Apple Neural Engine. It lives in the menu bar, you hold a hotkey to talk, and it types straight into whatever app has focus. Free, open source (AGPL-3.0), and it runs on both Intel and Apple Silicon Macs.

For an alpha it was surprisingly stable and light on resources. When someone asked me about latency in June, my answer was the reason I’d picked WhisperKit in the first place. On the Neural Engine it has a massive edge over whisper.cpp on CPU: it feels instant and keeps the machine cool. Accuracy is basically the same since the core models match, so the native Apple integration made it an easy call.

Paying Apple $99 so my mum can install it

Until April, installing VocaMac meant meddling with CLI commands. An unsigned app on macOS gets Gatekeeper warnings and right-click-open tricks, and for anyone who isn’t used to that, it’s a dead end.

So I paid for the Apple Developer Program. On 10 April I had a proper drag-to-Applications installer working, simple enough that my mum could use it, and I called it “worth $99/year imo /s”. The next day VocaMac v0.4.0-beta went out Developer ID signed and Apple notarized. Download, drag, grant the permissions, talk.

After that it was the usual grind. v0.6.1 in April fixed two startup crashes and a paste bug on non-QWERTY layouts, and the in-app update checker offered it to v0.6.0 users automatically. v0.7.0 in July added custom vocabulary for names and jargon, usage stats (words, WPM, streaks), a mic picker and a Homebrew cask, so updating is now just brew upgrade --cask vocamac.

Meanwhile, Vocalinux kept growing

The Linux app didn’t slow down while I was busy with the Mac. In mid July the 0.14 beta got picked up by Phoronix, It’s FOSS, FOSS Force and Linuxiac, and on 17 July Vocalinux became my first GitHub project to cross 500 stars.

On 28 July SwitchedToLinux reviewed it on YouTube. I’d been building it steadily for over a year, so watching a stranger install it and fumble through the settings had me sweating. Every wrong click, every awkward pause. But they got it working and they liked it, and as a first real review it hit harder than I expected.

v0.15.0 on 3 August brought a new settings panel, AppImage builds, around 33 speech languages, auto-pause and idle unload, and smarter Vulkan GPU picking. Remember the AppImage part, it comes back later.

One org for the whole family

By the summer, Vocalinux was one of several apps. There was VocaMac, a Windows version (VocaWin) and a phone app (VocaPhone), and a few active contributors were maintaining pieces of it with me. A shared org is simply easier for access and ownership than keeping all of that under a personal account.

So on 6 August everything moved under a new VocaHQ org. Same apps, same licenses, still free, and the old jatinkrmalik/... links redirect. Stars, issues, PRs and releases moved with the repos. The VocaPhone repo came over from a contributor’s own account a few days before the announcement.

The longer-term goal is in that README: set Voca up once and use it across whatever machines you own, desktop or phone, headless or interactive. The headless part arrived in September as VocaGateway, a transcription server you run on your own compute and point any of your machines at. Your other machines send their audio to it, and it stays on hardware you own.

At the end of August I was also asking for people to help test a beta on Windows. VocaWin is out now too.

VocaPhone, and three app stores

VocaPhone is an Android keyboard for voice dictation, with an iOS app alongside. On Android it plugs in as an input method, so dictation works in any text field. It runs models on-device and can also use a VocaGateway.

The keyboard part grew fast. One PR in mid August added a number row, keyboard heights, local English completions (switched off in password fields), a clipboard chip, emoji categories, spacebar cursor swipe, and a searchable model catalog with engine, size and language filters. By then I was typing some of my own replies on X with NVIDIA’s Parakeet 0.6B model running locally on my Android phone. On 3 September the public beta opened: Android 13+ builds and an iOS 17+ TestFlight.

Then came the stores. I had shipped Windows Phone apps and a Chrome extension before, but never to three stores in parallel, and each one checked for something different.

Google Play: prove people use it

Play wanted testers before production. On 18 August the tester list got an email with two links: the closed test, “the one Play counts toward review”, and an internal test that was already live for anyone who wanted it sooner. The build was 0.1.0-beta.16, and until Google reviewed the listing, Play showed the app by its package name with an “(unreviewed)” tag.

On 9 September Google granted VocaPhone production access. Play was the most straightforward of the three: run the closed test, wait, apply.

VocaPhone is live on Google Play now.

The App Store: the binary has to be right

I submitted VocaPhone 1.0 for iOS on 2 September. Apple had already flagged an earlier upload in August, and on 15 September it bounced builds 27 and 28, fourteen minutes apart, with the same error:

ITMS-90208: Invalid Bundle - The bundle VocaPhoneApp.app/Frameworks/onnxruntime.framework does not support the minimum OS Version specified in the Info.plist.

That error has nothing to do with your own code. A prebuilt framework you bundled declares a different minimum iOS version than your app does, and the upload pipeline rejects the whole build before a human ever looks at it.

The next day App Review came back with “Changes needed” on version 1.0. The email doesn’t say why; you have to open the App Review page in App Store Connect for that.

I got past both in the end, and VocaPhone is live on the App Store now.

F-Droid: prove you can build it from source

F-Droid barely looks at your listing. What it checks is whether it can build your app from source, and whether that build matches what you ship.

A contributor opened the fdroiddata merge request on 14 August, and it ran to 30 comments before the merge. Some asks were small: pin a full commit hash instead of a version tag, and drop a sudo block because the build server already runs JDK 21. The big one was reproducible builds.

VocaPhone ships two product flavors. The APK on our GitHub releases page was the full flavor, which bundles prebuilt native libraries: about 19 MB of ONNX Runtime and about 5 MB of sherpa-onnx. F-Droid doesn’t accept prebuilt binaries like that, so the fdroid flavor exists to drop them and compile whisper.cpp from a pinned submodule instead. That left two different APKs by design, and nothing for F-Droid to compare its own build against.

The fix was to publish the fdroid-flavor APK as its own release asset, signed by us. Then a reviewer pointed out that we had to decide on reproducible builds now, because switching from F-Droid’s signature to ours later would cut existing users off from updates. We chose upstream-signed reproducible builds from the very first F-Droid release, and the MR was merged on 3 October.

The funny part is that ONNX Runtime sat in the middle of both fights. Apple rejected the iOS build over its framework’s minimum OS version, and F-Droid needed a whole separate flavor to keep it out.

Hackaday couldn’t get it to work

On 15 September Hackaday ran a Linux Fu column on speech input. Vocalinux was in it. The writer said it looked nice, but a quick test kept complaining that his Intel extensions weren’t available, which made sense on his AMD CPU, and he never got it working. Handy was the one that worked for him. Fair enough, I had suggested Handy as a Vocalinux alternative on LibHunt myself back in January.

Late that night I introduced myself in the comments as the maintainer. I’d written Vocalinux on an AMD PC running Ubuntu, so an Intel extensions error was new to me, and I asked for his distro and the exact error.

He’d used the AppImage on openSUSE. The next morning he retried and it picked right up. A few minutes later he added that he had removed the model, and that the AMX messages only show up once a model is loaded. Either way, it was now working on his AMD machine.

From a public “never got it working” to working in under a day. I’ll take that.

Devin cleaned up my backlog

On 24 September I won my first giveaway ever, a $200 Devin plan from Cognition, for building VocaHQ. Its macOS VM (M4 Pro, 16 GB RAM) turned out to be handy for testing VocaMac too.

On 6 October I pointed it at Vocalinux and asked it to triage every open issue and PR, a backlog I’d been carrying since June 2025. Over about 10 hours it worked through the board bit by bit, ran end-to-end tests on a KDE desktop, and wrote its own skills for the job. Out of 60+ issues, I only had to bring in a different model for 2. Having Windows, Mac and Linux machines available to the agent made the biggest difference, because it could build each app on its native platform.

Seeing VocaMac on TechWiser

Four days ago I was watching TechWiser’s latest YouTube video about Mac apps over lunch, and they covered VocaMac. I’ve been building this in public since the start of the year and refining it bit by bit with the community, so seeing it pop up in someone else’s video was a validating moment. A lot of the credit goes to a contributor who revamped the UI and added a ton of features and models.

What I took away

Porting meant redoing almost everything except the idea. The engine, the installer and the way people get the app all changed between Linux and the Mac.

Each store checked something different. Play wanted a closed test before production, Apple wanted a binary that passed its upload checks and then a human sign-off, and F-Droid wanted to build the app from source and get the same APK we ship.

And most of this came from other people: user reports, PRs, and the few contributors who now maintain parts of it with me.

If you want dictation that stays on your device, on whatever you use: vocahq.com.
