item.title: A year of 3D printing: my giant creative hammer
item.description: A Flashforge AD5M, a printed enclosure, a dryer before TPU, a desk mount an LLM helped draft, an STL edited by an AI agent and an NFC tag for my dog.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve wanted a 3D printer for over 5 years. Finally, in July 2025, I was able to justify it 😁 And like any sane person, I bought the filament before the printer even showed up. “now we just wait for the 3d printer to show up (:”

So here goes: what I bought, what I printed, what I designed myself, where AI agents sneaked in, and what went wrong.

The BlackBox

Initial setup done! Let me introduce you to “The BlackBox”, aka the Flashforge Adventurer 5M (AD5M). CoreXY, incredibly fast print speeds and acceleration, auto levelling built in, and a textured PEI bed plate.

I debated going with the Pro model, but couldn’t justify the extra $150 when I can just print an enclosure myself. As a 3D printing newbie, that sounds like fun.

First up, some test prints on a black eSUN PLA Basic spool, and of course that means a Benchy. It came out incredibly detailed! There’s a video on X too.

Why did I think this would be a cheap hobby?

A couple of weeks in: “why did i think 3d printing would be a cheap and easy hobby lol”. The alt text on that photo was “How much filament is too much filament?”, so yeah, you know where my head is at.

The printer is the planned expense. Then come the spools, a storage bag kit to keep them dry, tools, and eventually a dryer (more on that below).

Even the small stuff sneaks up on you. Sample filament comes as a loose coil and I didn’t have a spare spool for it, so it got wrapped around a bottle. Jugaad ftw.

On the software side, I’m learning FreeCAD (open source) and Fusion 360 (the community version).

Printing stuff for the printer

So far I’ve mostly been printing small stuff for the printer itself. Next step: the enclosure I skipped the Pro model for. Spent my whole weekend printing and building it. Before and after:

Someone said it looks clean. Thanks! I call it The StormTrooper. I know it’s kinda meta, printing stuff for your 3D printer, on your 3D printer. Pretty cool eh?

Looks aside, I want it so I can experiment with TPU, ABS and the like.

Printing someone else’s model

Do you need a AA and AAA battery dispenser? No. Should you print one? YES.

This is the Multi Battery Dispenser from Printables, not my design. It took just under 2 hours on a 0.6 mm nozzle with 0.3 mm layer height, and used 87 grams of PETG Pro. Someone in the replies said it looks like a box magazine, and now that they mention it, it kinda does lol.

TPU, step 0: buy a filament dryer

November 2025, and I’m ready to try TPU. My entire tutorial is two lines:

how to 3d-print tpu in your fdm 3d printer? step 0 / buy a filament dryer

I went with the Creality Filament Dry Box 2.0. By the end of November it’s sitting right next to the printer, feeding filament straight in. That’s the photo at the top of this post.

The giant creative hammer

End of November, and this is how I’d describe it:

owning a 3D printer is like having this giant creative hammer where you go around the house to find problems and then solve them, would recommend buying 10/10!

That’s “The Art”. The printer is “The Artist”.

Someone asked what software I use to model these. Honestly, it depends on your skill level and the problem. For basic stuff, Tinkercad is enough. For advanced stuff, Blender or Fusion is pretty good. And you can find a lot of models on Yeggi and just print them.

Sketch, LLM, OpenSCAD: the under-desk mount

New Year 2026! I drew a rough sketch of an under-desk power brick mount with the S-Pen on my S23 Ultra, and gave it to an LLM to help generate a parametric 3D model in OpenSCAD. Use case #431 for the S-Pen.

The render, not bad tbh:

The slicer said about 41 minutes and 27 grams. The prints came out really well, so the power bricks are now mounted under my desk.

It’s modular enough to take a brick in and out. Bonus points: it keeps the floor clean. Happy wife, happy life!

I made it open source too: Open Source Universal Parametric Under-Desk Mount on Printables, with the SCAD file included. The walls are 4 mm thick with triangular fillets, it prints lying flat on its side so the layer lines run along the strap (no snapping), and it’s sized for #8 wood screws or M4 screws. Change the dimensions at the top of the file and you get a bracket for whatever you want under your desk.

Small fixes around the house (and the car)

A lot of it is small stuff. I made a quick model to mount my multimeter in style on my honeycomb storage wall. It’s a remix of a community model, and it’s up as the HSW Multimeter Holder v2 on Printables.

Then there’s the car. I printed a clip to hold the NACS <-> CCS charging adapter. Someone in the replies thought I was mounting a high-powered laser on my car. No bud, it’s just a NACS <-> CCS adapter for charging the car :D

Not everything has to be useful. Finally watched Project Hail Mary (10/10, would recommend!), so I printed this Grace model for my wife.

A $15 Pi Zero to babysit the printer

February 2026: just picked up a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W from Micro Center to manage the printer remotely. It’s mind blowing how much compute you get for just $15! A quad-core 64-bit A53 ARM CPU, 512 MB of SDRAM, and built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 4.2.

Raspberry Pis and I go back a long way, from the Pi 2 guides in 2015 to Pi-hole. When someone asked about Pi-hole under the tweet, yep, I already run Pi-hole and PiVPN on my RPi4.

I edited an STL with an AI agent, no CAD

My wife has an Xteink X4, a tiny e-reader that sticks to the back of your phone. I call it the antidote to doomscrolling. I wanted a better case for it.

I started with a community model of the case, but I didn’t like its textured back:

So I asked my AI agent to flatten it, then add a MagSafe ring recess, perfectly positioned for the camera bump on her Pixel 10 so it fits nicely.

Zero manual CAD work. I just described what I wanted, and Qwen 3.7 Max handled the Python and trimesh magic through OpenCode.

The final print is TPU 95A on a 0.4 mm nozzle, and it took 1h44m. The MagSafe ring is there because her Pixel 10 comes with Qi2 built in.

Someone asked if the design is open source, so a little late, but as promised, here it is: Xteink X4 E-reader TPU Flex Case with Flat Back and MagSafe versions on Printables.

Oh, and the AD5M is running open source firmware now.

An NFC tag for my dog

The latest one! I printed a tag for my dog Kylo’s collar, with an NFC tag inside that points to his page at j47.in/kylo, in case he ever gets lost. (NFC stickers and I go back a while too, all the way to 2016.)

Someone pointed out that whoever finds him lands on a page without my contact details up front. Fair point, but I don’t want to put my email and phone number up front on a public page and then get spammed till the end of time. (:

The Pointer Case Files

I’m also making a YouTube shorts series out of this, called Pointer Case Files. A simple pointer (my finger) points out life’s annoying little problems, like a wobbly table, messy cables or a misplaced remote, and then solves them with creative thinking and 3D printing. Each short is a new case. Basically the giant creative hammer idea, just on camera.

There are 10 so far. It starts with The Birth of The Pointer, and then there’s The Battery Chaos, The Frustrating Galaxy Watch Charger, The Humidity Horror and The Finishing Touch.

If you’re on the fence

It’s not a cheap hobby, so budget for filament and the bits around it, not just the printer.

You don’t need to design anything on day one. My battery dispenser was someone else’s model, and you can find a lot of models on Yeggi and print them directly. When you do want to design, Tinkercad is enough for basic stuff, and Blender or Fusion for advanced. For my under-desk mount, a rough sketch plus an LLM plus OpenSCAD came out really well, and because it’s parametric, one file can make a bracket for whatever you want under your desk.

Buy a dryer before you try TPU. Printing upgrades for the printer itself is kinda meta, but pretty cool, so go for it.

Once you have one, you start seeing problems everywhere, and every one of them looks like a nail. So yeah, this is your sign to buy that 3D printer!
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: My desks, 2018 to 2026: Cherry MX Blues, an ultrawide and an Airbnb table
item.description: Eight years of desk tweets: a 4K Dell and MX Blues, a 34-inch ultrawide over a walking pad, a vertical monitor, a dog crate desk and a G502 with weights.
item.content:encoded:
Every so often I post a photo of my desk on X with a list of everything on it. Lined up, those tweets make a decent changelog of how I work: what I bought, what I sold, and what made it across the world in a suitcase.

So here’s eight years of it in one place.

2018: Dev Setup Thursday

In August 2018 I posted a “Dev Setup Thursday”:

  • Laptop: Apple MacBook Pro with the Touch Bar (2017)
  • Monitor: Dell U2718Q, 27-inch 4K UHD
  • Keyboard: HyperX Alloy FPS Pro with Cherry MX Blues
  • Mouse: Logitech G300s

That MacBook shows up in two other tweets that year. The day before the setup post, Chrome was “taking over my mac”. On Christmas I was asking for StickerMule stickers, because my naked MacBook felt embarrassed in public and started throttling its CPU. Or maybe that was just Apple’s poor ventilation. I needed the stickers to verify, for science.

The MX Blues are loud and clicky, and I was still on them in late 2022. That matters later.

2022: tiling windows and neofetch

By August 2022 the monitor was busy. I posted a “sneak peek on my dev monitor”: Amethyst tiling an M1 Pro MacBook Pro into bashtop, ranger, a shell, neofetch and vim open on oh-my-zsh.sh, all on one screen. The first tweet in that thread was just “neofetch + oh-my-zsh == ❤️”.

Amethyst is an open source auto-tiling window manager for macOS. If you like the auto-tiling you get on Pop!_OS or Manjaro, it’s the closest thing on a Mac. It was my daily driver on the work machine, and it’s especially useful on an ultrawide, which is where this was going.

December 2022: work from home setup 3.0

In December 2022 I posted “Work from home setup 3.0”:

  • Monitor: a 34-inch UWQHD 144 Hz monitor from MSI, on a monitor arm
  • Keyboard: Keychron K8 Pro with G Pro Red switches
  • Mouse: Logitech MX Master 3S
  • Desk: a Green Soul electric sit-stand desk
  • Under the desk: a walking pad
  • And: a palm plant

About those red switches. Two weeks before this post I was on X saying I’d been eyeing a Keychron K2 v2 with Browns, that I was on HyperX Blues, and that I absolutely hated Reds because linear switches felt mushy. Then I bought the K8 Pro with Reds. In the replies to the setup post I admitted I got used to them pretty quickly. That’s all I have to say about that.

Four years after the naked-MacBook tweet, the laptop on the stand is covered in stickers, so that got sorted too.

The standing desk and the walking pad

Earlier that month someone asked about the best investment of 2022, and my answer was the standing desk. When someone called the thing underneath a treadmill, I had to admit it’s more of a walking pad. But even if you only stand for half your workday, that’s 1.5x more calories burned.

The desk is electrically height adjustable. In that photo it’s at about 120 cm, which is perfectly comfortable for me to walk and work at. In April 2023 someone in the replies pictured me sitting and walking at the same time like Peter Griffin, and I had to explain that the angle of the photo doesn’t do it justice. A month before that, someone asked what to buy, and I recommended the same Green Soul desk and chair, because together they did wonders for my back.

One tip for the monitor arm, from October 2023, after 8 months of it holding a 34-inch screen: if your tabletop isn’t very thick, wedge a solid block of wood into the clamp. It reinforces the clamp and gives the mount a wider grip.

Why the K8 Pro

The K8 Pro is my third mechanical keyboard, after a Razer BlackWidow with Greens and the HyperX with Cherry MX Blues. In April 2023 I asked X to choose between the Apple Magic Keyboard and the K8 Pro, and someone asked why I’d picked the K8 Pro over the K2 v2. It was a tough call, and three things decided it.

QMK/VIA support is the big one. I’ve built so many coding and workflow macros on it that it’s now hard to go back to any keyboard without it. It also ships with sound-absorbing foam and a silicone pad, so it sounds and feels premium out of the box. I’m not into lubing switches and adding foam myself yet, so that just works. And it’s a standard TKL layout. That makes it a bit bulky, but I’ve been typing for over two decades and muscle memory is a thing.

I’m also really digging the hot-swappable PCB, for whenever I go further into the custom world. In 2025 I still thought TKL was right for long coding sessions at a desk, with 60% boards making sense when you need something portable. I love my Keychron and wouldn’t trade it for anything, but on days when I travel and work, the Apple Magic Keyboard is the portable one.

May 2023: a vertical second monitor

In May 2023 I started test driving a second monitor, in portrait, mainly for code reviews, a persistent Slack window and Spotify. The other option was to mount it above the ultrawide. That keeps my neck moving up and down instead of side to side, but it needs a second monitor arm. I drew it out:

The two shapes are good at different things. On the ultrawide you can stack several editor windows side by side, which is great for refactors and writing unit tests. The vertical monitor is zen mode for writing new code: it only fits one editor window, but you see a huge amount of it at once.

I said I’d try it for a week and then decide. A month later it was still on the left, and still useful for code reviews and reference docs. It’s a Dell P-series, and in November someone on X turned out to have the exact same one.

In June 2023 I told someone choosing a monitor to get a 34-inch ultrawide over the usual 27-inch, partly because it “declutters your workspace by minimizing the need for dual monitors”. I had added the second monitor a few weeks earlier. Make of that what you will.

That ultrawide got a lot of use. In August 2023 I spread VS Code across it to read the Redis codebase at night (a topic I later gave a talk on). By December I was saying even 21:9 wasn’t wide enough for Chrome. And on Boxing Day 2023 I ran GTA III on my Galaxy S23 Ultra, projected onto it through Samsung DeX and played with an Xbox controller. Perfectly playable. The future is now, old man.

One thing on that desk never changed. In July 2023 I posted the Zen of Python poster that had been taped to my desk for more than seven years.

2024: a garage sale and an Airbnb table

Before all that, in February 2024 the desk was briefly a poolside table in Goa: “Why work from home when you can work from Goa?!”

On 1 August 2024, a month before relocating to the US, I announced a garage sale of everything I couldn’t take with me because of luggage limits. The desk was gone the same day. I also added the Apple Magic Keyboard and Magic Mouse to the sale.

The Keychron and the MX Master made the trip. In September 2024 I posted my old desk next to my new one, the setup back home in India on the left and the minimal setup in my temporary Airbnb on the right. The caption was a line from an old Hindi film song about stepping out of home, with a translation in the next tweet for everyone else.

Left: the Airbnb table, September 2024. Right: what I called “peak dev productivity setup” later that month. Don’t @ me.

That second one is a laptop stand and a keyboard on top of a dog crate, in front of the balcony door. Not a bad view, though.

Everything stayed in boxes for two months, and I finally unpacked in November 2024. The homelab side of that is in my homelabs before Zion. The same month I decided to build a PC for homelab experiments and the occasional game, and by 20 November I had the parts, including a Ryzen 7 9800X3D and an RX 7900 XTX. A gaming PC changed what the mouse had to do.

The PC got a new monitor too: an INNOCN 32M2V, a 32 inch 4K mini-LED that runs at 144 Hz.

The walking pad didn’t make the move. I left it behind in India.

The desk didn’t make it either. In Chicago I had to buy a new one.

Then I moved from Chicago to Mountain View, sold that desk, and bought another one here.

The mouse saga

In January 2024 I called the MX Master 3S the best mouse I’ve ever owned, mostly for the custom keymaps. In September 2024 it started double-clicking, so I opened it up. Later that month someone asked about its polling rate. My answer was that it’s not a gaming mouse, but on a 120 Hz MacBook display and a 120 Hz monitor I’d had no trouble with it.

The PC changed that. In December 2024 I was trying a Razer Basilisk V3, because the MX Master’s 125 Hz polling rate couldn’t keep up with my 144 Hz monitor, in games or even basic tasks. The stutter was noticeable even on the Bolt receiver. I was split between the Basilisk and a Logitech G502 HERO, which cost about the same.

In the end the Basilisk went back, and by August the G502 HERO had won. I’d been all in on the MX Master, but its materials started degrading, and the G502’s layers of customisation won me over. My hot take: the G502 HERO’s removable weights are the most underrated desk feature of the last decade. Featherweight for eight hours of work, loaded tactical anchor for gaming at night.

2026: power bricks and a 15-inch touchscreen

The desk keeps growing. Around New Year 2026 I sketched an under-desk power brick mount with the S-Pen, had an LLM help turn it into a parametric OpenSCAD model, printed it and mounted the power bricks under the desk.

In May 2026 I started testing a portable 15-inch touchscreen monitor just for coding sessions, with a coding agent CLI running over tmux. An absolute game changer, because now I could focus on my chess games without interruptions. (That was sarcasm.)

A lot of my coding doesn’t happen at a desk anymore. About half of it happens on the go, on my phone, which I wrote up in Coding on the Go.

What eight years of desk tweets add up to

The gear changed a lot. The K8 Pro is the constant: it’s in the setup 3.0 photo, the GTA photo, the Airbnb and the dog crate, and the QMK/VIA macros are why. The Reds I swore I’d hate turned out fine.

On screens, I’d still take one ultrawide over two small monitors, unless the second one is vertical and holds code reviews. The sit-stand desk was one of my best investments of 2022. Amethyst and an ultrawide go well together. And the mouse is the part that keeps changing: G300s, MX Master 3S, a Basilisk trial, and now a G502 with weights in it.

One thing on my desk wasn’t gear at all: the Zen of Python poster. In July 2023 it had been pasted on my desk for more than seven years, and the principles translated surprisingly well to Ruby, Go and Kotlin as I moved between orgs and projects. Simple is better than complex. That one applies to desks too. I just haven’t applied it to mine.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Coding on the Go: My Full-Stack Dev Environment Lives in My Phone Now
item.description: I used to think I needed a laptop. Then I dropped a phone into a lapdock, and now I ship code from hotel TVs.
item.content:encoded:
this is not a “laptop” 👆

I used to think I needed a laptop. Then I dropped a phone into a lapdock, and now I ship code from hotel TVs.

There’s a moment every traveling developer knows: you’re at an airport, in a hotel, at a coffee shop with bad wifi, and a critical bug lands in your repo. The Mac is in your hotel safe. The Linux box is at home. You have your phone.

For years, that meant: open GitHub mobile, read the issue, swear, and wait.

It doesn’t have to.

I’m writing this on a phone. Not “drafted on phone, polished on laptop.” This post was written inside a Termux session, inside a proot Ubuntu container, on a three-year-old Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra, with OpenCode as the coding agent and gh talking to GitHub. The setup is reproducible, cheap, and more capable than it looks in a photo.

A Dream 15 Years in the Making

This is not a new idea. I’ve been chasing it since the early 2010s, watching the industry get close and then walk it back.

2011: Motorola Atrix and Webtop.

The Atrix 4G had a “Laptop Dock”: a clamshell with a screen, keyboard, and battery, but no compute. You slid the phone in and got Ubuntu with Firefox and Nautilus.

I remember reading about it and thinking that’s the future. The hardware was too slow, the lapdock was overpriced, and the software was a gimmick. Motorola killed the line in 2012.

2015: Windows Continuum and the Lumia 950.

I was a Windows Phone fan (still am, in a quiet way). When Microsoft announced Continuum, the dream came back. Plug a Lumia 950 into a Display Dock and the phone threw a Windows-like desktop onto a monitor.

UWP apps scaled up. Keyboard and mouse worked. For a minute it looked like Microsoft had cracked it. Then Windows 10 Mobile died in 2019, and Continuum died with it. I had to let it go.

2017: Samsung DeX, and the long patient wait.

Samsung shipped DeX on the Galaxy S8: wired, dock-based, locked to their ecosystem. I watched. I waited. Year after year they kept iterating: DeX over HDMI, DeX over a single USB-C cable, DeX wireless, DeX on PCs, DeX on cars, DeX on TVs.

They even tried Linux on DeX in 2018 (actual Ubuntu on the phone), then Android 10 killed it in 2019. Samsung has been pushing this for nine years. They never quite nailed the software story. They did prove the hardware story, over and over: the phone can do this.

2025 to 2026: the ARM catchup.

And then, finally, the rest of the stack caught up. Two things happened in the last 3~4 years that made this dream actually work:

  1. Phone chipsets became genuinely desktop-class. A 2024 to 2026 flagship ARM SoC (Apple A18, Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, Exynos 2400, Google Tensor G4) has 8+ CPU cores, dedicated NPUs, multi-GHz clocks, and GPU compute that rivals a 2019 laptop. The Apple M-series proved you could put a Mac-class CPU on a phone-class power budget; the Android ecosystem followed. The phones in our pockets are now mini full-fledged PCs. They always have been, but now the silicon actually has the headroom.
  2. The ARM software stack matured. Linux on ARM64 went from “mostly works, lots of edge cases” to “first-class.” Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, and Arch all have solid aarch64 ports. The build tools, the container runtimes, the agentic CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, oh-my-openagent) are all native ARM64, no emulation. Termux + proot is now stable enough to run a real dev workflow for hours without breaking.
  3. The thing I love about phones, and the thing that’s always been true, is that they’re absurdly underutilized. Most people use them for WhatsApp, Instagram, and a few mobile games. The SoC spends 99% of its life idling, throttled, waiting. We’re running 8 cores, dedicated NPUs, and 8+ GB of RAM to scroll a feed. The same hardware, given the right software, can compile Go, run agentic refactors across 50 files, and serve a web app on localhost:3000 for testing. The hardware was never the bottleneck. The software was.

So here we are. 15 years after the Atrix, a decade after Continuum, 9 years into DeX, and the dream finally works. Not because someone had a brilliant new idea, but because the boring fundamentals (silicon, software, accessories) all matured in parallel until the moment arrived.

The Stack

The full chain, bottom-up:

  1. Android device. Any recent flagship with USB-C display output. I daily-drive a Galaxy S23 Ultra (2023), Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 for Galaxy, 8 cores, 12 GB RAM. It runs this whole stack without getting interesting in the heat. Older Samsung flagships work too if they do DeX. Pixel 8 and newer do Android’s own desktop mode over DisplayPort alt-mode. That is not “every phone since 2017.” The S8 needed a dock. A lot of Pixels before the 8 cannot drive an external display at all.
  2. A lapdock. This is the accessory that makes it feel real. A lapdock is a laptop shell: screen, keyboard, trackpad, speakers, battery, no motherboard. NexDock, Uperfect/Uplay, and a pile of AliExpress clones start around $200 to $300. USB-C in, clamshell out. The lapdock battery charges the phone, so a work day fits in a pocket plus a bag. Don’t want a lapdock? A $10 USB-C hub with HDMI-out, a USB-A port, and an SD slot turns a phone plus any monitor plus any keyboard into a desk. That’s the floor.
  3. Samsung DeX. Samsung’s desktop-mode UI. Since 2017, every Galaxy S/Note/Z Fold phone can output a real windowed desktop to an external display with proper keyboard, trackpad, and resize behavior. Not a stretched phone screen, an actual desktop.
  4. Termux. The F-Droid build (not the Play Store version, which is abandoned). Linux userland for Android: bash, gcc, python, go, the usual suspects, no root required.
  5. proot-distro + Ubuntu. Drop into a full Ubuntu 26.04 rootfs inside Termux. apt works, systemd doesn’t (proot is fakechroot-style, not a real container), but for 95% of dev work you don’t care.
  6. OpenCode. The open source coding agent, installed with a single curl pipe. Same TUI you’d get on a Mac.
  7. gh CLI. For repo operations, PRs, issues. Auth once, then it just works.
  8. An OpenCode Go API key. or whatever you already pay for. OpenCode will talk to Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Copilot, or Go. I use Go at $10/month; the catalog and the routing config live in the other post.

That’s it. No cloud VM, no remote box, no SSH tunnel. The whole dev environment runs on the device in your hand.

Why This Actually Works

“Why would you code on a phone?” is a fair question.

Three reasons that changed my mind:

1. The phone is not the bottleneck anymore.

The S23 Ultra has 12 GB of RAM, 8 ARM64 cores, and hundreds of GB of fast storage. I compile Go, run a local HTTP server, and let OpenCode fan out a few subagents, and the phone does not notice. “Phones are toys” died somewhere around Snapdragon 800. A three-year-old Ultra is more computer than most laptops that shipped in 2019.

2. The real trick is subscribed compute, not local compute

OpenCode, oh-my-openagent, Claude Code, Codex CLI: those are API clients. The model runs on someone else’s GPUs. The phone is the terminal. Same mental model as Codespaces or Gitpod, except the “cloud” is the model provider, the IDE is in your pocket, and you pay $10 to $20/month instead of per-minute for a remote box.

That changes the math. You can leave an agent looping for hours, refactor a service, write tests, and open a PR from hotel wifi, and the bill is the tokens.

3. You stay in control of your repo

This is the part I care about more than the form factor. Cloud coding products (Cursor Background Agents, Devin, and the rest) spin up a sandbox you do not own. You don’t watch the install. You don’t have the git config. The audit trail lives on their machine.

Here the agent runs in your filesystem, with your git and your gh auth. Every file it touches is a git diff away. Every command prints in the same Termux pane you started. If it does something dumb, Ctrl-C and git reset. If it does something good, git add -p and you read the hunks before you commit.

The agent is a tool in your hand, not a coworker in a VM you can’t SSH into.

Desktop Mode Is Coming to All Phones

The DeX question is the one I get most, so: Android is growing a desktop mode that is not Samsung-only.

Google shipped a DeX-like desktop session in Android 16. It started as a developer toggle in the September 2025 Pixel Drop (QPR1), on Pixel 8 and newer (DisplayPort alt-mode is the hardware gate; Pixel 7 and older don’t have it). By the March 2026 Pixel Drop (QPR3) it was on by default for those phones: plug in an external display, pick Desktop instead of Mirror, get a taskbar, free-form windows, keyboard and mouse. Google built it with Samsung. It is still rougher than DeX. It is also no longer a side quest.

Google has also said, in public, that they are putting the ChromeOS experience on Android internals (the Aluminium OS work, the “combine the PC and phone stacks” comments from late 2025). I would not bet a laptop purchase on the branding. I would bet that windowed Android on an external display is now a platform feature, not a Galaxy extra.

There is a Linux Terminal app too: a real Debian VM via the Android Virtualization Framework, KVM, its own kernel. On Pixel it is interesting. On Samsung, AVF is often disabled, which is why I still live in Termux plus proot on the Ultra. Don’t wait for Google’s VM if you have a Galaxy. The path below works today.

Everyone else has been quietly shipping a version of this for years. Motorola Ready For / Smart Connect on Edge and Razr. Huawei Easy Projection on the Mate 10/20/30. LG Screen+ on the Velvet and V60. If you want it polished today, Samsung is still the one. Pixel is native and early. Motorola already has it. The rest of Android has had a half-version of it for a long time.

The lapdock (NexDock, Uperfect, Uplay, the AliExpress specials) does not care which OEM is painting the windows. HDMI is HDMI.

This fragmentation is temporary. “Phone is a desktop” is becoming a stock Android feature. It will not be even across price tiers next year. It will be boring a couple of years after that.

The Setup, In 10 Minutes

1. Install Termux

Get it from F-Droid. Once installed, run:

pkg update && pkg upgrade
termux-setup-storage   # grants access to /sdcard if you want it

Pin Termux in Android recents and turn off battery optimization for it. Android will kill a 6-hour agent run the moment the screen goes off, and Samsung is extra enthusiastic about it (phantom process killer, “deep sleeping” apps). If a long session dies overnight, this is why.

2. Install Ubuntu via proot-distro

pkg install proot-distro
proot-distro install ubuntu # currently lands on 26.04; pin ubuntu:24.04 if you want fewer surprises
proot-distro login ubuntu

That’s it. You’re now in a real Ubuntu shell, with apt, gcc, python, the whole lot. A few things to know:

  • No systemd. systemctl is a brick. Start Postgres with pg_ctl, Redis with redis-server &, long jobs in tmux or screen. Docker-in-proot is a bad time; if you need containers, run rootless Docker on the Termux side, not inside the distro.
  • apt is fine. apt install -y git curl wget build-essential python3 nodejs npm ripgrep fd-find
  • Newer Ubuntu can be weird under proot. 26.04 works for me. If gdk-pixbuf starts wanting bwrap (needs real namespaces), pin ubuntu:24.04.
  • Termux home is bind-mounted. Files in ~/ on Termux and /root (or /home) inside Ubuntu are the same files. Edit in either place.

3. Install OpenCode

curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
opencode --version   # should be >= 1.4.x

It’s a Go binary. ARM64, no native deps, starts in under 200ms.

4. Authenticate

opencode auth login

Pick a provider. If you have OpenCode Go, pick that. $10/month, currently 27 coding models, dollar caps per model rather than one shared bucket. The routing config I actually run is in the Go + oh-my-openagent post. If you already pay for Claude, OpenAI, or Copilot, pick that. OpenCode does not care.

5. Install gh CLI

apt install -y gh
gh auth login

Pick HTTPS, paste a GitHub PAT (or use the device flow), and you’re done. You can now gh pr create, gh issue list, gh workflow run, all from the phone.

6. (Optional) Install oh-my-openagent

If you want the multi-agent setup (Sisyphus / Hephaestus / Oracle / Explore / Librarian, fallback chains, parallel subagents):

bunx oh-my-openagent install

Same ~/.omo/omo.jsonc I use on the laptop. It does not know or care that the kernel underneath is Android.

The Daily Workflow

Here’s a real session, slightly cleaned up:

# hotel room, TV as monitor via USB-C to HDMI
# (or lapdock clamshell open on the desk)
proot-distro login ubuntu
cd ~/code/payments-service

gh pr list --search "is:open review-requested:@me"
gh pr checkout 482

go test ./... -run TestRefundFlow

opencode
# > TestRefundFlow is failing in checkout/482. Read the test, read the
#   handler, find the race, fix it. Run the test until it passes.
#   Don't touch unrelated files.
#
# Sisyphus → Explore reads the code, finds the race
# Hephaestus writes the fix, re-runs the test
# Momus nags about unrelated edits
# Sisyphus: "Fixed. Test passes. Here's the diff."

git diff          # I actually read this
git add -p
git commit -m "fix race in refund flow"
git push

Total time: about 12 minutes, including my manual review. The agent did the investigation and edit. I did the validation and the push. The audit trail is in my terminal, in my git history, in my GitHub PR.

When I travel lighter, I do the same thing from a coffee shop with no external display, just the phone in DeX mode, the on-screen keyboard for short prompts, and a paired Bluetooth keyboard for the rest.

A $25 Logitech K380 + the phone + a USB-C cable to whatever screen is around is the entire “laptop.”

The Hardware Configurations

I’ve tested three setups. All work. Pick your poison:

The one I use most: lapdock on the desk, phone in via USB-C, lid open like a normal laptop. The lapdock battery keeps the phone alive, so I don’t end the day with 4%. Keyboard and trackpad are laptop-quality. Screen is a real 13 to 15” panel. It feels like a thin-and-light because, physically, it is one. The phone is the motherboard.

What This Setup Is Not Good For

A few honest limits:

  • GPU work. No CUDA, no ROCm, no local LLM at useful speed. Fine-tunes stay in the cloud. That’s fine; OpenCode was going to send the model off-device anyway.
  • Docker-in-Docker. Rootless Docker can live on the Termux side. Inside the proot, don’t bother. For services, apt and a process in tmux is simpler anyway.
  • systemd. No systemctl. pg_ctl, redis-server &, tmux new -d.
  • iOS. Termux is Android. iSH exists and it is a much weaker emulation layer. I don’t have a recipe for iPhone, and I’m not going to pretend I do.

For web work, Go services, Python, refactors, tests, PR review, long agent runs, even compiling C++: it works.

Why Am I Doing This?

The cost of “where” you code is falling off a cliff.

Ten years ago you needed a $1200 MacBook, fast wifi in a specific chair, and a disk image you were afraid to wipe. Today I need a phone, a screen, a Bluetooth keyboard, and a $10 to $20/month model subscription. The environment is in the pocket. The weights are in the API. The repo is on GitHub. Desktop mode is slowly becoming a boring Android feature. The SoCs that have always been tiny PCs are finally getting a userspace that treats them that way.

This is what I wanted in 2011, reading about the Atrix on a 4-inch screen and thinking “one day.” I am writing this from a phone. The PR is open. The test passed. The agent is already on the next task.

The install is about 10 minutes. The first time you push a fix from a hotel TV, the laptop starts to feel optional.

Related:

  • OpenCode Go + oh-my-openagent: The Complete Guide to SOTA Model Routing Without Hitting Limits, the model-routing config that runs on this setup.
  • Android 16 Desktop Mode / Samsung DeX / NexDock / proot-distro on GitHub / Termux on F-Droid

If you set this up, drop a comment with your hardware config. I’m collecting “phone-as-laptop” setups and want to see what others are running.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: I filed my Indian taxes as an NRI with AI agents
item.description: My first time self-filing an ITR, done end to end with Grok 4.5 in the grok build CLI. I built a neo-brutalist dashboard and a 158-page audit packet, and still overpaid by ₹5,550.
item.content:encoded:
Indian taxes are brutal. So I went neo-brutalism on them, with my own personalised dashboard to prepare my ITR for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27).

It was also my first year self-filing, with my (AI) agents. Going in, I was hoping I wouldn’t regret it ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Spoiler: I overpaid by ₹5,550, and I’d probably still do it again.

This started as two threads on X: the prep one in mid-July and the after-filing one two weeks later.

Why an NRI is filing in India at all

I lived in India (NCR and Bangalore) till 2024 and worked there for 12 years. Back then I was one of those FIRE aspirants, putting close to 60% of my paycheck into investments. That portfolio now throws off capital gains, dividends and interest on its own. Add a few past RSU grants and the stock/MF holdings, and there’s a fair bit to account for.

That income is in India, so I still have to file an ITR and pay taxes there. So I haven’t lived in India for 2 years, but I’m still contributing to nation-building. You’re welcome.

Why not a CA this time

Over the last few years I kept finding mistakes in my filings, so many that I was anyway playing the part of the CA. This year I figured I’d just file it myself.

The setup

If you have a coding client like Claude Code, Codex or opencode, these two skills are a good place to start:

  1. shivprime94/file-itr
  2. openaccountants/openaccountants

I used the two together for the due diligence, then got Grok 4.5 to build me a dashboard with a checklist so I could keep an eye on everything and verify it myself.

The document collection was all manual. I pulled a lot and lot and lot of documents into one folder on my PC, and by the time the dashboard was up it had 17 files loaded. Roughly:

  • Form 26AS (annual tax statement), for TDS credits
  • Form 16 + 12BA from my employer, for salary, RSU perqs and employer TDS
  • Form 16A from the REITs I hold
  • Interest certificates and savings statements from my banks, plus the home loan interest certificate
  • PPF transaction history, LIC premium statement and the NPS receipt
  • Mutual fund capital gains statement and the CAS from CAMS + KFintech
  • My broker’s tax P&L, for equity capital gains and dividends
  • AIS / TIS (deferred at first, because the portal was down)
  • A passport day-count for the residency status (only verbal at that point, the dashboard flagged that a written note would help)
  • Last year’s ITR, as a baseline

Grok 4.5 High in the grok build CLI

I did the whole thing end to end exclusively with Grok 4.5 High through the grok build CLI, plus a bunch of custom skills and scripts working off that document folder.

IMO grok-4.5-high sits right between the Sonnet and Opus class models, and it’s incredibly fast, so you can iterate very quickly.

I literally ended up pasting screenshots of complex ITR schedule forms side by side, and it could look at the data in the folder and explain each and everything properly.

The neo-brutalist dashboard

The dashboard was basically my working paper for the whole return, with a tab for pretty much everything:

Everything hung off a “confirmed decisions” table: new tax regime, non-resident (under 60 days in India), self-filing on the portal. From there it picked the form. ITR-1 was out because of the capital gains and NR status, ITR-3 and ITR-4 are for business income, so ITR-2 it was. It also laid out the filing flow in six steps, from locking in NR + new regime to e-verifying within 30 days.

About the look. I’ve been a backend/platform dev all my life, so I’m now on a mission to explore new design languages and systems and build myself custom dashboards that improve my productivity/efficiency (or at least my perception of it ;) ). This one is neubrutalism. If you want to learn a bit more about this design language, check out Neubrutalism: The Definitive Guide.

Gumroad by @shl has been the poster child for this look and feel, and it’s one of the first websites I remember adopting the style.

Filed, and overpaid

ITR-2 filed under the new regime as a non-resident, e-verified, challan paid. Turns out I overpaid by ₹5,550, which is one month of my coding plan, courtesy of the Indian govt.

The audit packet

Good thing is, I have incredibly detailed records in case I get audited, and I have up to 3 years to fix or amend my return. Bad thing is, the IT Dept is notorious for raising demand notices years after you file. Last year I got a notice to pay an extra ₹550 that was pending from 2016.

So after filing, the e-verify, the challan and all of that, I kept dumping everything into the same folder. Then I made the agent write a 400-line Python script that generates a 160-page (158, if you’re counting) audit packet PDF with everything end to end. The table of contents goes roughly like this:

  1. Filed return and acknowledgement: the ITR-2 ARN, the full form as filed, the self-assessment tax challan
  2. Working papers and checklist: a facts memo with the key numbers, the filing checklist, a digital exhibits and path map, and a JSON snapshot of the computation data
  3. TDS, 26AS, AIS and TIS
  4. Salary, Form 16 and employer TDS
  5. House property and home loan
  6. Bank accounts and interest
  7. Capital gains, including the Schedule 112A working
  8. REIT / InvIT Form 16As
  9. Other investments and exempt income (the CAS)

If I get a demand notice or an audit, or just need someone to review it later, I won’t have to scramble across bank websites, stockbrokers and mutual fund platforms to collect evidence. It’s all in one PDF.

I’m planning to do the same for my last 3 years of returns, just for peace of mind, and probably for my US tax filing too, so I have one single audit packet. I might also package it as a skill and publish it on a skill marketplace.

Was it worth all the effort?

Probably not. Did I learn a lot about taxation, and about how surprisingly good our income tax portal is? Absolutely yes.

Would I do it again? Well, I think so. With all the research I’ve done this time, I can probably cut the time by 60-70% next year and have everything on autopilot. I’m also banking on the models getting significantly better, cheaper and faster by then. So, cheers to that.

Disclaimer: DYOR. I am not a financial advisor.

item.title: Building cross-distro offline voice dictation for Linux (and why it took more than a model)
item.description: The story behind Vocalinux, from the missing Linux dictation gap to whisper.cpp, remote HTTP STT, Wayland text injection, and a tray app you can use every day.
item.content:encoded:
Linux is great at a lot of things. Voice typing has not been one of them.

On Windows and macOS you get system dictation that works in basically any app. On Linux you get cloud services, research scripts, and CLI tools that only make sense if you already know how speech stacks fit together. I wanted something closer to: press a shortcut, talk, text appears. Prefer offline. Free. Not tied to one distro.

That is Vocalinux. GPLv3 tray app. System-wide speech-to-text on X11 and Wayland. Default engine is whisper.cpp running on your machine. You can also pick OpenAI Whisper, VOSK, or a Remote API engine that talks to your own HTTP STT server (OpenAI-compatible or whisper.cpp’s server). Core path needs no account and does not send audio to a random SaaS.

This is the story and the technical path, not a feature dump.

The gap

I kept tripping over the same three constraints:

  1. Privacy. Mic audio is sensitive. Cloud STT is a non-starter for a lot of people (and a lot of workplaces).
  2. Daily use. A tool that only works as a terminal demo is not dictation.
  3. Linux realities. X11 and Wayland are different. GNOME and KDE are different. Text injection is harder than “call the API and print a string.”

Pieces of the puzzle already existed. whisper.cpp made local Whisper models practical. VOSK was light enough for older boxes. Projects like nerd-dictation showed people wanted FOSS options. What I did not find was a multi-engine tray app that treated Wayland as a real problem, stayed offline by default, and still let power users point at a home-lab GPU when they wanted to.

So I started building one.

A short timeline

Numbers as of mid-2026. The project is still beta on purpose.

When What
Early 2025 Design and early work around offline Linux dictation
April 2025 Public GitHub repo: jatinkrmalik/vocalinux
Late 2025 First tagged alphas (e.g. v0.2.0-alpha). Installer and engine choices start to harden
Early 2026 Alpha into beta (v0.5.0-beta and friends). Site at vocalinux.com. Multi-language work
Through 2026 Wayland/IBus reliability, settings UX, model selection, remote HTTP STT, nightlies
July 2026 v0.14.0-beta: custom modifier+key hotkeys, FunASR/SenseVoice over remote OpenAI-compatible APIs, more Wayland fixes, smarter whisper.cpp thread defaults on hybrid CPUs

Still beta because desktop Linux dictation has a long tail of compositor and input-method bugs.

What Vocalinux actually is

In practice:

  • Tray app with clear listening / processing state
  • Toggle or push-to-talk
  • Configurable shortcuts (presets, or any Ctrl/Alt/Shift/Super + key combo)
  • Four engine paths: whisper.cpp (default, local), OpenAI Whisper (local PyTorch), VOSK (local, light), and Remote API (HTTP to a server you control)
  • Vulkan GPU for whisper.cpp when available (AMD, Intel, NVIDIA)
  • One interactive installer that peeks at hardware and suggests an engine
curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux/main/install.sh -o /tmp/vl.sh && bash /tmp/vl.sh

First install is usually a couple of minutes with the default tiny whisper.cpp model. Bigger models cost RAM and latency for accuracy.

Stack: Python 3.9+, GTK 3 (PyGObject), the speech backends above, then a lot of stubborn work on audio capture and text injection.

Remote API (the fourth engine)

Local models are the default story. Remote is the escape hatch when your laptop is weak, you already run a Whisper box on the LAN, or you want one GPU server shared by a few machines.

How it works when Remote API is selected:

  1. Vocalinux still captures mic audio on the laptop (16 kHz mono PCM).
  2. Local VAD / end-of-utterance decides when a phrase is done.
  3. The buffer is packed as WAV in memory (not written to disk) and uploaded over HTTP.
  4. The server returns text; Vocalinux injects it into the focused window.

Two wire formats out of the box (docs: HTTP remote transcription):

Format Endpoint idea Examples
OpenAI-compatible POST /v1/audio/transcriptions Speaches, LocalAI, FunASR/SenseVoice servers, or a self-hosted stack that mimics OpenAI’s audio API
whisper.cpp server POST /inference The HTTP server binary from whisper.cpp

You are not locked into OpenAI’s cloud. Point the base URL at http://your-lab:8000 (or whatever you run). As of v0.14.0-beta, OpenAI-compatible remote mode also understands FunASR/SenseVoice-style model names (e.g. sensevoice) and cleans SenseVoice metadata labels before injection.

Same self-hosted server can back other clients on the network (phones, other desktops) if they speak the same API. Audio goes to your box, not a random vendor, unless you deliberately configure a public endpoint.

Remote does not replace offline mode. It is for people who want the tray UX on a thin client and the heavy ASR somewhere else they trust.

The hard parts

1. Recognition is only half the product

Getting a transcript string is easy. Users live in browsers, IDEs, chat, LibreOffice, terminals. The product is “text landed where the caret is,” not “something printed on stdout.”

That means:

  • Clipboard and paste paths when injection fails
  • IBus and input method restore on GNOME/KDE Wayland
  • Modifier keys still held when injection starts (fires shortcuts, garbles input)
  • Audio device indices that change between sessions

A lot of recent releases are those bugs, not new models. That is the right bias for desktop software.

2. Wayland is not “X11 but newer”

On X11 you could fake more with older tools. Wayland is stricter and more compositor-specific. Vocalinux spends time on injection paths for modern GNOME and Plasma, then spends more time fixing regressions when detection or engines move.

If you only test one DE, you ship “works on my machine” and break on the next Reddit thread.

3. Engine choice is a product feature

There is no single STT stack that wins for everyone:

Engine Role
whisper.cpp Default local path. Good speed/quality tradeoff, Vulkan-friendly, avoids PyTorch for many users
OpenAI Whisper Local PyTorch path; NVIDIA-oriented GPU story
VOSK Lighter local footprint on older hardware
Remote API Offload ASR to whisper.cpp server or any OpenAI-compatible STT (Speaches, LocalAI, FunASR/SenseVoice, etc.) while VAD stays local

The installer recommends something sane from RAM, GPU, and Vulkan. Settings keep model selection per engine so switching does not wipe preferences. Remote is configured with server URL, endpoint style, and model name when the server needs one.

4. Offline-first is a constraint, not a slogan

Offline means:

  • Models download once and run locally for the three local engines
  • No account for core dictation
  • Remote API is optional and explicit: you choose the host

Air-gapped and flaky-network laptops care about the first path. Homelab people care about the second. Both are valid; the default still does not require a network.

5. UX details show up before fancy models do

People notice tray icons, short audio cues, whether push-to-talk matches muscle memory, whether a pause between phrases inserts a space instead of gluing words, and whether hybrid CPUs cook because the STT library grabbed every core.

v0.14.0-beta is full of that kind of work: hotkeys, hybrid-CPU thread defaults, Wayland/IBus reliability, remote SenseVoice cleanup. Unsexy. Necessary.

Who it is for

Linux desktop users who want dictation without defaulting to cloud STT. People reducing keyboard load (RSI, accessibility, long writing sessions). Devs who live in terminals and editors but still want system-wide capture. Privacy-minded folks who want GPLv3 code they can read. Homelab users who already run Whisper (or FunASR) on a box and want a proper Linux client in front of it.

It is not a commercial Dragon replacement with a sales team. It is a community desktop app that should be good enough to leave running every morning.

What I would do differently (and what I would not)

I would not drop the offline default, the multi-engine design (including remote), or Wayland injection as core work.

I would start earlier on packaging (Flatpak, AUR, and friends) as a real channel, not only the install script. More automated DE matrix testing for injection. Clearer “what works where” docs from day one. Remote setup could use more opinionated presets for common servers so people do not have to read endpoint docs on a bad day.

Still open: broader packages, a better docs hub, and the endless DE/compositor bugs that only show up when real keyboards and layouts hit the wild.

Try it, break it, file issues

  • Site: https://vocalinux.com/
  • Source: https://github.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux
  • Remote HTTP setup: docs/HTTP_REMOTE.md
  • Changelog: https://vocalinux.com/changelog/
  • Compare / alternatives: https://vocalinux.com/compare/

If you try it on a weird Wayland setup, open an issue with distro, DE, and whether injection or recognition failed. Same for remote: say which server software and endpoint style you used. Those reports are how the history above got written.

I am still shipping betas on purpose. Desktop dictation on Linux only gets good if people use it in the wild and we keep fixing what they hit.

Disclaimer: I am the maintainer of Vocalinux. Feedback welcome on GitHub issues/discussions.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: I left GoDaddy after 15 years and moved every domain to Porkbun with zero downtime
item.description: Why I finally walked, how I picked Porkbun over Cloudflare and Namecheap, and the exact downtime-free playbook you can steal for any registrar move.
item.content:encoded:
Why I finally walked, how I picked Porkbun over Cloudflare and Namecheap, and the exact downtime-free playbook you can steal for any registrar move.

Fifteen years. That is how long I stuck with GoDaddy before I finally moved all my domains out. Eight of them, once I counted the parked ones I had forgotten I owned.

I kept putting it off because I assumed a migration meant a scary window where my sites would go dark. It turns out that fear is mostly misplaced. If you understand one simple thing about how domains work, you can move a whole portfolio and never drop a single request.

This is the guide I wish I had when I started. The method works for any registrar-to-registrar move. I will use my real migration as the worked example: GoDaddy out, Porkbun in, with most of my sites running on GitHub Pages.

Here is the post that kicked the whole thing off:

Jatin K Malik on X (formerly Twitter): “Devs, need your help! I’m planning to finally move away from @GoDaddy after 15 years of using them as my domain…

Why I finally left GoDaddy

I did not leave over one big betrayal. I left because of a hundred small ones that add up when you own more than a couple of domains.

If you have bought anything from GoDaddy recently, you know the checkout. It runs across seven or eight screens, and half of them have add-ons pre-selected for you. Click through too fast and you have signed up for a website builder, an email plan, and a security bundle you never wanted. Some of that even auto-enrolls: I have watched Microsoft 365 email and a “Websites + Marketing” plan attach themselves to domains I only wanted parked.

Then there is the pricing. WHOIS privacy, which almost every modern registrar throws in for free, is billed as a roughly twenty-dollar-a-year add-on. Renewals creep up quietly until a plain .com I have owned forever is renewing at three or four times what it should cost. And in early 2025 they cut the refund window from thirty days to seven, which tells you where their priorities sit.

None of it is illegal. It is just a business model built on hoping you are not paying attention. After fifteen years, I got tired of paying attention.

Jatin K Malik on X (formerly Twitter): “ok, I finally did it. after 15 years on @GoDaddy, moved all 7 domains off this week. it was never one big thing but…

The three contenders

Once I decided to leave, three names came up over and over: Cloudflare, Porkbun, and Namecheap. Here is how they actually compared for me.

Cloudflare is the cheapest by a hair and has genuinely excellent DNS. But it comes with two strings I did not love. You are forced to use Cloudflare’s own nameservers, and there is no human support unless you are on an expensive business plan.

Namecheap I ruled out on renewal math. That six-dollar first year balloons past fourteen at renewal, and I plan to own these domains for years, not months.

The .in domain that killed Cloudflare for me

There was also a hard blocker. One of my domains is j47.in, and Cloudflare Registrar does not support .in at all.

This is not a fluke. Cloudflare supports basically every generic TLD, but only a short list of country-code TLDs: .co, .io, .me, .us, .uk, .ca, .mx, .nz, .tv, .fm, .cc, and .ai. Almost every other national extension is missing, including big ones like .de, .fr, .it, .es, .eu, .au, .jp, and yes, .in. They also do not do internationalized or punycode domains.

So Cloudflare would have forced me to split my portfolio across two registrars. Porkbun handles .in and the rest of those ccTLDs happily, which meant one login for everything. That settled it.

Is Porkbun even trustworthy?

Fair question before you hand over eight domains. The pig branding does not exactly scream “enterprise.”

Porkbun has been around since 2014. It is the registrar arm of Top Level Design, a company that actually operates its own TLDs like .design, .ink, and .wiki, so these are people who work at the registry level, not just resellers. They are ICANN accredited, they crossed three million domains under management in late 2025, and they have been USA Today’s top-rated registrar three years running with a five-star Trustpilot average across tens of thousands of reviews.

The one honest knock: support is not 24/7. It runs 365 days a year but on business hours, so a 3am emergency waits until morning. For a batch of GitHub Pages sites, I could live with that.

The one idea that makes zero downtime possible

Almost nobody explains this part clearly.

A registrar transfer and your DNS are two separate systems. Moving who you pay for the domain does not, by itself, change where the domain points. The only thing that can take your site offline is your nameservers going quiet.

And that is the trap with GoDaddy specifically. If you use their default nameservers, the ones ending in domaincontrol.com, those stop answering the moment a domain leaves GoDaddy. So if you just yank the domain out, your DNS falls off a cliff.

The fix is simple once you see it. Move your DNS to the new home and confirm it is serving correctly before the registration transfer ever completes. Do it in that order and there is never a gap.

Step 0: map your DNS before you touch anything

You cannot recreate records you did not know you had. Before I started, I ran dig against every domain to build a full inventory of nameservers, where the site points, email, and verification records.

for d in yourdomain.com anotherdomain.com; do
  echo "==== $d ===="
  dig +short NS  "$d"     # who answers DNS today
  dig +short A   "$d"     # where the apex points
  dig +short www."$d"     # the www record
  dig +short MX  "$d"     # email, do NOT lose these
  dig +short TXT "$d"     # SPF, domain verification, etc.
  dig +short DS  "$d"     # DNSSEC, if present
done

This one pass saved me. It confirmed every domain was on GoDaddy nameservers, that none had DNSSEC, that seven of eight were plain GitHub Pages, and it caught the two landmines I talk about below.

Protip: Use EXODUS at checkout for transfers to save $1 / domain.

Porkbun on X (formerly Twitter): “You can transfer them all to us and have them in one place, you can still use Cloudflare for DNS and we will not lock you in…

The zero-downtime transfer, step by step

This is the sequence I ran for each domain. Porkbun documents a version of it, and it maps cleanly onto any registrar that lets you edit DNS before the transfer finishes.

  1. Leave the domain locked at the old registrar. Counterintuitive, but the lock is what stops the transfer from completing before your DNS is ready.
  2. Start the transfer at the new registrar. When it asks for the auth or EPP code, the domain is still locked so you do not have a usable one yet. Enter a placeholder to get past the screen. (Porkbun posts transfer coupons on their socials from time to time, so it is worth checking before you pay, I just used XX.)
  3. Rebuild your DNS at the new registrar. Re-enter every record from your dig inventory, formatted exactly the same. Take your time here.
  4. Switch the nameservers at the old registrar to the new ones. For Porkbun that is curitiba, fortaleza, maceio, and salvador dot ns.porkbun.com. Because you pre-loaded the records in step 3, the site keeps resolving through the switch.
  5. Wait 24 to 48 hours for the nameserver change to propagate, then verify (see below).
  6. Unlock the domain and copy the real auth code from the old registrar.
  7. Finalize the transfer with the real code and approve the confirmation email. Since your DNS already lives at the new host, this last step has zero effect on your live site.

The magic is in the order. By the time the registration actually moves, your traffic has already been served by the new nameservers for a day or two.

If your sites are on GitHub Pages

Most of mine were, which made the DNS side trivial. GitHub Pages needs the same handful of records everywhere:

A      @     185.199.108.153
A      @     185.199.109.153
A      @     185.199.110.153
A      @     185.199.111.153
CNAME  www   yourusername.github.io

Two tips that are easy to miss.

  • Add your custom domain in the repo’s Pages settings before you point DNS at it, otherwise you leave a small window for someone to hijack the subdomain.
  • And since GitHub’s IP addresses never change during a move, its Let’s Encrypt certificate just keeps working. Re-tick “Enforce HTTPS” after the dust settles and you are done.

The gotchas that will bite you

The generic steps are easy. The details are where sites break.

Email is the big one. One of my domains routed mail through Mailgun. A single missed MX record there means silently broken email, and email failures are the kind you notice a week too late. If a domain has any mail on it, open the old DNS panel by hand and copy every last record, including SPF and DKIM entries that often hide on a subdomain like mg.yourdomain.com where an apex dig will not show them.

Do not transfer a domain that is about to expire. I had one expiring in about four weeks. Transfers can take several days, and if one stalls past the expiry date you can actually lose the domain. If it is close, renew it at the old registrar first to buy a safe year, then move it later.

Kill DNSSEC before you move. If a domain has DNSSEC enabled, remove it at the old registrar first. Mismatched keys after a transfer cause resolution failures that look exactly like an outage. Mine had none, which I only knew because I checked the DS records up front.

Keep your verification TXT records. Several of my domains had Google site-verification strings. Losing them does not cause downtime, but it quietly breaks Search Console and anything else tied to that proof. Carry them over.

How to verify each move

After the nameserver switch, three commands tell you everything:

dig +short NS  yourdomain.com    # should now show the new registrar's nameservers
dig +short A   yourdomain.com    # should still show the right target IPs
curl -sI https://yourdomain.com  # expect a 200

If the nameservers have flipped and the site still answers on HTTPS, you are safe to finalize the transfer.

Was it worth it?

Completely. Eight domains now live under one clean dashboard, at flat pricing, with privacy and SSL included and nobody trying to upsell me at checkout. The whole batch moved without a second of downtime, because at no point was there a gap between the old DNS answering and the new DNS taking over.

super clean dashboard

If you have been sitting on a GoDaddy account you have outgrown, the move is far less scary than it looks. Map your DNS, rebuild it at the new home first, switch nameservers, verify, and only then finish the transfer.

The 60-second cheatsheet

  • Inventory every domain with dig (NS, A, www, MX, TXT, DS)
  • Pick a registrar that supports all your TLDs (check ccTLDs like .in carefully)
  • Renew anything near expiry before you move it
  • Remove DNSSEC on the old side
  • Leave the domain locked, start the transfer, rebuild DNS at the new registrar
  • Switch nameservers, wait 24 to 48 hours, verify with dig and curl
  • Unlock, grab the real auth code, finalize
  • Re-check email, HTTPS, and any verification records
  • Start with your least important domain as a test run

Start small, prove the process on one throwaway domain, then run the rest on autopilot. That is exactly how I did it, and I only wish I had done it years ago.
