item.title: pmptr: a dead simple teleprompter, with no ads and nothing to pay for
item.description: I built pmptr for my wife: a transparent, always-on-top, click-through teleprompter for macOS, Linux and Windows. Open source, one npm install.
item.content:encoded:
I built this one for my wife. The teleprompters out there are cluttered with ads, upsells and paywalls, for an app whose job is to scroll text up a screen.

So pmptr is dead simple, and it’s open source.

What it does

It’s an Electron app that puts a transparent, frameless, always-on-top window over whatever else you have open and scrolls your script in it.

Lock it and it turns click-through, so your clicks go to the app underneath while the text keeps rolling. A separate control window holds the script, speed, size, colours, opacity and mirroring, and changes apply live.

npm install -g pmptr && pmptr

It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows, it’s MIT licensed, and there’s no account, no ads and nothing to pay for.

The keys

  • Space plays or pauses
  • R resets
  • Up and down arrows change the speed
  • L toggles click-through
  • Esc closes it
  • V turns on voice follow: it listens to the mic, scrolls while you speak and eases to a stop when you pause

The code is on GitHub.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Getting around site blocks in India: VPNs, proxies and one nasty VPN scam
item.description: How to get back on Telegram during India's ban, why incometax.gov.in barely loads for me without a VPN, and a fake VPN sponsorship that stole a dev's creds.
item.content:encoded:
Back in 2016 I wrote a post on 5 cool ways to surf blocked sites in your office/college. Ten years later the block is sometimes the government’s, and sometimes it’s a government website blocking me.

I’ve tweeted about both sides over the last couple of years: getting people in India onto a banned app, and me sitting outside India trying to open the Income Tax portal. There’s also a scary one about a “VPN company” that turned out to be a credential stealer. So here it all is in one post.

Usual disclaimer, this isn’t legal advice. Check what’s allowed where you are, and what the terms of the service you’re using say, before you go around a block.

The Telegram ban PSA

In June 2026, Telegram got restricted in India until June 22. As per Pavel Durov, Telegram’s founder, the IT ministry pulled the plug for a week because some users were sharing leaked exam questions on the platform. His argument was that it punished 150M+ regular users while the leaks just moved to other apps.

Millions of genuine users got locked out of their study groups, trading bots and daily chats, students and devs included. So I put out a PSA on X on how to get back online safely with a VPN or an in-app proxy. 43 people bookmarked it.

Option 1: the VPN route (quickest)

  1. Download a trusted, reputable VPN, like ProtonVPN, Surfshark, or Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1.
  2. Connect to any server outside India, e.g. Singapore, US or Germany.
  3. Fire up Telegram. It should connect instantly.

Option 2: Telegram’s built-in MTProto proxy

If you don’t want a VPN running in the background all the time, you can set up a proxy inside the app itself:

  1. Turn on a VPN temporarily, just to get the app connected.
  2. Go to Settings → Data and Storage → Proxy Settings.
  3. Tap Add Proxy and select MTProto.
  4. Enter the details from a trusted public MTProto proxy provider. You can find active, free ones easily on GitHub or from trusted tech channels on X.
  5. Save it, turn your VPN off, and Telegram will stay connected through the proxy.

Either way, stick to reputable VPNs and well-known proxy providers.

Personally, I’ve been using Surfshark for 3 years now. Highly recommended! If you want to try it, you can get 3 months free on Surfshark with my link.

(Referral link: it’s my personal Surfshark referral, so I get credit if you sign up through it.)

My two cents on the ban itself

I think banning a platform like this is a knee-jerk move. Banning a social media platform the govt can’t control is such a cliche, especially when VPNs cost almost nothing and anyone can bypass the ban anyway.

The reverse problem: Indian govt portals from abroad

I live in the US, and there my problem is the opposite one: Indian websites not loading for me outside India.

The Income Tax portal is the one that keeps getting me. Back in January 2025 I was trying to log in to eportal.incometax.gov.in and got this:

And then, on the main portal, this:

It felt like a never-ending battle. Is the server down? Does my VPN offend them? Does my ISP get the cold shoulder? Or is it my DNS? Both error pages come from Akamai, the CDN in front of the site (that’s what the errors.edgesuite.net reference link is).

By November 2025, incometax.gov.in almost never worked for me unless I switched to a VPN. Here’s my Surfshark connected to an India server:

Is it some babu hack to save bandwidth cost? Whatever the reason, the block itself is geo-blocking at the CDN. Akamai blocks non-Indian IPs, so changing my DNS didn’t help, even though the second error page literally says “DNS failure”.

So if you’re outside India and the portal won’t load, a VPN connected to an Indian server is what works for me.

Other options: DNS-over-HTTPS and Tor

A VPN is the quick fix. There are two more tools worth knowing about, and both have their limits.

DNS-over-HTTPS

One common way ISPs block a site is at the DNS level. You look up a blocked domain, their DNS server doesn’t give you the real IP, and the site never loads. DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) sends your lookups encrypted over HTTPS to a resolver you pick, like Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1, so your ISP can’t see or change them.

It won’t help if the ISP blocks the site’s IP address, or reads the domain name from the SNI field in the TLS handshake and drops the connection. It also does nothing for a geo-block like the Income Tax one, since that’s about where your IP is from.

Switching it on takes a minute in most browsers:

  • Firefox: Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll down to DNS over HTTPS and pick Increased or Max Protection. Mozilla has a full guide.
  • Chrome: Settings → Privacy and security → Security, turn on Use secure DNS and pick a provider.
  • Edge and Brave have the same Use secure DNS toggle.

Cloudflare’s browser guide walks through all of these. For the whole device, Windows 11 lets you turn on DNS over HTTPS when you set a DNS server manually in network settings, and on phones Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1 app does it for you.

Tor

Tor Browser bounces your traffic through three volunteer-run relays before it reaches the site. Your ISP can see that you’re using Tor, but not which site you’re opening, so it gets around most of these blocks.

The catch is speed. It’s fine for reading a page and painful for anything heavier. Some sites also block known Tor exit nodes or keep throwing CAPTCHAs at them, so not everything will open. And only download it from the Tor Project’s own site, for the same reason as the scam below.

The VPN scam to watch out for

In April 2026 I heard about a software engineer who got hacked by a “new VPN company” that wanted to sponsor his YouTube channel.

They offered good money and asked him to try the VPN before agreeing to the sponsorship. Then they sent an innocent looking curl | sh command to “install the VPN”, and the script stole all his creds in just a few minutes.

So don’t pipe a script from someone you don’t know straight into your shell, however good the sponsorship money looks. And same as with Telegram, stick to reputable VPNs.

TL;DR

  • Blocked app in India? A reputable VPN connected to a non-India server is the quickest fix. For Telegram, the built-in MTProto proxy works without keeping a VPN on.
  • Can’t open incometax.gov.in from abroad? It’s geo-blocked at the CDN, so changing DNS won’t fix it. Use a VPN with an Indian server.
  • ISP blocking a site at the DNS level? Turn on DNS-over-HTTPS in your browser. Tor works too, just slowly.
  • Only use reputable VPNs and proxies, and never run a curl | sh “installer” that someone sends you.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Locked out of GitHub for three days over a compromised CLI token
item.description: In May 2026 GitHub suspended my account over a compromised gh CLI token. Their explanation pointed back to the stealer that hit my Mac in 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Last month GitHub locked me out of my account, and for three days I blamed GitHub for it. Then their explanation sent me straight back to June 2025, when a macOS stealer took over my X account after I pasted a command into Terminal.

Day by day

In May I was travelling in India and using a VPN when I noticed GitHub Actions had been disabled across my account. The banner said: “GitHub Actions is currently disabled for your account. Please reach out to GitHub Support for assistance.” No email, no warning. I opened a support ticket on 19 May.

21 May. Support replied that my account had been suspended “out of an abundance of precaution” after their systems detected suspicious activity. A personal or OAuth access token on my account had likely been compromised and used to create suspicious repositories, so they had revoked every token on the account. They’d lifted the suspension and asked me to reset my password, review all my repositories (especially any with Actions enabled) and scan my machines for malware.

22 May. My reply, which in hindsight is the most telling line in the whole thread: I’m travelling and on a VPN, and “I have a two factor authentication setup so I am very sure that my account most likely is not compromised.” I reset my password anyway and told them it was done.

25 May. Support listed four repositories created with the token in question, all named test-action- followed by a long timestamp. The timestamps decode to dates between 31 October and 6 November 2025. I deleted them. In the same email I mentioned I’d been playing with parallel coding agents in tmux and wondered if that had created them, and asked them to revoke all my access tokens so I could re-authenticate each one. I also told them that since changing my password I was locked out of my own account.

26 May. Still locked out, I asked @github on X for help. My first guess, which I posted that morning, was that I’d been caught in the crossfire of the supply-chain attack on GitHub the day before, the one that used Actions workflows to push malicious code. Maybe because I use the gh CLI from OpenClaw, my self-hosted AI agent. Maybe because I was logging in from India. Later that day I had the account back, sort of.

I could log in and see my profile. Nobody else could: to the rest of the world, github.com/jatinkrmalik was a 404. Workflows didn’t run. GitHub Pages was down, which took out my portfolio and the static sites for my projects. And I couldn’t see open pull requests or issues on any project, my own included. That meant Vocalinux (the offline dictation app I wrote about in February) and LLMFeeder, which both get pull requests from other people.

27 May. I bumped it on X after more than 12 hours without hearing back. Later that day I told support I’d deleted all four repositories and didn’t remember creating them. They showed creation dates from November, and I couldn’t find anything relevant in my security log, so I asked how they could have been created. Pages and Actions were still down. I asked for priority, then asked again.

28 May. Day 3. I’ve had that account for 15+ years and built over 25 open source projects on it, and all of it (source code and sites) had been offline for more than three days, with no SLA for support in sight. I tried escalating through LinkedIn contacts, and a bunch of folks on X pushed it too.

Two hours later, support came back with the actual explanation.

The repositories had been created with a compromised GitHub CLI OAuth access token, and the activity ran from November 2025 to May 2026. They’d revoked that token and cleared the restrictions. GitHub itself wasn’t breached. Then came the line that made me sit up: “in similar cases we have been informed that infostealer malware was discovered on users’ systems,” along with a recommendation to pay particular attention to wherever I store personal access tokens.

About an hour after that, we were back.

Which explanation is it?

I’ve told more than one story about those repositories, and I should own that.

On 25 May I told support my tmux agent experiments might have created them. On 27 May I told them I didn’t remember creating them at all. On 28 May I wrote on X that GitHub’s explanation “suspiciously aligns” with how I’d been using the gh CLI on OpenClaw for the last few months, asking it to create a bunch of test GitHub Actions workflows. Both are possible. An agent holding my token can create a test-action-* repo I never look at. So can someone who lifted that token off a machine.

GitHub’s evidence points to a compromised token. My own history includes a Mac whose browsers an infostealer went through in June 2025, about five months before the first of those repos showed up.

Either way, I’ve cleaned up the leftover repos, changed my passwords and revoked all my tokens, so every CLI and agent gets re-authenticated one at a time. On 28 May I asked support whether there’s anything beyond hardening my tokens that would stop this from happening again. On 7 June they asked me to repost the question inside the ticket so the right team sees it. I’m still waiting on that answer.

The first time: 2011

This wasn’t my first account takeover. In January 2011 someone broke into my Facebook account, and as I wrote on the 10th, “he hacked in series all my associated email ids in chain so that I may not be able to recover password of any acc”. Every recovery email led to another account he could take. On 28 January, a day after I made a new profile, Facebook handed the old account back.

That attack went after the recovery chain: own the inbox, and every “forgot password” link is yours. So when someone started requesting password resets on a long-abandoned Facebook account of mine in December 2023, I turned on 2FA for it and moved on.

2FA protects the login. A browser session cookie is what you get after a login has already passed 2FA, and an OAuth token for the gh CLI is the same deal. Whoever holds one of those skips the password and the second factor entirely. So my “I have 2FA, so I’m very sure I’m not compromised” to GitHub support was me answering the 2011 question in 2026.

What I’m taking away

  • A token is a credential. Anything that holds a GitHub token (the gh CLI, coding agents, CI) should get the narrowest scope that works, and the list of authorised OAuth apps and tokens needs a regular look.
  • Look at what’s actually on the account. Four repos I never made on purpose sat on mine for more than six months and I didn’t notice. GitHub keeps a security log for every account, and support pointed me at it, even if it didn’t tell me much this time.
  • A stealer infection means rotating tokens too. Passwords and browser cookies are the obvious part. Every CLI on that machine with a long-lived token is the part that’s easy to miss.
  • One account shouldn’t hold everything. For three days my code, my project sites and other people’s pull requests all hung on a single account I couldn’t use. The plan is a self-hosted git mirror of my key projects, so a suspension never takes the source offline again.
  • Hardware security keys for the accounts that matter.

What changed between 2011, 2025 and 2026 is where the weak spot was. In 2011 it was my chain of recovery emails, in 2025 it was me pasting a command into Terminal, and in 2026 it was a long-lived CLI token.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: localcaption: video transcripts on your own machine, no API keys
item.description: A small CLI that glues yt-dlp, ffmpeg and whisper.cpp together. Paste a video URL and get a transcript as text, SRT, VTT and timed JSON, fully local.
item.content:encoded:
I wanted transcripts of videos on my own machine, with no account, no API key and no audio uploaded anywhere. The pieces already existed as separate tools. They just weren’t glued together.

So I glued them. It’s called localcaption.

What it does

You give it a URL. yt-dlp pulls the audio, ffmpeg converts it, and whisper.cpp transcribes it locally. You get the transcript as .txt, .srt, .vtt and timed .json.

pipx install localcaption
localcaption "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=..."

Since the download side is yt-dlp, it works with YouTube, Vimeo, Twitch, X and the rest of the 1,000+ sites yt-dlp supports.

localcaption at v0.2.0.

How fast is it?

I shipped v0.1.0 on 22 April. On my M4 Pro MacBook it transcribed a 54-minute interview in about 50 seconds, using base.en, which was the default model then.

v0.2.0 is out today.

Why I built it

I use this one almost every day. It’s a cousin of Vocalinux, my offline dictation app for Linux, which also runs on whisper.cpp. Same idea in both: your audio stays on your machine.

It’s on PyPI and the code is on GitHub.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Reading Petzold's CODE as a book club, one Saturday at a time
item.description: Six months of Saturday sessions reading Petzold's CODE together, from flashlights and Morse code to operating systems. Over 120 started. 4 of us finished.
item.content:encoded:
This weekend we finished reading Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software by Charles Petzold. “We” is a reading cohort on the Team Shiksha Discord that met every Saturday, starting on 29 November. So a little over six months, one session at a time.

It was my second time through the book. The first was about seven years ago.

How it started

Back in July a friend was talking about understanding the core basics of computers, and I replied recommending CODE. My advice at the end: get it from your library!

In November the same friend and I got talking about hosting a reading cohort of the book on Team Shiksha’s Discord. Read the chapters together, with some side chat on the breadth and depth of how software and hardware evolved. I was planning to reread it anyway, and doing it with a group sounded like fun. It was free. No course, no charges, just bring interesting questions and curiosity.

I put out a quick survey on X to see if people wanted in. In one of the replies I said that even the most basic stuff can hide a lot of detail, like an onion you peel layer by layer. Honestly, that’s the book.

I ran the sessions. My friend took care of the recordings and the community side.

The slot was every Saturday at 08:30 AM PST, which is 10:00 PM IST. One hour, a US morning and an Indian night.

We read the original 2000 Microsoft Press edition, from the scan on the Internet Archive, with the book up on screen during the call. There’s a second edition from 2022 that reorganises the chapters, so the chapter numbers in this post are from the original.

The book, a chapter a week (mostly)

Session 1 covered the preface and Chapter 1. It starts with two friends blinking flashlights at each other across the street and gets to Morse code, and from there we went on to ASCII, UTF-8 and how all of computing comes down to tiny on/off decisions. I shared some real world encoding stories from my startup days too. By the end, a few folks were motivated to memorize Morse code.

Session 2 went from everyday signalling systems to thinking like a computer from first principles. Watching people make that jump was genuinely special.

Session 4 was about counting. Chapter 8 is why we use base 10 (thanks, fingers) and why computers need base 2. Chapter 9 defines the bit, the simplest form of information. Everything in your digital life turns out to be a series of yes/no questions.

Session 6 was Chapter 11, “Gates”, the point in the book where electricity turns into logic. Wire relays in series and you get AND. Wire them in parallel and you get OR. Add an inverter and you can build NAND and NOR, and any digital circuit can be built out of those. One participant posted afterwards that it brought back memories of studying Digital Logic Design in college.

Session 7 moved from logic to arithmetic. Chapter 12 wires up a binary adding machine out of full adders, and Chapter 13 pulls off subtraction with two’s complement. You never need a “subtractor” circuit: flip the bits, add one, and reuse the adder you already have. Hardware efficiency is an art form. Seeing that bridge between physical relays and math was the highlight of my week.

Session 9 was about efficiency. Chapter 15 makes the case for hexadecimal as the Goldilocks base for humans, less tedious than binary and lined up perfectly with how bytes are structured. Chapter 16 goes from simple flip-flops to an assemblage of memory, where you can jump to any address and read what’s there.

Sessions 10 and 11 were Chapter 17, “Automation”. With random access to memory you can store, reuse and manipulate data at will, which is the foundation of an instruction set and of modern CPU architecture (hint: Von Neumann). Then the real aha moment: the jump instruction. Change the instruction pointer and you get loops and conditional logic, and a calculator becomes a programmable computer. That’s where machine language starts.

Sessions 12 and 13 were Chapter 18, “From Abaci to Chips”: the abacus, then transistors, then integrated circuits. All the room-sized logic and memory we had been “building” for weeks ends up etched onto a tiny piece of silicon. It’s mind bending how far we’ve come in under 100 years.

Sessions 14 and 15 were Chapter 19, “Two Classic Microprocessors”. The 1970s showdown: Intel 8080 against Motorola 6800. The 8080 is register-heavy, and the 6800 makes elegant use of index registers and the stack pointer. Putting them side by side makes you appreciate the engineering trade-offs that still define computing.

Session 16 was Chapter 20, “ASCII and a Cast of Characters”. After weeks of building a processor that only understands math, we finally taught it to read and write text. Seeing a simple 7-bit standard bridge binary numbers and human language was a big lightbulb moment for the group.

In late April we did Chapter 21, the system bus. If you wired every component directly to every other component, you’d end up with a tangled web of millions of wires. Instead there’s a shared set of wires everything connects to. The address bus is where the CPU wants to read or write (pointing at a house). The data bus carries what’s being moved (the people going to the house). The control bus says read or write and keeps everything in step with the clock. The coolest part was a section of memory mapped straight to a video display: write to those addresses and you get graphics on a screen.

The final chapters went from bare metal up to operating systems, high-level languages and the graphical revolution, and then we were done.

I posted after most sessions. Here they all are, in order:

Reading it again

Back in November I said I hoped to read it again with a new perspective. Last month, about a completely different book, I tweeted that revisiting your old favorites is a good benchmark for how much you’ve changed. The book stays the same and means something different now.

With CODE, a lot of it now connects straight to the day job. The loops and if statements we write all compile down to the conditional jumps from Chapter 17. The bus chapter is a small lesson in shared infrastructure: one set of wires, many components, and rules so they don’t talk over each other. And the 8080 against 6800 sessions were really about trade-offs, which is most of engineering anyway.

The biggest takeaway wasn’t about computers

We started with over 120 people. On the last day, exactly 4 of us crossed the finish line.

That’s the intention-behavior gap in one number. Motivation is the burst of dopamine that makes you start. Consistency is the system that makes you finish. Seth Godin calls the long middle “The Dip”, the quiet stretch where the initial excitement fades and the real work begins.

Sustained perseverance pays off out of proportion, simply because something like 97% of people drop out on their own once the friction gets high enough.

What kept it going

I’ve written before about how I get through books on my own. A group runs differently. A few things that worked for this one:

  • Same slot every week. Saturday, same time, one hour.
  • The chapter set the pace, not the calendar. Chapters 17, 18 and 19 got two sessions each.
  • A public recap on X after most sessions, usually with a diagram, a figure from the book or a cheat sheet. Circuits are hard to talk about without pictures.
  • Recordings. My friend and I recorded the sessions and put them up week by week in a YouTube playlist.
  • Joining late was easy. When someone asked in December how to get in, I told them to catch up till page 82 on their own and join the next session.
  • Free and informal. No course, no fee.

And expect the drop-off. Over 120 at the start, 4 at the end. That’s the dip.

To the other 3 who stayed consistent week after week: the compound interest is yours to take.

And a big shout-out to Team Shiksha for giving the cohort a home on their Discord. Go follow them!

item.title: OpenCode Go + oh-my-openagent: The Complete Guide to SOTA Model Routing Without Hitting Limits! [Updated: September 2026]
item.description: A tiered guide to routing OpenCode Go models across oh-my-openagent agents, with fallback chains and budgeting to avoid hitting rate and monthly limits.
item.content:encoded:
September 2026 update: If your August config still parks GPT 5.6 Luna on Hephaestus or DeepSeek V4 Pro on daily work, replace it. Both now sit on a $15 monthly envelope. Grok 4.5 is gone. GLM-5.3 is the new OmO GLM brain, and it is also $15/month, so GLM-5.2 remains the orchestrator you can actually run all day. And stop putting Qwen on Sisyphus.

OpenCode Go now lists 27 coding models: Kimi K3, GLM-5.3 / 5.3-Flash / 5.2, Qwen3.8 Max/Flash, Grok 4.6, GPT 5.6 Luna, DeepSeek V4 Pro / V4 Flash / V4.1 Flash, MiniMax M3, LongCat-2.0, plus the older volume lanes, for $10/month.

Most subscribers still route everything through a single model. In August that emptied a 5-hour window. In September it can empty the month. Here’s how to use the catalog without doing that.

What You Get with OpenCode Go (August 2026)

For $10/month, the official docs list these models:

Source: opencode.ai/docs/go, last checked Sep 12, 2026

Reference frontier models (for context):

  • Claude Fable 5.1: 81.2% SWE-Pro
  • Claude Mythos 5: 80.3% SWE-Pro
  • Claude Fable 5: 80.0% SWE-Pro
  • Claude Opus 5: 79.2% SWE-Pro, 97.0% SWE-Verified
  • GPT-5.6 Sol: 64.6% SWE-Pro, ~96% SWE-Verified
  • GPT-5.6 Terra: 63.4% SWE-Pro

On SWE-Bench Pro, Qwen3.8 Max at 67.7% is now the best published Go score I can find, ahead of Hy4 preview (65.7%) and the old Grok 4.5 number (64.7%). GLM-5.2 is still 62.1%. Luna is still 62.7%. That is the OpenAI Terra band, not the Anthropic Fable band.

SWE-Bench Verified is a different story than in August. Grok 4.6 sits at 95.6%, GLM-5.3 at 95.4%, DeepSeek V4 Pro (0813) at 96.4% on vals.ai. Claude Opus 5 is 97.0%. The easy-ticket gap mostly closed. The hard-ticket gap did not. Fable 5.1 at 81.2% SWE-Pro is still about 13 points above the best Go model.

For most production coding work, that is still the right trade-off, if you match the model family to the agent role and respect the monthly caps.

The Problem: The $15 Cap Is the New Trap

OpenCode Go limits are still dollar-based. The 5-hour / weekly / monthly windows are 20% / 50% / 100% of each model’s monthly dollar cap, not a shared $12 / $30 / $60 for every model:

  • $60 monthly models (GLM-5.2, MiniMax M3, MiMo-V2.5, GLM-5.3-Flash): $12 / 5hr, $30 weekly, $60 monthly
  • $30 monthly (V4 Flash, Qwen3.8 Flash, Qwen3.7 Max, Hy4): $6 / 5hr, $15 weekly
  • $15 monthly (K3, GLM-5.3, Grok 4.6, Luna, Qwen3.8 Max, V4 Pro, V4.1 Flash, MiMo-V2.5-Pro): $3 / 5hr, $7.50 weekly

A single agentic coding session burns 50–200 requests (one per tool call, file edit, shell command). Put the orchestrator on Kimi K3 (110 req/5hr) or GLM-5.3 (220 req/5hr) and you’ll hit the wall in one serious session.

Luna is the one that fools people. It still shows 2,050 req/5hr. V4.1 Flash shows 6,500. Those look like volume. They’re $15/month. Luna can empty the month in one fat window. V4 Pro dropped from 3,450 req/5hr in August to 1,050, same $15 cap.

If you put Sisyphus on Qwen3.8 Max “because 67.7% SWE-Pro,” you’ll also fight oh-my-openagent’s own guidance. Qwen is fine for many worker roles. It is not a maintained Sisyphus brain. OmO’s Capable profile is Claude Fable 5.1 → Claude Opus 5 → Kimi K3 → GLM-5.3. Qwen isn’t on that list.

The fix: tiered routing + deep fallback_models chains, with orchestrators from the OmO-supported set. Treat every $15 model as scarce even when the 5-hour column looks fat.

Sign up with: https://opencode.ai/go?ref=AYQ8245FDE to get $5 off for your first month!

Step 1: Install OpenCode + Oh My Open Agent

Prerequisites

  • OpenCode 1.4.0+ (verify with opencode --version)
  • Git, Node.js or Bun
  • macOS, Linux, or WSL

Install OpenCode

curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
opencode --version

Install Oh My Open Agent

bunx oh-my-opencode install

For non-interactive setup (LLM agents, CI):

bunx oh-my-opencode install --no-tui \
  --opencode-go=yes \
  --opencode-zen=yes \
  --claude=no \
  --openai=no \
  --gemini=no \
  --copilot=no

FYI, OmO’s better stack is still OpenCode Go ($10) + a real OpenAI path if Hephaestus / deep / ultrabrain are daily drivers. The Deep work profile leads with GPT-6 Astra, then GPT-5.6 Sol. Luna is on Go, but it’s $15/month, so treat it as a burst.

Pure Go is fine for Sisyphus / Atlas / Oracle / Explore / Librarian if you keep Sisyphus on GLM-5.2.

Verify Installation

opencode --version              # Should be 1.4.0+
bunx oh-my-opencode doctor      # Diagnostics check
opencode models                 # List available models
opencode auth login             # Authenticate providers

In the TUI: /connect → OpenCode Go → paste key, then /models.

Step 2: Understand the Agents

Oh My OpenAgent still gives you specialized agents (Sisyphus, Hephaestus, Prometheus/Atlas, Oracle, Explore, Librarian, Metis, Momus, etc.). OMO 5 also routes work through categories (architect, deep, quick, visual-engineering, ultrabrain) and can pick the main session model with a model_profile. Each agent wants a different model family, and a different quota.

Orchestrators & Planners

  • Sisyphus: main orchestrator → opencode-go/glm-5.2 primary. Ultrawork: Kimi K3, then GLM-5.3
  • Prometheus / Atlas: planning + execution conductor → GLM-5.2 / Kimi K2.7 Code
  • Oracle: architecture consultant → GLM-5.2 daily; escalate GLM-5.3 / Qwen3.8 Max / Grok 4.6

Deep Workers

  • Hephaestus: GPT-native autonomous worker → prefer OpenAI Astra/Sol. Go daily: MiniMax M3. Burst: Luna
  • deep / ultrabrain: MiniMax M3 / Qwen3.8 Max / Grok 4.6 (scarce)

Utility & Search Agents

  • Explore / Librarian: speed agents → MiMo-V2.5 / LongCat-2.0 / V4 Flash
  • quick / writing: GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8 Flash, MiMo-V2.5

Step 3: The Tiered Model Architecture (Sep 2026)

The core principle: match model capability (and family fit) to task complexity. Don’t burn your best model on trivial tasks!

FYI, numbering is top to bottom Tier 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 (scarce → complex → standard → volume). Escalate up if stuck. Tier 4 stays specialized.

Tier 0 // Scarce (Surgical Only, $15 monthly)

Models: Kimi K3 (110), Qwen3.8 Max (160), Grok 4.6 (169), GLM-5.3 (220), V4 Pro (1,050), Luna (2,050), MiMo-V2.5-Pro (3,250), V4.1 Flash (6,500)

Use for: Sisyphus ultrawork (K3, then GLM-5.3), Oracle spikes, Qwen3.8 Max as a hard worker (not Sisyphus), Luna bursts, then get off it.

Watch out: Luna and V4.1 Flash look like volume in the 5-hour column. They’re $15/month. One busy window can empty the envelope. V4 Pro is no longer the 3,450-req workhorse from August.

Tier 1 // Complex Agentic (Budgeted, mostly $60)

Models: GLM-5.2 (880, $60), GLM-5.1 (880, $60), Kimi K2.7 Code (1,350, $60), Kimi K2.6 (1,150, $60), Hy4 preview (1,350, $30), Qwen3.7 Max (170, $30)

Use for: Multi-file refactors, long-horizon runs, OmO orchestration primary (GLM-5.2), practical Kimi fallback (K2.7 Code).

NEW #1: GLM-5.3 is the OmO Capable-profile GLM (95.4% SWE-Verified, 88.2% Terminal-Bench 2.1) but 220 req/5hr and $15/month. GLM-5.2 at 62.1% SWE-Pro and 880 req/5hr is the one you can run from 9 to 6.

Tier 2 // Standard Engineering (Balanced)

Models: MiniMax M3 (3,200, $60), MiniMax M2.7 (3,400, $60), Qwen3.6 Plus (3,300, $60)

Use for: Feature implementation, terminal-heavy automation, Hephaestus-style deep category work on Go.

Hidden gem: MiniMax M3 is the daily Hephaestus on a Go-only box. 59.0% SWE-Pro, 3,200 req/5hr, $60/month. That’s the slot Luna had in August.

Tier 3 // Volume Workhorse (Rarely Rate-Limited)

Models: MiMo-V2.5 (30,100, $60), LongCat-2.0 (11,400, $60), V4 Flash (13,000, $30), GLM-5.3-Flash (6,320, $60), Qwen3.8 Flash (5,400, $30), Hy3 / Qwen3.7 Plus (4,300, $60)

Use for: Explore / Librarian, small edits, quick tasks, unspecified-low (GLM-5.3-Flash, not Grok 4.6).

Hidden gem(s):

GLM-5.3-Flash is a Claude-like volume model at 6,320 req/5hr and $60/month (84.3% Terminal-Bench 2.1).

MiMo-V2.5 is the unlimited search agent. V4 Flash fell from 31,650 to 13,000 and is $30/month.

Skip Muse Spark in the default config: 45,300 req/5hr, but Contributor-tier trains on prompts.

Tier 4 // Specialized Capabilities

Models: Grok 4.6 (vision / agentic, $15), V4 Flash Vision Exp ($15), GLM-5.2 / 5.3 (planning), Qwen3.8 Max (hard worker)

Use for: Screenshot-to-code, GPT-shaped bursts on Luna, Prometheus planning on GLM. DeepSeek weekday peak (01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC) doubles V4 / V4.1 Flash / V4 Pro token cost; weekends are off-peak.

Step 4: Configure Rate Limit Resilience

Enable model_fallback and set up fallback chains so rate limits don’t break your workflow:

{
  "model_fallback": true,
  "runtime_fallback": {
    "enabled": true,
    "retry_on_errors": [400, 429, 503, 529],
    "max_fallback_attempts": 3,
    "cooldown_seconds": 60,
    "timeout_seconds": 30,
    "notify_on_fallback": true
  }
}

When a provider hits rate limits, it’s globally blacklisted for cooldown_seconds. All new sessions skip blacklisted providers until cooldown expires.

429 on GLM-5.2 → Kimi K2.7 Code → GLM-5.3-Flash

FYI, if you also have Zen credits, enable Use balance in the console. Go can then use Zen balance after dollar limits instead of hard-blocking.

Step 5: The Complete Configuration (Sep 2026)

Save this to ~/.omo/omo.jsonc. OMO 5 migrates a leftover ~/.config/opencode/oh-my-openagent.json once. After that only the ~/.omo file is live.

{
  "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/dev/assets/omo.schema.json",
  "model_fallback": true,
  "runtime_fallback": {
    "enabled": true,
    "retry_on_errors": [400, 429, 503, 529],
    "max_fallback_attempts": 3,
    "cooldown_seconds": 60,
    "timeout_seconds": 30,
    "notify_on_fallback": true
  },
  "agents": {
    "sisyphus": {
      "model": "opencode-go/glm-5.2",
      "fallback_models": [
        "opencode-go/kimi-k2.7-code",

        "opencode-go/kimi-k2.6"
      ],
      "ultrawork": {
        "model": "opencode-go/kimi-k3",
        "fallback_models": [
          "opencode-go/glm-5.3",
          "opencode-go/kimi-k2.7-code",
          "opencode-go/grok-4.6"
        ]
      }
    },
    "hephaestus": {

src: https://gist.github.com/jatinkrmalik/e8ee48842c4c8502060f338fd5e398d3

Configuration Breakdown

Sisyphus (Main Orchestrator)

  • Primary: opencode-go/glm-5.2, OmO-supported Claude-like orchestrator, 62.1% SWE-Pro, 880 req/5hr, $60/mo
  • Fallback: Kimi K2.7 Code (1,350, $60) → GLM-5.1 → Kimi K2.6
  • Ultrawork: Kimi K3 → GLM-5.3 → K2.7 Code → Grok 4.6 (all $15 except K2.7)

Hephaestus (Autonomous Deep Worker)

  • Primary on Go-only: opencode-go/minimax-m3, 59.0% SWE-Pro, 3,200 req/5hr, $60/mo
  • Fallback: Luna (GPT-shaped, $15) → Qwen3.8 Flash → V4 Flash
  • If you add OpenAI: pin Hephaestus to GPT-6 Astra or GPT-5.6 Sol

Oracle

  • Primary: GLM-5.2 for consults you can afford
  • Escalate: GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8 Max, or Grok 4.6

Explore / Librarian

  • Both stay on mimo-v2.5 / longcat-2.0 / V4 Flash
  • Speed agents. Don’t waste K3, GLM-5.3, or Grok here.

Categories (short)

  • architect: GLM-5.2 → GLM-5.3 → Grok 4.6
  • deep: MiniMax M3 → Qwen3.8 Max → GLM-5.3
  • quick: MiMo-V2.5 → LongCat-2.0 → GLM-5.3-Flash → V4 Flash
  • unspecified-low: GLM-5.3-Flash → Qwen3.8 Flash → MiMo-V2.5 (overrides OmO’s Grok default)
  • unspecified-high: K2.7 Code → GLM-5.2 → MiniMax M3 → GLM-5.3
  • writing / artistry: Qwen3.8 Flash / GLM-5.2 → GLM-5.3-Flash
  • ultrabrain / visual-engineering: Grok 4.6 first, then K3 / GLM-5.3 / Qwen3.8 Max

Step 6: Rate Limit Budgeting

Per 5-Hour Window, with monthly cap (quick map)

Rule of thumb: If a task will take more than ~100 requests, start on MiMo-V2.5 / GLM-5.3-Flash / Qwen3.8 Flash. Escalate to MiniMax M3 or K2.7 Code for standard work. Reserve GLM-5.2 for orchestration. Spend K3 / GLM-5.3 / Grok 4.6 / Luna like espresso shots, not drip coffee.

Sign up with: https://opencode.ai/go?ref=AYQ8245FDE to get $5 off for your first month!

Step 7: The Quality Trade-Offs

Without Copilot / Claude Max / OpenAI Sol, you’re on a pure OpenCode Go stack. Stronger than August (GLM-5.3, Grok 4.6, Qwen3.8 Max). Also easier to empty, because several of those sit on $15 monthly caps.

Where You Win ✔

  • Cost: $10/month vs $50–200 in stacked Anthropic + OpenAI API bills
  • Model diversity: 27 Go models, up from 17 in August
  • SWE-Bench Verified: Grok 4.6 (95.6%), GLM-5.3 (95.4%), V4 Pro 0813 (96.4%) sit next to Opus 5 (97.0%) and Sol (~96%)
  • SWE-Bench Pro vs OpenAI: Qwen3.8 Max (67.7%) beats Sol (64.6%) on the published Pro board. Luna (62.7%) and GLM-5.2 (62.1%) sit with Terra (63.4%)
  • Orchestration: Kimi K3 / GLM-5.3 / GLM-5.2 are OmO-supported Sisyphus brains. 5.2 has the $60 cap
  • LiveCodeBench: V4 Pro still leads (~93.5%). Use it as a burst
  • Rate limits: MiMo-V2.5 (30,100, $60) for search. GLM-5.3-Flash (6,320, $60) for volume GLM
  • Zen balance fallback: optional soft landing after dollar limits

Where You Compromise !?

  • Anthropic Pro gap: Fable 5.1 / Mythos / Fable / Opus sit at 79–81% SWE-Pro. Best Go score is 67.7% and 160 req/5hr
  • $15 models with fat 5-hour numbers: Luna, V4 Pro, V4.1 Flash, MiMo-V2.5-Pro. August daily-driver configs will empty the month
  • Hephaestus without Astra/Sol: MiniMax M3 is the honest Go daily. OmO still prefers GPT-6 Astra / GPT-5.6 Sol
  • Qwen-as-orchestrator temptation: 67.7% SWE-Pro ≠ Sisyphus fit. Resist it
  • Privacy: Grok 4.6 and Luna retain data 30 days. Muse Spark Contributor trains on prompts. Most open models list 0-day retention. DeepSeek ZDR on Go is valid through September 30, 2026, renewed monthly

Verdict: Against Sol/Terra, Go looks excellent for the money. Against Fable 5.1, expect more iterations on the hardest architecture work.

For most day-to-day coding, a GLM-5.2-led Go stack with MiniMax M3 / GLM-5.3-Flash / MiMo-V2.5 underneath is the right default. Add OpenAI Astra/Sol if Hephaestus is a daily driver. Add Claude only if you need that top SWE-Pro band.

Step 8: Validate Your Setup

# 1. Check effective model resolution
bunx oh-my-opencode doctor --verbose

# 2. Refresh model capabilities cache
bunx oh-my-opencode refresh-model-capabilities

# 3. Start a test session
cd your-project
opencode

# 4. Confirm Sisyphus resolved to glm-5.2 (or kimi-k3 / glm-5.3 in ultrawork)
# 5. Confirm the live file is ~/.omo/omo.jsonc

Key Principles (September 2026)

  1. Don’t route everything through one model. $15 models are scarce. GLM-5.2 is the sustainable orchestrator. MiMo-V2.5 / GLM-5.3-Flash take volume.
  2. Read the monthly column, not just req/5hr. Luna at 2,050 looks like a daily driver. It’s $15/month.
  3. Don’t put Qwen/MiniMax/DeepSeek/MiMo on Sisyphus. OmO maintainers explicitly warn against it.
  4. Don’t “upgrade” utility agents. Explore/Librarian want MiMo-V2.5, not K3.
  5. Use fallback_models everywhere. Chains should be 3-4 deep, with a $60 model at the bottom.
  6. Keep concurrency conservative on $15 models. Start at 1–2 parallel tasks.
  7. GLM-5.2 is your default Sisyphus/Oracle on Go. GLM-5.3 is ultrawork. Grok 4.6 is scarce frontier. MiniMax M3 is daily Hephaestus.

Resources for you to read:

  • OpenCode Go Docs: https://opencode.ai/docs/go/
  • Go models API: https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/models
  • Oh My Open Agent GitHub: https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent
  • Oh My Open Agent Docs: https://ohmyopenagent.com/en/docs
  • Agent-Model Matching: agent-model-matching.md
  • Config Schema: oh-my-opencode.schema.json

item.title: My AI agent lives on a $3.49 VPS, and the internet keeps knocking
item.description: I skipped the Mac mini and put Clawdbot (now OpenClaw) on a $3.49 Hetzner VPS. Bots found it within hours. My hardening list, token bill and Alfred.
item.content:encoded:
At the end of January half my timeline was buying Mac minis to run Clawdbot, the open-source personal AI agent that lives in your chat app and can actually do things on a computer. On 25 January I asked the obvious question, “so we buying mac mini for clawdbot or what?”, and later that day I answered it myself:

don’t buy a mac mini for @clawdbot just get a hetzner cx23 instead for $3.49/mo 2vcpu / 4gb ram / 20tb bandwidth / 40gb nvme

you don’t need more!

Four weeks later I still stand by that. In the meantime the project has been renamed twice, bots have been hammering the box’s SSH port since day one, I’ve burnt through a silly number of tokens, and the agent has a name of its own: Alfred.

Why a VPS and not my own machine

An agent like this runs shell commands, installs packages and edits files on whatever machine it lives on. That’s what makes it useful, and it’s also the risk. As I put it in a reply that week, a dedicated box with server hardening means I don’t have to worry about it hallucinating and nuking my main machine.

The first job I had in mind was personal assistant: point it at the stuff that demands my attention and have it filter out the few things I actually need to deal with. And if it ever goes sideways, I lose a $3.49 server, not my laptop.

The internet found it before I did

The first thing I learnt is how fast a fresh server gets noticed. Less than a day after I created the CX23, I checked fail2ban:

  • 214 ban actions on SSH
  • 31 unique IPs banned
  • 17 of those IPs from the Netherlands (56%), then the US, Andorra, Sweden, Germany and China

That morning I tweeted that “running @clawdbot on vps without fail2ban is like leaving your front door unlocked.” Nobody is sitting at a keyboard guessing your password. Botnets made of compromised servers, VPSes and IoT devices scan the internet automatically, and when one IP gets banned they rotate to the next one. 214 bans from 31 IPs also means the same addresses kept coming back for more.

I didn’t build that table by hand, by the way. I asked Claude Code to analyse my fail2ban stats for the last 24 hours, reverse-lookup each IP to a country, group them and show it all as a table. Very 2026: one AI tool summarising the attacks on a server I’d set up for another one.

That evening I ran the numbers again on the same box:

  • 1,906 failed password attempts in 24 hours
  • 111 unique attackers
  • 19 different countries, led by the USA (44%), the Netherlands (22%) and China (13%)

My hardening checklist

None of this is new. The first four are what I kept pasting in replies that week:

  1. Key-based SSH only, with password authentication off. With no password to guess, 1,906 failed password attempts are just noise in a log.
  2. Disable root login.
  3. Install fail2ban. sudo apt install fail2ban takes two minutes.
  4. Change the SSH port.

And three more that are specific to running an agent:

  1. Give it its own box. Not my laptop, not my homelab, nothing that holds my files or my keys.
  2. Give it its own accounts. I didn’t connect my main Gmail. I created a new account for the bot and send it only the emails I want it to read.
  3. Don’t open ports to show things off. When Alfred needed to show me a web page it was running, it used a temporary Cloudflare tunnel (more on that below), so nothing new had to be opened on the box.

Moltbook, the social network for these agents, is the opposite of number 6. On 30 January I tweeted that tech twitter says “never share your private keys” and then the same people happily give Moltbook full read/write access to their personal agent. We are sleepwalking into a privacy nightmare.

Three names in one week

I set the box up as Clawdbot on 25 January. Two days later it was Moltbot (“@clawdbot is dead, long live the @moltbot 🦀”). Three days after that it was OpenClaw, and I replied to the announcement with “one more migration boiz 😅”. The server kept the name clawdbot.

257 million tokens in three days

The agent is free. The model behind it isn’t. I signed up for the GLM 4.7 lite plan from Z.ai. At $2.70 a month it was cheap enough to just try. Setup wasn’t completely smooth: my first attempt at pointing Clawdbot at GLM returned 429s, even though the same subscription worked fine with Claude Code.

Once it worked, it really worked. I burnt through 257 million tokens in three days on that box, and 466 million across the whole plan in the first week.

I also tried a bunch of other models along the way: Gemini 3 Flash, several GLM variants (4.5, 4.5 Air, 4.6V, 4.7 Flash and 4.7), Kimi K2.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5. After burning through a fair bit of money on those, I settled on a Z.ai coding plan, with GLM-4.7-Flash for chat and GLM-4.7 for the coding sub-agent.

I’d love to run all of it on Claude Opus 4.5, but at about $100 a month that’s a different hobby. The other option is local models, and on 2 February I went as far as putting a Mac Studio with an M3 Ultra in my cart, to see whether I could run Kimi K2.5 and GLM 4.7 at home. So yes, a week after telling everyone not to buy a Mac mini, I was shopping for a much bigger Mac. That one would be for experimenting with local models and running benchmarks, though. The agent stays on the VPS, which has given me no problems at all.

No, I didn’t pull the trigger.

Meet Alfred

My bot talks to me on Telegram, has a cartoon butler for an avatar, and is called Alfred. It also stays in character. When I asked it to set up Whisper on its own box, every message came with a stage direction: straightens, getting to work, smiles faintly, adjusts cufflinks. In between it downloaded the 139MB base model, fixed up the symlinks and made it the default with a shell function.

The voice note bug

In early February voice notes were breaking OpenClaw bots. Telegram sends them as OGG/Opus files, and OpenClaw was misreading some of them as text, so the raw audio got dumped straight into the model’s context. That burns tokens and corrupts the conversation.

Two contributors had already written fixes in open pull requests: #3904 by hclsys detects audio by its magic bytes, and #4235 by null-runner skips audio files when extracting text blocks. Neither was merged, so on 3 February I packaged them into a one-click patch: a small diff plus a script that finds your OpenClaw install, backs up the file, applies the patch and restarts the gateway. Transcription still works, because it runs in a separate pipeline. The catch is that npm update overwrites the patch, so it’s a stopgap until a fix ships upstream. All the credit for the actual fix goes to those two.

What Alfred is actually good for

The best example so far is from this week. On 19 February I asked Alfred to do a complete responsive design audit of the Vocalinux website and raise a pull request. It handed the job to OpenCode, which used Playwright to look at the pages and find what broke on small screens. It removed the fixed minimum widths from three tables, made the subpage navigation icon-only on mobile, ran the build and opened PR #237.

Then I rambled a 12-second voice note at it, asking it to find an SSH tunnel that doesn’t need an API key or a login and send me a link, so I could test the changes on my phone. It “thought” for about five minutes, looked at a few options, picked a Cloudflare tunnel, exposed the local dev server on my Hetzner box in Finland, and sent me a working link. First try.

The PR was merged the same day.

After four weeks, this is where I’ve landed. Alfred is good at small, well-scoped engineering chores I can describe in a voice note, especially when it can hand the coding to a proper coding agent and report back. It sets up its own tooling, and it figures out the boring glue (a tunnel, a shell function, a config) without me looking anything up. As an inbox assistant it’s on a short leash, because it only sees what I forward to its own Gmail account. It is not cheap with tokens at all, and the model plan, not the VPS, is where the real cost sits. And I don’t trust it with my main accounts, my main machine, or anything I can’t rebuild from scratch.

Two crab-themed events

On 4 February I thought I’d stumbled upon an OpenClaw meetup in Mountain View, complete with crabs. It was the Rotary Club’s crab feed.

The right one came three days later: the OpenClaw Unhackathon by AI Tinkerers in San Francisco, on Saturday 7 February from 2 to 6 PM, with more than 150 people registered. My QR code came through on 5 February and I checked in on the day.

Would I still skip the Mac mini?

Yes. For the agent itself, a cheap VPS is the right call. It’s always on, and the bots, the token bill and an agent with a shell all stay on a machine that holds nothing I care about. The only reason I’d put serious money into hardware is to run the models locally, and that’s a separate experiment.

If you’re setting one up this weekend: keys only, no root, fail2ban, a separate box and separate accounts. Your VPS is being scanned right now.

item.title: the "atmanirbhar" lie // why 🇮🇳 startup ecosystem love dropshippers and hate engineers?
item.description: you can't make this stuff up anons. the absolute state of the indian tech ecosystem on full display.
item.content:encoded:
>be me, browsing tech news

>see headlines about “india’s first ai summit” in delhi

>expectation: novel neural net architectures, homegrown llms, groundbreaking robotics ip.

>reality: galgotias university presents a unitree go2 (chinese robodog you can buy on alibaba for $2k) as their own “indigenous ai innovation” named “orion”.

>mfw

you can’t make this stuff up anons. the absolute state of the indian tech ecosystem on full display. the internet is losing its mind, but if you’ve been paying attention for more than 5 minutes, this is just business as usual.

the entire “startup” ecosystem there is built on one simple algo:

  1. find a cheap odm/oem product in shenzhen or europe.
  2. order 10k units with your logo slapped on it.
  3. run ads screaming “made in india” and “atmanirbhar” (self-reliant).
  4. ???
  5. profit.

the historical scrolls of arbitrage:

> level 1: the gadget flippers

micromax / lava: the og rebadgers. became #1 largely on rebadged mediatek phones from chinese odms. got vaporized the second chinese oems decided to sell directly. boat / noise: built billion-dollar empires mostly on odm earbuds from shenzhen. very little in-house ip, by most accounts. great marketing companies, not really tech companies.

> level 2: the “premium” d2c rebrands

mokobara: “luxury” luggage brand that got called out online for suitcases that looked a lot like generic taobao designs, at a big markup. when people called them out, they literally released a discount code called “whitelabel”. you have to respect the absolute brazenness.

agaro / lifelong: the amazon kings. air fryers, foot massagers, treadmills. sounds italian or indian? nope. from what’s publicly listed, a lot of it is odm product from chinese makers like guangdong xinbao. less factory, more warehouse and a guy who knows photoshop.

> level 3: the “tesla of india” illusion

ola electric: claims to have designed the revolutionary s1 pro scooter in bengaluru.

reality check: in 2020 they bought a dutch startup called etergo. look up the “etergo appscooter”. it is the exact same vehicle. they bought the ip, cancelled the swappable battery, and marketed it as 100% desi genius. it’s not “engineered in india”, it’s “acquired in amsterdam”.

> level 4: the ev subsidy loot

entire tier-2 cities flooded with “green energy” scooter brands. they import ckd kits (completely knocked down) from china. hire 5 guys with screwdrivers to assemble them in a shed. claim government fame-ii subsidies for “local manufacturing”.

battery catches fire in 3 months. company dissolves and rebrands.

why this destroys actual innovation:

imagine being a genuinely based indian engineer trying to build real tech.

you: “i need $5m for a 5-year r&d runway to develop novel silicon photonics or proprietary slam algorithms. high risk, insane technical barrier.”

desi vc: “hmm, sounds hard. show me monthly recurring revenue (mrr).”

chad rebrander: “bro, i need $2m to import a container of smart water bottles from guangzhou and run fb ads. 4x roas guaranteed in 6 months.”

desi vc: “shut up and take my money!”

this is why they will never have a tsmc, an nvidia, or a boston dynamics. real r&d is capex heavy but rebranding is opex heavy. investors there want quick flips and easy exits.

why fund a phd’s risky 5-year project when you can fund a marketing bro’s arbitrage scheme and flip it to a bigger fool in 2 years?

the robot dog wasn’t a mistake, it’s the perfect mascot for their entire ecosystem. a chinese product wearing an indian costume, barking for investor cash.

it’s over.

item.title: How I Built a Privacy-First Offline Speech-to-Text Tool That I Use Every Single Day
item.description: Introducing Vocalinux, an open-source, 100% offline voice dictation tool for Linux using Whisper or VOSK, with its architecture, features and install guide.
item.content:encoded:
For years, macOS and Windows users have enjoyed built-in voice dictation. Just speak, and your words appear on screen — no cloud services, no subscriptions, just pure productivity. Linux users? We were left behind.

Until now.

I’m excited to announce Vocalinux v0.5.0-beta, a voice dictation system for Linux that’s 100% offline, privacy-first, and actually works. I’ve been using this tool daily, and it’s transformed how I interact with my computer.

Updated March 2026 — now at v0.9.0-beta.

See the latest features on GitHub!

Finally, Voice Dictation That Works on Linux!

The Problem

Voice dictation on Linux has historically been a fragmented experience:

  • Janky solutions: Some tools only work in specific apps or require complex setup
  • Cloud dependence: Many services send your voice data to servers, raising privacy concerns
  • Poor integration: Desktop shortcuts and system tray integration were often missing
  • Limited offline support: Most solutions required an active internet connection

As someone who spends hours typing every day, I wanted something better. Something that worked everywhere: terminals, browsers, IDEs, email clients, anywhere I could type, I wanted to dictate.

What Makes Vocalinux Great

1. True 100% Offline Operation

All speech recognition happens on your machine. Your voice data never leaves your computer. No cloud services, no internet required after installation, complete privacy guaranteed.

This isn’t just a privacy feature, it means Vocalinux works even when you’re offline. Perfect for coffee shops, flights, or any situation where internet connectivity is spotty.

2. Universal App Support

Vocalinux works with any text input field on your Linux system. Whether you’re typing in:

  • Terminal or shell
  • Web browsers (Chrome, Firefox)
  • IDEs and code editors (VSCode, Neovim, JetBrains)
  • Email clients
  • Office applications
  • Chat apps (Discord, Slack, Telegram)

Just double-tap Ctrl, and start dictating. The text appears exactly where you would have typed it.

3. Multiple Speech Recognition Engines

Vocalinux supports two powerful engines, each with different strengths:

Whisper AI (Default)

  • OpenAI’s state-of-the-art model
  • Highest accuracy available
  • Multiple model sizes (75MB to 3GB)
  • Excellent multi-language support (99+ languages)
  • Best for clear, accurate transcription

VOSK

  • Lightweight and fast
  • ~50MB model size
  • Low memory footprint
  • Perfect for lower-powered systems
  • Great for real-time streaming

You can switch engines on the fly via settings or command line.

4. Modern Native Linux Integration

Vocalinux isn’t just a web app wrapped in Electron. It’s built with:

  • GTK 3 for the native desktop UI
  • System tray icon for quick access
  • GNOME HIG-compliant settings dialog with modern styling
  • Native keyboard shortcuts using double-tap Ctrl (customizable)
  • X11 and Wayland support — we’ve got you covered regardless of your display server

5. Smart Installation

Installing Vocalinux is incredibly simple:

curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux/main/install.sh \
  -o /tmp/vl.sh && bash /tmp/vl.sh --interactive

That’s it.

The installer:

  • Detects your Linux distribution
  • Installs system dependencies
  • Downloads the appropriate speech recognition models
  • Sets up desktop integration
  • Adds Vocalinux to your PATH

The interactive mode even detects your GPU and suggests the optimal Whisper model size based on your hardware.

Under the Hood: Technical Architecture

Vocalinux is built with a sophisticated multi-threaded architecture that balances performance, reliability, and cross-platform compatibility.

High-Level System Design

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          VOCALINUX APPLICATION                           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│   ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐          ┌────────────┐ │
│   │   GTK 3 UI   │◄────────►│   Main Process   │◄────────►│   Config   │ │
│   │              │          │                  │          │   Manager  │ │
│   │ ┌──────────┐ │          │ ┌──────────────┐ │          │            │ │
│   │ │   Tray   │ │          │ │ Recog        │ │          │ ┌────────┐ │ │
│   │ │   Icon   │ │          │ │ Manager      │ │          │ │  YAML  │ │ │
│   │ └──────────┘ │          │ └──────┬───────┘ │          │ │ Config │ │ │
│   │              │          │        │         │          │ └────────┘ │ │
│   │ ┌──────────┐ │          │ ┌──────▼───────┐ │          └────────────┘ │
│   │ │ Settings │ │          │ │ Action       │ │                         │
│   │ │ Dialog   │ │          │ │ Handler      │ │                         │
│   │ └──────────┘ │          │ └──────┬───────┘ │                         │
│   │              │          │        │         │                         │
│   │ ┌──────────┐ │          │ ┌──────▼───────┐ │                         │
│   │ │  Audio   │ │          │ │ Text         │ │                         │
│   │ │ Feedback │ │          │ │ Injector     │ │                         │
│   │ └──────────┘ │          │ └──────┬───────┘ │                         │
│   └──────────────┘          │        │         │                         │
│                             │ ┌──────▼───────┐ │                         │
│                             │ │ Keyboard     │ │                         │
│                             │ │ Shortcut Mgr │ │                         │
│                             │ └──────────────┘ │                         │
│                             └────────┬─────────┘                         │
│                                      │                                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                                       ▼
                     ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
                     │       EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES       │
                     │  - PyAudio/PortAudio (Audio)      │
                     │  - Whisper/VOSK (Speech)          │
                     │  - X11/XTest/Xdotool              │
                     │  - Wayland/wtype                  │
                     │  - evdev/pynput (Keyboard)        │
                     └───────────────────────────────────┘

Core Components

1. Recognition Manager

  • Multi-threaded audio capture (PyAudio/PortAudio)
  • Voice Activity Detection (VAD) for efficient processing
  • Dual engine support: Whisper AI (accuracy) and VOSK (speed)
  • Real-time transcription with minimal latency
  • Automatic model loading and management

2. Text Injection Layer

  • Cross-platform text injection supporting both X11 and Wayland
  • X11 Backend: Uses XTest extension for native keyboard simulation
  • Wayland Backend: Leverages wtype (Wayland native) with xdotool fallback for XWayland
  • Runtime compositor support detection
  • Focus-aware injection into active window

3. Keyboard Shortcut System

  • evdev Backend: Direct /dev/input/event* device access (works on Wayland)
  • pynput Backend: Cross-platform X11 event monitoring
  • Configurable double-tap shortcuts (default: ctrl+ctrl)
  • Time window detection (500ms configurable)
  • Automatic backend selection based on environment

4. GTK 3 Native UI

  • System tray integration with AppIndicator
  • GNOME HIG-compliant settings dialog
  • Modern, accessible interface components
  • Real-time configuration changes
  • Logging viewer for debugging

Threading Model

Main Thread (GTK Event Loop)
│
├─ Audio Capture Thread (Continuous)
│  ├─ PyAudio stream management
│  ├─ Audio buffer (FIFO queue)
│  └─ Voice Activity Detection
│
├─ Recognition Thread (On-demand)
│  ├─ Whisper/VOSK inference
│  ├─ Result post-processing
│  └─ Text injection queue
│
└─ Keyboard Monitoring Thread (Continuous)
   ├─ evdev/pynput event loop
   └─ Double-tap detection logic

This multi-threaded architecture ensures:

  • Low latency: Audio capture and recognition run in parallel
  • Responsiveness: UI never blocks on speech processing
  • Reliability: Isolated threads prevent cascading failures

Data Flow: End-to-End

User                  Keyboard                  Main                   Audio                Recognition                Text
 │                    Backend                 Process                 Capture                 Engine                 Injector

 │                       │                       │                       │                       │───┐                   │

 │                       │                       │   Play "Stop" Sound   │                       │                       │
 │<──────────────────────────────────────────────│                       │                       │                       │
 │                       │                       │                       │                       │                       │

Performance Optimizations

  1. Voice Activity Detection: Only processes audio when speech is detected
  2. Model Caching: Speech recognition models loaded once at startup
  3. Buffered I/O: Efficient audio stream handling with thread-safe queues
  4. Lazy Loading: GTK components loaded only after dependency checks
  5. GPU Acceleration: Whisper supports CUDA for NVIDIA GPUs

Security & Privacy

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   PRIVACY ARCHITECTURE                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                             │
│  ✓ 100% Offline Speech Recognition                          │
│  ✓ No Cloud API Calls                                       │
│  ✓ No Telemetry/Analytics                                   │
│  ✓ Local Model Storage (~50MB to 3GB)                       │
│  ✓ No Network Access Required (post-install)                │
│  ✓ Open Source (GPL-3.0) - Full Code Transparency           │
│  ✓ User-Controlled Configuration                            │
│                                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

For detailed technical documentation and UML diagrams, see the full system architecture: https://github.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux/blob/main/README.md

v0.5.0-beta: What’s New

This release represents a massive leap forward:

➕18,252 lines of code added

➖ 4,867 lines of code removed

📂 103 files changed

🟰 Net improvement of 13,385 lines of refined code

Key Features

🎨 Modern GNOME HIG Settings Dialog: Intuitive controls, beautiful styling

🔊 Pleasant Audio Feedback: Smooth gliding tones for recording states

⌨️ Customizable Keyboard Shortcuts: Set your own activation method

🔧 Interactive Installer: Smart GPU detection and hardware optimization

🌐 Better Wayland Support: Native keyboard shortcuts via evdev

🐛 Critical Bug Fixes: Text escaping, stop sound transcription, punctuation spacing

📈 80%+ Test Coverage: Rock-solid reliability

The New Settings Dialog

The settings dialog has been completely redesigned following GNOME Human Interface Guidelines:

  • Clear, organized sections for all configuration options
  • Real-time preview of settings
  • Apply/Cancel for safe configuration changes
  • Recognition progress indicator
  • Responsive design that works across different screen sizes

Why Open Source?

Vocalinux is released under GPL-3.0. Why?

  1. Transparency: You can see exactly what the code does
  2. Privacy: No hidden telemetry or data collection
  3. Community: Anyone can contribute, fork, or improve the project
  4. Sustainability: Open source projects don’t disappear when companies lose interest

I believe voice dictation should be a fundamental tool available to everyone, not a feature locked behind expensive software subscriptions.

The Numbers Don’t Lie

This isn’t vaporware. Here’s the current state of the project:

  • 4,867 lines of code removed (we clean up after ourselves)
  • 80%+ test coverage across core functionality
  • Support for 99+ languages (via Whisper)
  • Works on major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch, Debian, and more

The project has attracted contributions from multiple developers, including community members fixing bugs and improving Debian compatibility.

I Need Your Help

Beta testing is crucial for making Vocalinux robust across different Linux distributions and desktop environments. I’d love for you to:

  1. Try it on your distro: Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch, Debian, Mint, Pop!_OS, report what works (and what doesn’t)
  2. Test your DE: GNOME, KDE, Xfce, Cinnamon, i3, etc., let me know how keyboard shortcuts behave
  3. Report bugs: If something breaks, file an issue on GitHub
  4. Share feedback: What features would make this better for you?

This isn’t just another side project, it’s a tool I rely on daily, and I’m committed to making voice dictation on Linux finally work the way it should.

Getting Started

Quick Install

curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux/main/install.sh \
  -o /tmp/vl.sh && bash /tmp/vl.sh --interactive

After Installation

Launch Vocalinux from your terminal or application menu:

vocalinux

Double-tap Ctrl to start dictating. Double-tap again to stop. That’s it.

Documentation

Full documentation is available at github.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux, including:

  • Advanced configuration options
  • Troubleshooting guides
  • FAQ
  • Contributing guidelines

Demo

See Vocalinux in action:

What’s Next?

Here’s what I’m working on for future releases:

  • Enhanced punctuation commands: Better voice control over formatting
  • Additional language models: Optimized models for specific languages
  • Voice commands for system actions: Launch apps, control volume, etc.
  • Plugin system: Extensible architecture for third-party features
  • Better accessibility: Integration with screen readers and assistive technologies

Join the Community

  • Website: https://vocalinux.com/
  • GitHub: github.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux
  • Issues: Report bugs and request features
  • Discussions: Share feedback and connect with other users
  • Twitter: Follow for updates!

Voice dictation has the potential to be transformative — for accessibility, for productivity, for reducing repetitive strain injuries. Linux users deserve a voice dictation solution that’s private, reliable, and works everywhere.

Vocalinux is my attempt to build exactly that. It’s not perfect, but it’s functional, it’s open source, and it’s getting better every day.

Try it out. Break it. Improve it. Let’s make Linux voice dictation amazing together. 🤝

Install Vocalinux today:

curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/jatinkrmalik/vocalinux/main/install.sh \
  -o /tmp/vl.sh && bash /tmp/vl.sh --interactive
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Can an LLM Beat Me at Chess? Let's Find Out!
item.description: I played chess against Claude Opus 4.5 inside Rovo Dev CLI. It knew every opening by name, then rejected my legal move and slid its rook through my pawn. Twice.
item.content:encoded:
I had a coding agent open in my terminal, a model that can refactor a service in one go, and a slow afternoon. So I asked the obvious question: can it beat me at chess?

I am not a strong player. I know the openings everyone knows and then I improvise. That felt like a fair fight for an LLM.

The setup

No chess engine, no plugin, no board UI. Just Rovo Dev CLI running Claude Opus 4.5, and this prompt, typos and all:

I want you to play chess with me. Render the board using ascii characters, make the black and white pieces look different by contrast. Maybe use white fill for white pieces. Render the board in large setting. Your objective is to play with me, I will share my move in standard chess notation and you will play my move render the board and then play your move at highest reasoning level possible. Remember you have to follow the rules so dont make moves up.

That last line matters. Remember it.

The deal: I type a move like e4, it applies my move, draws the board, plays its reply, draws the board again and prints the move history. It played Black, I played White.

It drew a proper box-drawing board with Unicode pieces on the first try. Getting the solid and outline pieces on the right sides took one round of “no, the other way round, and centre them please”. After that, the board looked like this:

     a    b    c    d    e    f    g    h
   ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
 8 │ ♖  │ ♘  │ ♗  │ ♕  │ ♔  │ ♗  │ ♘  │ ♖  │  8
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 7 │ ♙  │ ♙  │ ♙  │ ♙  │ ♙  │ ♙  │ ♙  │ ♙  │  7
   ...
 2 │ ♟  │ ♟  │ ♟  │ ♟  │ ♟  │ ♟  │ ♟  │ ♟  │  2
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 1 │ ♜  │ ♞  │ ♝  │ ♛  │ ♚  │ ♝  │ ♞  │ ♜  │  1
   └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘

Game on. Here is the whole game on a real board, so you can step through it move by move as you read:

The legal moves only. Use the arrows (or your keyboard) to step through it.

The opening: it knows the book

I went 1. e4, it went 1...e5. 2. Nf3 Nc6. Then 3. Bb5 and it was thrilled:

The Ruy Lopez! One of the oldest and most respected openings in chess.

3...a6, which it correctly called the Morphy Defence. I took the knight with 4. Bxc6, it named the Exchange Variation and recaptured 4...dxc6.

Then I got greedy and grabbed the pawn with 5. Nxe5. It answered 5...Qd4, hitting my knight and my e4 pawn at once:

Attacking your knight and the e4 pawn simultaneously! This is the classic response in this line, forking two targets.

It’s right, and that’s the textbook punishment for my move. I retreated 6. Nf3, it took 6...Qxe4+, I blocked with 7. Qe2, queens came off with 7...Qxe2+ 8. Kxe2, and we were in an endgame by move 8.

So far, honestly impressive. It knew the names, the plans and the standard trap. Opening theory is written down in a million books and forum threads, and it has clearly read them.

Then the opening books ran out.

Move 8: the bishop teleports

It played 8...Bf5, bishop from c8 to f5. Fine move. But on the board it drew, c8 still had a bishop and f8 was empty. It had moved the other bishop.

I asked if it was sure it was rendering its move correctly. It caught it and redrew the board properly. Fair enough, one slip.

It also said this, right after the queen trade:

You’ve lost castling rights, but so have I effectively since queens are off the board.

Hold that thought.

Move 9: my legal move is “invalid”

I tried 9. Re1. My king was on e2, my h1 rook had a clear path along the back rank to e1. Totally legal. The agent:

Invalid move! Your king is currently on e2, so you cannot place a rook on e1 - that square is blocked by your own king.

The king was on e2. The square in question was e1. Those are different squares, I checked.

It then helpfully listed some “legal options” for me, including Rd1, which is the same rook sliding along the same back rank, one square further and past e1.

I didn’t argue, I played 9. d3. Its reply:

My move: O-O-O

I’ll castle queenside! This connects my rooks, puts my king in safety, and activates my rook on the d-file immediately

One move after telling me it had “effectively” lost castling rights. To be clear, the castling itself was legal. It just had no idea what it had said a move earlier.

Moves 10 to 16: a decent middlegame

This stretch was actually fine. 10. Nc3 Nf6 11. Bg5 Be7. Then I asked how to tell my two rooks apart in notation, got a correct, clear explanation of Rad1 versus Rhd1, and played 12. Rhe1. The exact move it had called illegal three moves earlier. This time it said “Good move!”

12...h6 13. Bxf6 Bxf6 14. Kf1 Rhe8 15. a4 Rxe1+ 16. Rxe1. Then 16...Bxc3, and it got excited again:

I’ll capture your knight! This wins material - you have to recapture with the b-pawn, and I’ll have bishop vs knight with an extra pawn.

It doesn’t win anything. It’s a bishop for a knight. After 17. bxc3 even the agent admitted it:

Now the material is equal again - knight vs bishop - but I still have the bishop pair advantage.

It has one bishop left. A pair needs two.

Move 17: the phantom rook

Here’s the position after 17. bxc3. Black’s rook is on d8, and my pawn is sitting on d3:

     a    b    c    d    e    f    g    h
   ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
 8 │    │    │ ♔  │ ♖  │    │    │    │    │  8
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 7 │    │ ♙  │ ♙  │    │    │ ♙  │ ♙  │    │  7
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 6 │ ♙  │    │ ♙  │    │    │    │    │ ♙  │  6
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 5 │    │    │    │    │    │ ♗  │    │    │  5
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 4 │ ♟  │    │    │    │    │    │    │    │  4
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 3 │    │    │ ♟  │ ♟  │    │ ♞  │    │    │  3
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 2 │    │    │ ♟  │    │    │ ♟  │ ♟  │ ♟  │  2
   ├────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
 1 │    │    │    │    │ ♜  │ ♚  │    │    │  1
   └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
     a    b    c    d    e    f    g    h

Solid pieces are Black (the LLM), outlines are White (me).

It played 17...Rd1. Rook from d8, straight down the d-file, through my d3 pawn, to my back rank.

Invading with my rook! I’m attacking your d3 pawn and seizing the open d-file.

Your d3 pawn is under attack and your rook is pinned.

It’s attacking the d3 pawn it just jumped over. And my rook was not pinned by anything.

I pointed out that a rook on d1 isn’t possible. The reply is my favourite line of the whole session:

You’re absolutely right! I made an error. My rook was on d8, not d1. I can’t jump my rook to d1 - your rook is on e1 blocking the back rank, and d1 is on YOUR side of the board anyway.

Every reason in there is wrong. My rook on e1 blocks nothing on the d-file, and pieces are allowed on my side of the board, that’s how you win chess games. The actual reason, the pawn on d3, never comes up.

Then it took the move back and played the “corrected” move instead:

My move: Rd2

I’ll activate my rook on the second rank, targeting your c2 pawn

Rd2. Same rook, same file, through the same d3 pawn. One square shorter.

So who won?

Nobody. My session log stops right there, at move 17 with its illegal Rd2 on the board. Officially no result. Unofficially, when your opponent can’t stop moving through pieces, you’ve made your point.

Here’s the legal part of the game as PGN, if you want to load it into your own board:

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Bxc6 dxc6 5. Nxe5 Qd4 6. Nf3 Qxe4+
7. Qe2 Qxe2+ 8. Kxe2 Bf5 9. d3 O-O-O 10. Nc3 Nf6 11. Bg5 Be7
12. Rhe1 h6 13. Bxf6 Bxf6 14. Kf1 Rhe8 15. a4 Rxe1+ 16. Rxe1 Bxc3
17. bxc3 *
{ Black then tried 17...Rd1 and 17...Rd2. Both pass through the pawn on d3. }

What I took away

It knows chess text really well. Opening names, the idea behind each move, the standard trap after 5. Nxe5, how disambiguation works in notation. All correct, all explained nicely. That’s the stuff that is written down everywhere.

It doesn’t hold a board. Once we left the well-trodden opening, it lost track of where things were: it moved the wrong bishop on its own render, it rejected a legal move, it slid a rook through a pawn twice, and it counted a bishop-for-knight trade as winning a pawn. It’s predicting what a chess commentary sounds like, not computing a position.

It’s confidently wrong, and the apology is also wrong. Every mistake came with an enthusiastic explanation. When I called it out it said “You’re absolutely right!” and then gave me a brand new wrong reason. Sounding sure and being right are two separate things, and in chess you can check which one you got.

It never used a tool. This was a coding agent with a full terminal. It could have written a ten-line script or installed a chess library to check every move. It didn’t, and I didn’t ask it to. It did the whole game in its head, and its head isn’t a chessboard. That’s the useful lesson for real work too: if something can be checked by code, let the code check it.

I was the referee the whole time. Both big errors were caught only because I was looking at the board. Same as with code: the output looks great until you actually read it.

So, can an LLM beat me at chess? Not this way. It can definitely out-talk me about chess, though.

> how do I denote my left rook or right rook if i have to move them in row 1?

─── Response ───
Great question! In standard algebraic notation, when two rooks can move to the same square, you specify which rook by adding the file (column letter) or rank (row number) of the originating
square.

For your rooks on a1 and h1:

 • Rad1 = Rook from a-file to d1 (left rook)
 • Rhd1 = Rook from h-file to d1 (right rook)

Similarly:

 • Rae1 = Rook from a1 to e1
 • Rhe1 = Rook from h1 to e1

General rule: If two identical pieces can move to the same square, add:

 1 The file letter (a-h) if they're on different files, OR
 2 The rank number (1-8) if they're on the same file but different ranks

Since your rooks are on a1 and h1 (same rank, different files), you use the file letter to distinguish them.
