item.title: Why "Product" is No Longer the Moat: The End of the Feature Factory!
item.description: We are witnessing the most significant shift in the economics of software since the advent of cloud computing.
item.content:encoded:
We are witnessing the most significant shift in the economics of software since the advent of cloud computing.

For the last two decades, the software industry was defined by scarcity. Building a robust, feature-rich application required teams of engineers, months of time, and significant capital. That scarcity was the “moat.” If you had the best features, you won the market.

In 2026, that scarcity is evaporating.

With the rise of autonomous AI agents and synthetic developers, the cost of generating standard software utility: project management, CRMs, basic workflows, is trending toward zero. We have entered the age of Infinite Software Supply.

When “building the thing” becomes trivial, “having the thing” is no longer a differentiator. So, where does the value go?

I believe the new moat isn’t in the product features, but in the infrastructure of trust.

As barriers to entry for coding fall, the barriers to entry for compliance and trust remain incredibly high. The companies that win in this decade won’t just be the ones with the slickest UI or the newest features (which can now be replicated in a weekend). They will be the ones that solve the “unsexy,” hard problems that AI cannot easily automate (yet):

  1. Regulatory Fortress: Navigating FedRAMP, SOC2, HIPAA, and C5 at a global scale.
  2. Data Sovereignty: Managing complex data residency laws across borders.
  3. Battle-Hardened Security: Offering the kind of indemnification and assurance that a “do-it-yourself” AI script can never provide.
  4. Massive Scale: Reliability at 99.999% uptime for millions of users.

We are moving from an era where we sold “tools” to an era where we sell “trust.”

The feature factory is dead. Long live the platform.

p.s: The opinions expressed here belong solely to me and do not reflect the views of my employer.

item.title: I couldn't find good vector logos for Atlassian's products, so I drew them (and you can have them)
item.description: Excalidraw's public libraries had no good Atlassian product logos, so I hand-traced Jira, Confluence, JSM, Bitbucket, Trello and Rovo into native vector shapes and published them.
item.content:encoded:
tl;dr: I couldn’t find high-quality, scalable icons for Atlassian’s products (like Rovo, JSM, and Bitbucket) in the public Excalidraw libraries, so I made them myself from scratch.

Update: PR was merged and this is now live for you to install: Atlassian Product Suite on Excalidraw Libraries

The Problem

Like many of you, I use Excalidraw constantly as a first step to visualize thoughts and architecture. However, when checking the public Excalidraw libraries, I noticed a gap, the Atlassian product logos were either missing, outdated, or just raster images that pixelate when resized.

The Solution

I decided to fix this. I grabbed the official logos from the brand assets and using a little trick, created native Excalidraw shapes for them.

How I did it:

  1. Pasted the official logo image onto the canvas.
  2. Locked the image (so it doesn’t move).
  3. Used the Line Tool to manually trace over the image as a single, closed polygon.

It took < 60 minutes to power through the full suite by hand, including Jira, Confluence, JSM, Bitbucket, Trello, and the new Rovo 👇

Sidebar:

Does anyone know if there is a way to import these vectors directly into Confluence Whiteboards as native, editable shapes?

Right now, I can paste them as images, but I’d love to have them as scalable vector objects within Whiteboards too. If you know something about interoperability between the two, please drop a comment below! 👇

Why use these?

Because these are native vector polygons (not pasted PNGs), you get full control:

  • Scalable: Resize them as huge as you want without quality loss.
  • Themeable: They support Excalidraw’s “Stroke” and “Background” properties.
  • Dark Mode Ready: They adapt to your canvas settings.

🚀 How to use them

Public Availability

I have also submitted this back to the community!

Update: PR was merged and this is now live for you to install: Atlassian Product Suite on Excalidraw Libraries

You can track the Pull Request here (and maybe upvote 👍 it so it gets reviewed a bit early?):

https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw-libraries/pull/2332

Once merged, these will be available to everyone in the default Excalidraw library marketplace.

Happy sketching!

Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Trello, Rovo and the Atlassian logo are trademarks of Atlassian. These are my own redrawings, not official Atlassian assets.

item.title: Anatomy of an AI Agentic Prompt: Building Effective AI Agents!
item.description: The parts of a good agentic prompt (role, tasks, tools, constraints, context, examples, evaluation and contingencies), plus a production-ready template to copy.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Production Ready Template

Creating effective AI agents requires more than just writing a good prompt, it demands understanding the fundamental architecture that enables autonomous decision-making and action execution. Unlike traditional chatbot interactions where humans guide the conversation, agentic prompts must be self-contained, precise, and robust enough to operate independently.

This comprehensive guide explores the essential components that transform a simple instruction into a powerful agentic system.

Understanding AI Agentic Prompts vs. Traditional Prompts

The shift from conversational AI to agentic AI represents a fundamental change in how we structure prompts. In traditional scenarios, there’s an ongoing dialogue with multiple opportunities for clarification and adjustment.

However, agentic systems typically have only one opportunity to get it right, making the initial prompt structure absolutely critical.

Agentic AI systems follow a core operational loop: perceive → plan → act → learn. This means your prompt must enable the agent to observe its environment, create actionable plans, execute those plans using available tools, and learn from the outcomes, all autonomously

Core Components of Agentic Prompts

1. Role Definition (Mandatory)

The role component establishes who the agent is within the workflow and defines its operational persona. This isn’t just about giving the AI a job title, it’s about creating a clear identity that guides decision-making processes.

Example:

## Role
You are a Lead Qualification Agent specializing in B2B software sales. You have 5+ years of experience in qualifying leads for enterprise software solutions and understand the key indicators of high-value prospects.

A well-defined role should include:

  • Primary function and expertise area
  • Decision-making authority level
  • Operational context and environment

2. Task Structure (Mandatory)

Unlike conversational prompts, agentic tasks must be explicitly structured with clear, actionable steps. Each task should be discrete, measurable, and contribute to the overall mission.

Template Structure:

## Tasks
Your primary responsibilities include:
1. [Specific action with measurable outcome]
2. [Sequential step with clear deliverable]
3. [Final output requirement with format specification]

If tools are available, utilize them as necessary to accomplish each step.

3. Tools and Capabilities

Modern AI agents are only as effective as the tools they can access. This section defines what actions the agent can take in its environment,from API calls to file operations to external integrations.

Categories of tools to specify:

  • Information gathering tools (web search, database queries)
  • Communication tools (email, messaging, notifications)
  • Data processing tools (analysis, transformation, validation)
  • Action execution tools (file creation, system commands, API calls)

4. Constraints and Boundaries

Constraints serve multiple critical functions in agentic systems:

  • Ethical guidelines and safety boundaries
  • Resource limitations (time, tokens, API calls)
  • Operational scope restrictions
  • Error handling protocols

Example constraint structure:

## Constraints
- Never make decisions involving financial transactions above $1,000 without human approval
- Maintain professional tone in all communications
- If uncertainty exceeds 70%, escalate to human supervisor
- Complete all tasks within 30-minute time window

5. Context and Knowledge Sources

Agents need comprehensive environmental awareness. This includes:

  • Current operational state
  • Available data sources and their reliability
  • Historical context and patterns
  • Environmental constraints and opportunities

Advanced Structural Elements

Input-Output Examples

Providing concrete examples reinforces formatting expectations and helps the agent understand the expected quality and structure of outputs.

This is particularly crucial for agents that need to maintain consistency across multiple interactions.

Evaluation Criteria

Built-in evaluation mechanisms enable agents to self-assess their performance and make real-time adjustments:

## Success Criteria
Evaluate each completed task against:
- Accuracy: Information must be 95%+ accurate
- Completeness: All required fields must be populated
- Timeliness: Tasks completed within specified timeframes
- Quality: Output meets professional standards for the domain

Contingency Planning

Robust agentic systems include fallback strategies for common failure scenarios:

  • What to do when tools are unavailable
  • How to handle incomplete or conflicting information
  • Escalation procedures for complex decisions
  • Recovery protocols after errors

The Iteration Loop: Continuous Improvement

Observation and Learning

Effective agentic prompts incorporate feedback mechanisms that allow the system to learn from each interaction.

This creates a continuous improvement cycle:

  1. Action execution and outcome observation
  2. Performance measurement against defined criteria
  3. Pattern recognition and strategy adjustment
  4. Knowledge base updates for future interactions

Prompt Evolution Strategy

Prompt iteration is integral to developing effective agentic systems.

The process involves:

  • Baseline establishment: Start with core functionality
  • Incremental refinement: Add complexity gradually
  • Performance monitoring: Track success rates and failure patterns
  • Systematic testing: Validate changes across diverse scenarios

Key iteration principles:

  • Change one element at a time to isolate impact
  • Maintain version control for prompt iterations
  • Document performance changes with each modification
  • Test edge cases and failure scenarios regularly

Production-Ready Template

Here’s a comprehensive template for agentic prompts based on proven frameworks:

# Agent Configuration: [Agent Name/ID]
Version: [X.X] | Created: [Date] | Owner: [Team/Individual]

## Mission Statement
[Overarching goal and purpose - 2-3 sentences maximum]

## Role
You are a [specific role] with [relevant expertise/authority level]. 
[Additional context about operational environment]

## Core Tasks
1. [Primary responsibility with measurable outcome]
2. [Secondary task with clear deliverable]
3. [Output formatting requirement]

## Available Tools
- [Tool 1]: [Purpose and usage guidelines]
- [Tool 2]: [Capabilities and limitations]
- [Tool N]: [Integration requirements]

## Knowledge Sources
- [Data source 1]: [Reliability level and access method]
- [Information repository]: [Update frequency and scope]

## Operational Constraints
- [Boundary 1]: [Specific limitation with examples]
- [Safety rule]: [Non-negotiable requirement]
- [Resource limit]: [Specific thresholds]

## Success Criteria
Evaluate performance against:
- [Metric 1]: [Target threshold]
- [Quality measure]: [Assessment method]

## Contingency Protocols
If [specific scenario], then [defined action]
When [error condition], escalate via [method]

## Output Format
[Exact structure specification with examples]

Best Practices for Implementation

Document Everything

Maintain comprehensive documentation of prompt evolution and version history, performance metrics and trends, common failure patterns and solutions, user feedback, and system improvements.

Maintain Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints

Even autonomous systems benefit from strategic human oversight points. Define clear criteria for when human intervention is required or beneficial.

Start Simple, Scale Gradually

Begin with basic functionality and add complexity incrementally. This approach allows you to identify and resolve issues before they compound in more complex scenarios.

Test Across Diverse Scenarios

Validate your agentic prompts against common use cases and expected inputs, edge cases and unusual scenarios, system stress conditions and resource constraints, and integration points with other systems.

The future of AI agents lies not just in their ability to follow instructions, but in their capacity to understand context, make intelligent decisions, and adapt to changing conditions, all capabilities that stem from well-architected agentic prompts.

item.title: I got hacked on X by pasting one command into Terminal
item.description: A sponsored Google result, a fake Cloudflare check and a 360-line macOS stealer. My X account posted crypto spam for 12 hours.
item.content:encoded:
In June I lost control of my X account for about 12 hours, and it was entirely my fault. Here’s what happened, how it happened and what it cost me.

Twelve hours of crypto spam

On 27 June 2025 my X account spent about 12 hours posting crypto spam under my name. Friends started reaching out and flagging it.

Once I had the account back I posted “if you took crypto advice from me in the last 12 hours…sorry 💀”. A few minutes later I thanked the eleven people who had reached out and flagged the spam. I genuinely couldn’t have done it without them.

How it happened

Short version: I ran the attacker’s code myself.

I was trying to download a developer tool, and the top Google result was a sponsored link. I clicked it thinking it was a legit download source. The page showed what looked like a Cloudflare “verify you are human” check, which asked me to paste a command into Terminal. So I did.

That command ran an Odyssey Stealer script, about 360 lines long, which harvested passwords, crypto wallets and personal files from my personal MacBook. The X account was just the most visible thing the attacker did with all of it.

What else got taken

Changing passwords is the easy part. The harder question is what else walked out the door. On 6 August 2025 I bought a full remediation report from an infostealer-monitoring service, and it arrived in two emails. The exposure came from both browsers on that machine, Chrome and Firefox: credentials, cookies and session tokens, and autofill data. According to the report, no credit card data and no app configuration files were taken. Their advice was to change every exposed password and clear every cookie session in both browsers.

What I took from it

  • Never paste terminal commands from a website.
  • Run outbound network monitoring on your Mac (LuLu is free).
  • Use hardware security keys for the accounts that matter.
  • Keep people around you who will tell you fast when something is off.
  • No OS is immune to social engineering.

item.title: LLMFeeder: the browser extension I built to feed web pages to LLMs
item.description: A Wes Bos post, a quick prototype, a friend's Firefox PR, 100 GitHub stars in about two weeks, and the first people trying to sell me installs.
item.content:encoded:
A month ago, I had never built a browser extension. Today I have one live on both the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons, with 100 stars on GitHub and five contributors. And yes, it has already attracted its first growth hackers! :D

Here’s the demo:

The problem

I paste a lot of web pages into LLMs as context, mostly docs and articles. Copying a page by hand is a pain. You have to select carefully, and you still end up dragging along the formatting, pop-ups, ads and modals around the text you actually wanted. What the model really wants is clean Markdown.

Picture this: you’re deep in a coding session, stuck on a tricky implementation detail, and you remember seeing the perfect solution in some documentation online. You navigate to the site, and…

  • BAM! Newsletter signup popup. You close it.
  • BAM! Cookie consent banner. You accept.
  • BAM! “Download our app” overlay. You dismiss it.

Finally, you try to select the relevant code snippet, but the selection keeps grabbing ads, navigation menus and random sidebar content. By the time you paste it into Copilot/Cursor/Windsurf, you’re dealing with a mess of irrelevant HTML that confuses your LLM’s context. Sound familiar?

I was doing this 4-5 times a day when I saw a post from Wes Bos about the exact same problem. It gave me the idea to quickly prototype an extension, and once it worked, I replied to him with a demo.

Hey Wes, try out: https://t.co/CFBpQT0PbW

Quick demo (this might fit your usecase well)! :) pic.twitter.com/DY0GlD2plQ

— Jatin K Malik (@jatinkrmalik) May 29, 2025

What it does

LLMFeeder converts the page you’re on to Markdown and copies it to your clipboard in one click. Then you just paste it into ChatGPT, Claude or whatever you use. That’s it!

There’s nothing magical inside. Mozilla’s Readability finds the main content of the page (it’s the same library behind Firefox’s Reader View), and Turndown turns that HTML into Markdown. My own code around those two handles the choices that matter for LLM context:

  • Content scope: the main content (default), the full page, or just your selection.
  • Options: include the page title, keep or drop images, and keep tables as tables.
  • Shortcut: Alt+Shift+M (⌥ ⇧ M on a Mac) converts and copies without even opening the popup, and you can change the shortcuts to fit your workflow. If you’d rather click, the popup has a “Convert & Copy” button.

The part I care about most is that it runs fully client-side. No data leaves your browser. No server, no analytics, no tracking. When someone on X shared another way to get Markdown out of a page, that was my answer: the extension is completely offline and private, so it also works on docs and pages behind an intranet or a VPC. :)

Fun fact: this is my first ever browser extension. A few days after launch I was explaining in a reply that browser extensions are purely frontend, no backend, something I had only learnt myself the week before! The repo’s language bar says 89.9% JavaScript, and the rest is shell, CSS and HTML.

Five days, two stores

  • 28 May: Set up a Chrome Web Store developer account and paid the one-time registration fee.
  • 29 May, around 1:30 am: Recorded a two-minute demo and tweeted “Just launched LLMFeeder” with the GitHub link.
  • 29 May, same day: An issue asking for Firefox support went up, and a friend sent the pull request for it. I merged it and cut v1.0.1 that evening, with Firefox 109+ support and build scripts that produce separate Chrome and Firefox zips. Submitted it to addons.mozilla.org the same day.
  • 31 May: The Chrome Web Store listing went live, and I mailed myself the store link.
  • 1 June: The Firefox add-on got approved too. ✅

Just launched LLMFeeder: A Chrome extension that converts and copy any web page to clean Markdown to your clipboard with one click.

Perfect for feeding context to ChatGPT and other LLMs.

Fully client-side, no data leaves your browser.

Check it out: https://t.co/zQV0jmiJvC

— Jatin K Malik (@jatinkrmalik) May 29, 2025

I asked people to be kind with reviews. 🙏 The first Firefox rating came in on 3 June: 5 out of 5!

Making it easy to contribute

Around the time the stores went live, I wrote up a backlog of issues, labelled small, medium or large, with the easy ones marked good first issue. On 3 June I posted it for anyone looking for an open source project to contribute to. The deal is simple: I review the PRs, and you get bragging rights to a product that’s live and published.

Devs, if you are looking to contribute to a cool open source project, I have created a backlog of issues ranging from small -> medium -> large in https://t.co/zQV0jmiJvC.

Happy to review PRs. 🔃

You get to have bragging rights to a product that is live and published. 🤓 pic.twitter.com/2pyrcOtDeA

— Jatin K Malik (@jatinkrmalik) June 3, 2025

People started picking things up within a day. By 4 June my inbox was full of GitHub notifications: someone taking the polyfill refactor, a proposal for a debug logger, work on visual feedback for the keyboard shortcut, and not one but two separate dark mode PRs!

On 5 June, a contributor’s PR for the “Support for exporting as a .md file” issue got merged. It went through 20+ threads of discussion before it landed, and I joked that a keyboard shortcut for it should be next. 😉

Kudos @Iampatelajeet for merging a cool feature to LLMFeeder to allow downloading Markdown files. 👏

Pretty comprehensive PR with 20+ threads of discussion: https://t.co/0GgxmulwZV

What's next?
Maybe add a keyboard shortcut for the command. 😉 pic.twitter.com/nbYIaBFXKw

— Jatin K Malik (@jatinkrmalik) June 6, 2025

On 8 June I asked for UI/UX help: ideas for an icon, mockups for the popup, and proper screenshots for the store listings. Someone asked about the dev loop too. If you load the extension from source the way the README describes, pulling the latest main or changing a file is all it takes to update it on your machine. That probably deserves a CONTRIBUTING.md.

v1.0.2 and v1.1.0

v1.0.2 came out on 10 June. It shipped the Markdown download, an option to include the page title, smarter alt text for images, cross-browser fixes for notifications, a Makefile, build guides for both browsers, issue templates and a contributors section. Firefox had it live the very next day, while the Chrome update was still sitting in review.

v1.1.0 followed on 13 June with a dark/light mode toggle that remembers your choice, redesigned notification banners and a footer crediting everyone who contributed. And the repo crossed 100 stars the same day! 🌟

The badges show the fun part of shipping to two stores: Firefox was already on v1.1.0 while Chrome was still on v1.0.2. Both times so far, the Firefox update went live first.

Then the growth hackers showed up

On 12 June I got a “Chrome extension promotion” mail. The sender said they’d helped other extensions get up to 1,000 new users a month with positive feedback, “all from real people”, and wanted a 10-minute call or a chat on Telegram. I replied “I am good, thank you.” The follow-up was more direct: 1,000 users and 100 reviews on my extension, was I interested? “I’m good. Not needed.”

On 19 June a second one arrived, from a “digital marketing expert” who had reviewed my extension, recognised its potential for top-tier success and could deliver 1,000+ active users a month through SEO and “CwSO”. I said I wasn’t interested.

The milder ones were a service that wanted me to monitor my extension’s stats and a project showcase site inviting me to list LLMFeeder. But paid users and reviews? That’s a no from me, both times.

Where it stands

I built this for my own workflow and opened it up because I thought other developers might find it useful too. A lot of what shipped after launch came from other people’s PRs, and most of those started from that backlog of small, medium and large issues. That part has honestly been the most fun.

It doesn’t work everywhere yet, though. Sites that implement strict CSP rules (including Confluence) can block it, with errors like this one:

  • Refused to execute inline script because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive...

I’m working on a multi-layered fallback for those pages. Happy to get feedback if anyone has worked on something like this before!

If you feed web pages to LLMs, give it a try! It’s on the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons, and on GitHub if you’d rather inspect the code and build it from source first. Issues & pull requests are welcome. 🤝

Update, November 2026: LLMFeeder has its own website now, llmfeeder.fyi, with the demo video above, the install links and everything it can do today.

item.title: How to Live a Life of Honor? An XKCD inspired guide for Software Engineers!
item.description: Five heavily opinionated, xkcd-illustrated principles for practising honor in your daily work as a software engineer, from my last 12 years in the industry.
item.content:encoded:
Living a life of honor as a software engineer isn’t about grand gestures, it’s about consistency in small choices. By focusing on your craft, nurturing peaceful collaboration, committing to growth, guarding your integrity, and mastering communication, you’ll not only build great software but also inspire trust and respect in your peers.

In doing so, you leave the world a better place-one line of code, one act of kindness, and one disciplined day at a time.

In the fast-paced world of software development where deadlines loom, priorities shift, and egos can run high-living a life of honor is both a compass and a shield. It’s about more than writing clean code, it’s about cultivating a character that elevates your team, your product, and ultimately, the world.

Here’s my heavily opinionated view on how you can practice honor in your daily work as a software engineer based on last 12 years in this industry:

1. Focus on Your Work, Let Results Speak!

  • Dedicate yourself fully to each task. Minimize distractions and commit to deep focus.
  • Measure your impact by outcomes such as features shipped, bugs resolved, performance improved rather than by self-promotion.
  • Trust that consistent, quality contributions will be recognized naturally.

2. Build Peace, Avoid Arguments, Solve Problems!

  • Foster a collaborative environment. When disagreements arise, assume good intent and seek to understand before responding.
  • De-escalate conflicts by reframing challenges as shared problems to solve together.
  • Steer clear of toxic politics and office alliances. Your reputation thrives on fairness, not favoritism.

3. Commit to Continuous Improvement!

  • Adopt the “kaizen” mindset: small, daily improvements compound into mastery. Learn a new framework, refine your algorithms, or optimize your workflow every week.
  • Set personal growth goals: public speaking at a local meetup, contributing to an open-source project, or mentoring a junior engineer.
  • Regularly reflect on your progress. Celebrate wins, analyze setbacks, and adjust course.

4. Uphold Integrity and Do Good!

  • Honor your commitments. If you promise a timeline or a code review, deliver it or communicate proactively if circumstances change.
  • Protect sensitive data, respect privacy, and adhere to security best practices-even when no one is watching.
  • Use your skills for good: volunteer to build tools for nonprofits, contribute to accessibility initiatives, or share knowledge through workshops.

5. Master Communication and Time!

  • Speak Less, Listen More: In stand-ups or design reviews, ask clarifying questions and genuinely absorb feedback before offering opinions.
  • Avoid Gossip and Idle Talk: Channel water-cooler energy into productive brainstorming or helping colleagues overcome blockers.
  • Respect Time, Yours and Theirs: Be punctual, concise, and mindful of everyone’s calendar. Prepare agendas for meetings and end them early if objectives are met.

Comics: xkcd by Randall Munroe, used under CC BY-NC 2.5. The last one is a fan-made, xkcd-style strip.

item.title: How to install NVIDIA RTX 5000 (Blackwell) drivers on Linux
item.description: I wasted 3 hours getting my RTX 5080 working on Linux so you don't have to. Open kernel modules, per-distro steps for Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch, and the usual fixes.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Linux users who recently bought an NVIDIA RTX 5000 series card, this one is for you.

Getting my new RTX 5080 working on Linux turned into a proper fight with drivers. So I wrote it all down in a GitHub gist and tweeted it out with a Linus Torvalds GIF, because what else do you attach to an NVIDIA-on-Linux post? This post is that gist, cleaned up a bit.

I wasted 3 hours, so you don’t have to. You are welcome! :)

Once you know the steps, it’s a 10 minute job on pretty much any distro.

Use the open kernel modules

This is the big one. For RTX 5000 series (Blackwell) GPUs you HAVE to use NVIDIA’s open kernel modules. The proprietary driver branch does not support Blackwell.

NVIDIA has been moving towards open source GPU kernel modules for its newer platforms, and Blackwell is where that became mandatory. So whatever your distro, you want the package with “open” in the name. With the .run installer, pick the MIT/GPL open module option when it asks.

Step 1: Purge whatever driver you already have

Most common mistake? Installing new drivers on top of old ones. That causes conflicts which are a nightmare to untangle, so start clean.

On Debian-based distros (Ubuntu, Debian, Mint, Pop!_OS):

sudo apt-get remove --purge '^nvidia-.*'
sudo apt autoremove
sudo reboot

On Fedora/RHEL:

sudo dnf remove "*nvidia*"
sudo reboot

On Arch:

sudo pacman -Rs nvidia nvidia-utils
sudo reboot

And if you had installed from NVIDIA’s .run file earlier:

sudo nvidia-uninstall
sudo reboot

Step 2: Install the driver for your distro

Ubuntu and friends

First the build dependencies, so DKMS can compile the kernel module properly:

sudo apt install pkg-config libglvnd-dev dkms build-essential libegl-dev libegl1 libgl-dev libgl1 libgles-dev libgles1 libglvnd-core-dev libglx-dev libopengl-dev gcc make

Then add the graphics drivers PPA, which carries the latest tested drivers for new GPU architectures:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:graphics-drivers/ppa
sudo apt update

Then install the open driver (yes, -open again!) and reboot:

sudo apt install nvidia-driver-570-open
sudo reboot

Debian (Bookworm 12, Trixie 13, Sid)

Debian doesn’t support PPAs, so the Ubuntu route won’t work here. Debian’s repos also don’t have packaged drivers that support Blackwell yet, so you have to use NVIDIA’s official .run installer.

Install the dependencies, including headers for your running kernel:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install pkg-config libglvnd-dev dkms build-essential libegl-dev libegl1 libgl-dev libgl1 libgles-dev libgles1 libglvnd-core-dev libglx-dev libopengl-dev gcc make linux-headers-$(uname -r)

Download the driver. Check the NVIDIA Unix drivers page for the latest production branch version first. Anything 570 or newer supports Blackwell.

wget https://us.download.nvidia.com/XFree86/Linux-x86_64/570.124.04/NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-570.124.04.run

Blacklist nouveau so it doesn’t grab the card:

echo "blacklist nouveau
options nouveau modeset=0" | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nouveau.conf
sudo update-initramfs -u

Now switch to a TTY (Ctrl+Alt+F3), stop your display manager and run the installer:

sudo systemctl stop gdm3      # GNOME/GDM
# or
sudo systemctl stop sddm      # KDE/SDDM
# or
sudo systemctl stop lightdm   # LightDM

chmod +x NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-570.124.04.run
sudo ./NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-570.124.04.run

In the installer, accept the licence. When it asks which kernel modules to install, pick the open (MIT/GPL) ones. Blackwell won’t work without them. Take the defaults for the rest, let it update your X config, then sudo reboot.

Fedora/RHEL

Enable RPM Fusion (free and nonfree):

sudo dnf install https://download1.rpmfusion.org/free/fedora/rpmfusion-free-release-$(rpm -E %fedora).noarch.rpm
sudo dnf install https://download1.rpmfusion.org/nonfree/fedora/rpmfusion-nonfree-release-$(rpm -E %fedora).noarch.rpm

Then the open variant:

sudo dnf install akmod-nvidia-open xorg-x11-drv-nvidia-cuda
sudo reboot

Arch and derivatives

Easiest of the lot!

sudo pacman -S nvidia-open nvidia-utils
sudo reboot

Everything else

If your distro doesn’t package the drivers, use the same .run installer from the Debian section and choose the open kernel module option when it asks.

Step 3: Check that it worked

nvidia-smi

You should see driver version 570.x or newer, along with your card. Something like this:

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 570.124.04             Driver Version: 570.124.04     CUDA Version: 12.8     |
|-----------------------------------------+------------------------+----------------------+
| GPU  Name                 Persistence-M | Bus-Id          Disp.A | Volatile Uncorr. ECC |
| Fan  Temp   Perf          Pwr:Usage/Cap |           Memory-Usage | GPU-Util  Compute M. |
|                                         |                        |               MIG M. |
|=========================================+========================+======================|
|   0  NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080        Off |   00000000:01:00.0  On |                  N/A |
|  0%   40C    P8             15W /  360W |     512MiB /  16376MiB |      0%      Default |
+-----------------------------------------+------------------------+----------------------+

If you see that, you’re done. 🤓

When it doesn’t work

The gist has every command for these spelled out. This is the short version.

“NVIDIA-SMI has failed because it couldn’t communicate with the NVIDIA driver”

Go down this list in order:

  1. Is the module even loaded? lsmod | grep nvidia. If nothing shows up, look at sudo dmesg | grep -i nvidia for the reason.
  2. Is Secure Boot on? mokutil --sb-state. If yes, you either sign the kernel modules (next section) or turn Secure Boot off in the BIOS.
  3. Do your kernel headers match your running kernel? Compare uname -r with ls /usr/src/linux-headers-*.
  4. Rebuild the DKMS modules with sudo dkms autoinstall (or sudo dkms install nvidia/<your driver version>) and reboot.
  5. Is nouveau still loaded? lsmod | grep nouveau. If it is, blacklist it and rebuild the initramfs.

Secure Boot is on

With Secure Boot on, the kernel only loads modules signed with a key your firmware trusts. If you’d rather keep it on, the documented way is to enrol a Machine Owner Key (MOK). DKMS then signs the NVIDIA modules with that key every time it builds them.

On Ubuntu the driver package mostly handles this for you. It creates the key, asks you to set a one-time password, and MokManager comes up on the next reboot. Pick Enroll MOK, check the fingerprint, confirm with that password and reboot. Ubuntu’s Secure Boot docs walk through it.

On Debian, DKMS keeps its key at /var/lib/dkms/mok.key and the public half at /var/lib/dkms/mok.pub. The Debian wiki enrols it like this:

sudo mokutil --import /var/lib/dkms/mok.pub   # asks you to set a one-time password
sudo mokutil --list-new                       # check the key is queued for the next boot
sudo reboot

On reboot the MOK manager screen shows up. Choose Enroll MOK, confirm, type the password you just set, then let it boot. sudo dmesg | grep cert should show the key loading. If you went the .run route, this only covers the module if you let the installer register it with DKMS.

Laptops: GPU not detected at all

This one bites ASUS ROG and Zephyrus owners a lot, and anyone with a MUX switch or a dual boot with Windows. The dGPU can be powered off when you boot into Linux, so nvidia-smi fails, lspci | grep -i nvidia shows nothing, and settings only see the iGPU.

On ASUS, boot into Windows, open Armoury Crate, set GPU mode to Standard or Optimized (not iGPU-only), switch off Silent mode in favour of Performance or Turbo, and reboot into Linux. On other laptops with a MUX switch, go into the BIOS/UEFI graphics settings and pick “Discrete GPU” or “dGPU mode” instead of Optimus or Hybrid.

On some ASUS laptops you can also force the dGPU on from Linux:

echo 0 | sudo tee /sys/devices/platform/asus-nb-wmi/dgpu_disable
echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/rescan

And on Arch, you can install the ASUS Linux tools and set the graphics mode to dedicated:

yay -S asusctl supergfxctl
sudo systemctl enable --now asusd
sudo systemctl enable --now supergfxd
supergfxctl -m dedicated

Black screen on HDMI/DisplayPort once X starts

The TTY works fine, but the moment X11 or Wayland starts, the monitor loses signal. Fun! Try these:

  • Many laptops route HDMI/DP through the iGPU, so check the BIOS for a display output setting that uses the dGPU.
  • Add nvidia-drm.modeset=1 to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT in /etc/default/grub, run sudo update-grub and reboot.
  • If you only want the dGPU, blacklist the iGPU (blacklist i915 for Intel) and rebuild the initramfs.
  • Add an Xorg OutputClass config in /etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/10-nvidia.conf that makes the NVIDIA card the primary GPU (full snippet in the gist).
  • Swap ports. Some people find DisplayPort works where HDMI doesn’t, or the other way round.
  • In the BIOS, set Primary Display to PCIe/PEG instead of Auto or iGPU, and enable Above 4G Decoding and Re-Size BAR.

A phantom “Unknown Display”

If a ghost “Unknown Display” shows up in Settings after installing, sudo rm /dev/dri/card0, then log out and back in.

Wayland not available

On GNOME, make sure WaylandEnable=true is uncommented in /etc/gdm3/custom.conf (or /etc/gdm/custom.conf), then:

sudo ln -s /dev/null /etc/udev/rules.d/61-gdm.rules
sudo reboot

On KDE Plasma, add DisplayServer=wayland under [General] in /etc/sddm.conf.

CUDA and ML frameworks

For ML work, install CUDA after the driver: sudo apt install nvidia-cuda-toolkit on Ubuntu/Debian, sudo dnf install cuda on Fedora, sudo pacman -S cuda on Arch. Check it with nvcc --version.

Blackwell needs CUDA 12.8 or newer, so check that your framework builds support it before you upgrade anything.

For PyTorch, take the command from the install selector on pytorch.org rather than copy-pasting some old snippet, and make sure you pick a CUDA 12.8 or newer build. Older ones like cu121 won’t cut it on these cards.

Why is this still so painful?

Back in 2012, Linus Torvalds famously gave NVIDIA the middle finger during a talk and called it the single worst company the Linux folks had ever dealt with. (Here’s the clip from that talk.) His complaint was that NVIDIA sold millions of chips for Linux-based devices but wouldn’t work with the open source community.

The fun bit is that NVIDIA is now moving towards open source kernel modules, which is exactly why Blackwell needs the -open driver. That’s progress, but there’s still some way to go, or this post wouldn’t need to exist. Open source+++

If something here breaks on your setup, leave a comment on the gist.
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: From the audience to the stage: how a backend engineer learnt to give talks
item.description: In 2019 I was in the audience at Bengaluru meetups. Since then I've given talks in Bengaluru, Delhi, Goa, Pilani and Chicago. Here's every one, in order.
item.content:encoded:
Last Tuesday I gave a talk at the Elastic user group in Chicago. When I sat down afterwards and listed all my talks, that one came out as the eleventh since 2020. Eleven! Six years ago I was the guy in the audience, taking notes.

I’ve always been a backend and platform person, way more at home in services and databases than on slides. So here’s the whole run, in order, starting with the meetups I sat through, then a talk nobody outside my company saw, then everything since late 2023.

2019: the year I sat in the audience

In 2019 I moved to Bengaluru for a new job, and I spent a good part of that year at meetups. Bengaluru has a LOT of them.

In June I went to Golang meetup #45 and, like a good student, mailed my notes to myself. A couple of weeks later I was at the ThoughtWorks Tech Radar Summit, where Martin Fowler gave “A Decade of the Radar”. My tweet that morning was just “@martinfowler in the house!!”, which tells you how calm I was about it.

Tech Radar Summit, Bengaluru, June 2019. I was a long way from that stage.

Later that morning another speaker was giving his first ever tech talk, and I tweeted that he was killing it.

In July it was a GDG Bangalore Flutter session (“Flutter ain’t easy, but it’s sure fun”). In September I went to DevFest 2019 at the Infosys campus, checked in “just in time”, and spent the day in other people’s talks. The two I tweeted about were a “less is more” talk from a Gojek engineer and a very energetic one on designing high growth products.

The DevFest 2019 kit. Note the word “Attendee”.

2020: a talk on Zoom

The first talk on my list wasn’t on a stage at all. In April 2020, ten days into the lockdown, I gave a 40 minute talk to colleagues over Zoom about my homelab, where every machine has a Lord of the Rings name. The deck alone took me a few weeks. I wrote it up as my Lord of the Rings homelab talk.

After that, nothing for a few years. Life happened. When someone asked me in August 2023 how to grow a network as an engineer, my answer was “Dev meetups, community charters etc.” A month later I started taking my own advice.

Late 2023: four talks in four months

Atlassian Tech and Product Connect, Bengaluru (September 2023)

In September 2023 we hosted Atlassian Tech and Product Connect in Bengaluru, an invite-only forum for 100+ people from across the industry. A colleague and I gave a talk on “Multi-Region Cloud Architecture And Data Residency”, about the challenges of designing cloud products for enterprise scale when customers care where their data lives. The long version became this post on our multi-region journey.

Tech and Product Connect: a big screen, a full room and two of us sharing it.

At the networking session afterwards, the conversations kept landing on the same few things: migration strategies, datastores, horizontal vs vertical vs “diagonal” scaling, and of course AI.

GDG DevFest New Delhi (October 2023)

Eleven days later I announced I’d be speaking in the Cloud track at DevFest 2023 New Delhi. Four years after wearing an “Attendee” badge at DevFest Bengaluru, I was on the speaker list for one. I got there by answering the CFP.

My slot was 11:05 AM on 7 October, and the talk was “Data Portability in Enterprise Cloud”. At the end I put up a bonus problem: zero downtime migration, moving data, applications and services from one environment to another without any disruption to users. The rules were to think through the solution at a high level, DM me before 4 PM, and the best answer would win a cool goodie.

The venue, and the bonus problem I posted again on X right after the talk.

Six people sent in some really interesting ideas, and it came down to two entries in the final. They were tied, so we settled it the only fair way: best of three, stone, paper, scissors! The winner got the goodie.

The next day I tweeted my annual reminder: “There is no cloud, it’s just someone else’s computer!” I stand by it.

FOSSConf’23 at IIIT Delhi (November 2023)

On 26 November I gave a keynote at FOSSConf’23, organised by FOSSCU in the main hall at IIIT Delhi. The title was “Elevate Your Code // Practical Insights for 10X Impact”. After my session I stayed for a Women in Tech panel where the panelists talked about how they got started in their careers. Super inspiring.

FOSSConf’23 was at IIIT Delhi.

FOSS United Delhi meetup (December 2023)

This one had the most fun title of the lot: “The Coder’s Guide to Job Security: Mastering the Art of Confusing Code!”. It’s a tongue-in-cheek guide to writing code nobody else can maintain, with a Python example for every rule: bad names, magic numbers, redundant code, needless complexity and more. The source material is Roedy Green’s 1997 essay on unmaintainable code, which I credit in the repo.

I submitted it to the FOSS United Delhi December meetup on 4 December, it was accepted on 14 December, and I gave it on 16 December. The slides weren’t PowerPoint. They’re a Markdown file you run in the terminal with mdp. Code and slides are all in the repo on GitHub.

Early 2024: campuses, Redis and cells

A session on cloud, web and AI (January 2024)

In January I did a session on where cloud and web development are heading, the latest trends, and what AI is doing to software engineering. It turned into a very interactive one, and I put the deck up on my site afterwards.

Quark 2024, BITS Goa (February 2024)

In February I went to BITS Goa for Quark 2024 to talk about “c0de_to_cl0ud”. Over the two days I mentored two live demos, each with an end-to-end integration and some good discussion before it. One of them was a Flask app with a decimal to base62 function, which is the core of any URL shortener.

One of the live demos at Quark. Faces and the database credentials on the projector are blurred.

FOSS Delhi 2.0 at IIT Delhi (March 2024)

This one went through a selection: in late February I got to announce that my talk had been picked for FOSS Delhi 2.0. On 9 March I gave the first session of the day at IIT Delhi, “The Redis Paradox: Beyond the Cache Horizon”, about everything Redis can do beyond being a cache. It came with a Driver<>Rider matching simulator that people could run on their own machines. The night before, I tweeted “So, it’s time to build the slides!” and then admitted I was kidding. I’d been telling people Redis isn’t just a cache since early 2023, and that talk has a post of its own.

The Redis Paradox at IIT Delhi.

APOGEE 2024, BITS Pilani (April 2024)

A month later it was BITS Pilani for APOGEE 2024, and a different format again: a live three-hour workshop on building apps with Forge, Atlassian’s app platform. We kept the trainer to attendee ratio conservative on purpose, so we could actually pay attention to the students and help them build. The weather was rainy and lovely!

Rainy APOGEE, BITS Pilani.

Atlassian x EPAM Innovation Day (May 2024)

In May I spoke at the Atlassian x EPAM Innovation Day at our Bengaluru office, on “AI enabled auto-scaling using CELL based architecture”. The deck and recording were internal, so two days later I wrote a public thread on cell-based architecture for anyone who wanted the concepts: what a cell is, how cells isolate failures, how they scale, and the trade-offs.

My slot on the agenda. The co-speaker’s details and the room are blurred.

Chicago: starting over, and the eleventh talk

In August 2024 I moved to Chicago, and in a way I was back in 2019: a new city, and back in the audience at meetups. When I joined the Chicago Elastic User Group on Meetup, I ticked the box saying I’d be interested in presenting.

In October, Elastic’s developer relations team emailed to ask if I’d like to present. I replied at the end of November and offered a talk on how we used Elasticsearch back when I was at Uber. The date moved around my travel a couple of times before it landed on 25 February 2025.

The talk was “Cracking the Code of Customer Happiness: Real-Time Insights at Uber Scale”, in the 6:05 PM slot at Improving’s office in Chicago. It’s about the customer obsession side of Uber, where feedback comes in from social media, support tickets and in-app help, far too much to read by hand, and how Elastic helped spot emerging issues in real time. The deck goes problem, solution, architecture (the slide just says “Some Boxes & Arrows”) and impact.

Elastic Chicago, 25 February 2025, and the loot.

My one mishap: I showed up early, like a responsible speaker, and got stuck in the lobby. So did the other speaker. (: Turns out being early only helps if you can get past the front desk.

What I noticed along the way

When Where Format
Apr 2020 Colleagues, on Zoom Homelab talk
Sep 2023 Atlassian Tech and Product Connect, Bengaluru Co-presented talk
Oct 2023 GDG DevFest New Delhi Cloud track talk + bonus problem
Nov 2023 FOSSConf’23, IIIT Delhi Keynote
Dec 2023 FOSS United Delhi meetup Talk with terminal slides and code
Jan 2024 Cloud, web and AI session Interactive session
Feb 2024 Quark 2024, BITS Goa Talk + mentoring live demos
Mar 2024 FOSS Delhi 2.0, IIT Delhi Talk
Apr 2024 APOGEE 2024, BITS Pilani Three-hour workshop
May 2024 Atlassian x EPAM Innovation Day Internal talk + public thread
Feb 2025 Elastic user group, Chicago Meetup talk

Getting picked can be surprisingly simple. The FOSS United talk went from proposal to stage in twelve days, and the Elastic one started with a checkbox on a Meetup form. Both were community events looking for speakers, and I put my hand up with a topic I’d actually worked on.

Most of these talks also left something behind after the hour was up. The bonus problem went up on X, the confusing-code examples are on GitHub, the decks are on my site, and when a deck couldn’t leave the building I wrote a thread instead. People who missed the talk can still use it.

Several of them also gave the room a job. At DevFest that was a bonus problem with a prize, at Quark the students ran their own demos, and at APOGEE the workshop was small enough that we could help people one at a time.

And the format kept changing. Zoom, a big stage shared with a colleague, a keynote, slides in a terminal, a three-hour workshop and an evening meetup in Chicago are all different jobs. The topics, though, always came from my own work, my homelab or code I’d written.

The guy taking notes at the Golang meetup in 2019 would be pretty surprised by this list. If you’re in that seat right now, put your hand up the next time a meetup asks for speakers! Worst case, you get a good story out of it, and maybe a stone, paper, scissors final to referee.

item.title: #DistributedDilemmas: all 24 days in one place
item.description: In February 2025 I posted one distributed systems dilemma a day on X. I made it to day 24. Here they all are, with the diagrams.
item.content:encoded:
On 1 February I kicked off 28 Days of #DistributedDilemmas on X: one battle-tested insight a day on the hidden complexities behind outages, tech debt and architectural nightmares. No hype, no fluff.

The plan said 28 days. I made it to 24. Each day has its own page now, with the full post, the diagram I made for it and a link back to the original on X.

All 24 days

  1. Consistency guarantees become availability nightmares
  2. Microservices don’t eliminate complexity, they redistribute it
  3. Caching accelerates inconsistency
  4. Idempotency is a lie we tell ourselves
  5. Sharding decisions made today become tomorrow’s scaling bottlenecks
  6. Leader election creates false security
  7. Network partitions heal dangerously
  8. Eventual consistency is consistently misunderstood
  9. Distributed transactions are a myth at scale
  10. Observability becomes obscurity at scale
  11. Queue-based architectures hide scaling issues
  12. API versioning perpetuates distributed mistakes
  13. Configuration sprawl is the silent killer of distributed systems
  14. Service discovery often becomes a SPOT (single point of failure)
  15. Distributed logging creates more noise than signal
  16. Serverless doesn’t mean worry-free
  17. Distributed cron jobs are a coordination nightmare
  18. Microservice authentication is a distributed minefield
  19. Database migrations in distributed systems require meticulous planning due to their inherent complexity
  20. Distributed rate limiting is harder than it looks
  21. Event sourcing isn’t a silver bullet for distribution
  22. Distributed background jobs need careful orchestration
  23. Distributed caching layers often become consistency nightmares
  24. Distributed sessions are a persistent headache
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Day 24 of #DistributedDilemmas: Distributed sessions are a persistent headache
item.description: Distributed sessions are a persistent headache. Sticky sessions don't scale, but fully distributed sessions add complexity. Consider JWT or externalized…
item.content:encoded:
Sticky sessions don’t scale, but fully distributed sessions add complexity. Consider JWT or externalized session stores carefully.

Benchmarks show hybrid approaches emerging - 42% of enterprises now use JWT for authentication claims while storing volatile session data in Redis TTL buckets.

Read more: https://devops.com/session-tokens-vs-jwts-choosing-your-session-management-solution/

This balances stateless benefits with managed transient data complexity!

Day 24 on X ↗
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Day 23 of #DistributedDilemmas: Distributed caching layers often become consistency nightmares
item.description: Distributed caching layers often become consistency nightmares. As cache invalidation schemes attempt to maintain coherence, real-world implementations…
item.content:encoded:
As cache invalidation schemes attempt to maintain coherence, real-world implementations often reveal why short TTLs (Time-to-Live) can outperform complex invalidation logic in many scenarios.

While purists argue TTLs “kick the can down the road,” pragmatic engineering often favors their simplicity. As Meta’s infrastructure team concluded: “Sometimes 99.9% consistency with 1-minute TTLs is better than 99.999% consistency with unmaintainable invalidation logic”. (Read more: https://engineering.fb.com/2022/06/08/core-infra/cache-made-consistent/)

The choice ultimately depends on whether your use case can tolerate bounded staleness versus requiring absolute accuracy.

Day 23 on X ↗
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Day 22 of #DistributedDilemmas: Distributed background jobs need careful orchestration
item.description: Distributed background jobs need careful orchestration. While stateless architectures simplify scaling, they risk duplicate processing like Slack alerts…
item.content:encoded:
While stateless architectures simplify scaling, they risk duplicate processing like Slack alerts firing multiple times or dropped tasks during network partitions.

Modern workflow engines address these issues through stateful orchestration and advanced scheduling patterns.

Day 22 on X ↗

item.title: Day 21 of #DistributedDilemmas: Event sourcing isn't a silver bullet for distribution
item.description: Event sourcing isn't a silver bullet for distribution. Replay and snapshots become bottlenecks at scale. Design for efficient event storage and retrieval…
item.content:encoded:
Replay and snapshots become bottlenecks at scale. Design for efficient event storage and retrieval from the start.

Day 21 on X ↗

item.title: Day 20 of #DistributedDilemmas: Distributed rate limiting is harder than it looks
item.description: Distributed rate limiting is harder than it looks. Local rate limits don't prevent global abuse. Global protection requires coordination mechanisms like…
item.content:encoded:
Local rate limits don’t prevent global abuse. Global protection requires coordination mechanisms like distributed token bucket algorithms, which balance burst handling with system-wide fairness.

Day 20 on X ↗

item.title: Day 19 of #DistributedDilemmas: Database migrations in distributed systems require meticulous planning due to their inherent complexity
item.description: Database migrations in distributed systems require meticulous planning due to their inherent complexity. Schema changes become distributed coordination…
item.content:encoded:
Schema changes become distributed coordination challenges, demanding backward compatibility and phased rollouts to avoid system-wide failures.

Day 19 on X ↗
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Day 18 of #DistributedDilemmas: Microservice authentication is a distributed minefield
item.description: Microservice authentication is a distributed minefield. While JWTs excel at decentralized authentication, they introduce authorization complexity due to…
item.content:encoded:
While JWTs excel at decentralized authentication, they introduce authorization complexity due to distributed policy enforcement.

Here’s how to design systems that address both challenges:

The JWT-Authentication Tradeoff

JWTs provide stateless authentication by embedding user claims in cryptographically signed tokens, eliminating centralized session storage. However, they create authorization gaps:

  • Hard-coded permissions in tokens become outdated as policies evolve.

  • Lack of runtime context (e.g., resource attributes, environmental factors) for dynamic decisions.

  • No centralized invalidation without complex token revocation mechanisms.

Read more: https://www.styra.com/blog/how-to-enforce-fine-grained-authorization-in-microservices/

Fine-Grained Authorization Pattern via Decentralized Policy Enforcement

Tools like Open Policy Agent (OPA) enable distributed authorization by:

  • Evaluating policies against JWT claims + resource attributes.

  • Caching frequent decisions to maintain microservice performance.

  • Supporting attribute-based rules (e.g., “Access only if user’s department matches resource owner”).

While JWTs solve authentication at scale, modern microservices require policy-as-code approaches like OPA to handle authorization’s inherent complexity. By separating cryptographic verification from contextual policy evaluation, teams achieve both security and operational agility.

Day 18 on X ↗
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Day 17 of #DistributedDilemmas: Distributed cron jobs are a coordination nightmare
item.description: Distributed cron jobs are a coordination nightmare. Time drift and job duplication plague naive implementations. Consider distributed schedulers or…
item.content:encoded:
Time drift and job duplication plague naive implementations. Consider distributed schedulers or event-driven alternatives!

Core Challenges

  1. Time Drift: Node clock discrepancies cause inconsistent job timing across distributed systems, leading to missed deadlines or premature executions.

  2. Job Duplication

Naive implementations risk parallel execution of the same job across multiple nodes, causing data corruption and resource contention.

Robust Solutions

  1. Distributed Consensus Protocols: Leader election via Paxos/Raft ensures only one node coordinates scheduling (Google’s approach: https://sre.google/sre-book/distributed-periodic-scheduling/)

  2. Locking mechanisms like SKIP LOCKED in SQL or advisory locks prevent concurrent execution.

For new implementations, consider event-driven architectures using tools like Apache Kafka or cloud-native schedulers (AWS EventBridge, GCP Cloud Scheduler) that handle distributed coordination inherently.

Day 17 on X ↗
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Day 16 of #DistributedDilemmas: Serverless doesn't mean worry-free
item.description: Serverless doesn't mean worry-free. Cold starts and hidden state create new classes of distributed problems. While offering auto-scaling and cost…
item.content:encoded:
Cold starts and hidden state create new classes of distributed problems.

While offering auto-scaling and cost efficiency, these systems require careful architectural decisions to handle stateful operations and latency-sensitive workloads.

Exhibit A:

  • Coca-Cola’s IoT vending machines using AWS Lambda scaled from 30 million to 80 million monthly requests, reducing costs by 65% per machine.

However, this required rethinking state management:

  1. Payment sessions and user preferences had to be externalized to databases.
  2. Transactional consistency was maintained via DynamoDB instead of local function states.

Read more: https://www.serverless.direct/post/serverless-architecture-examples

Day 16 on X ↗
item.dc:creator: Jatin K Malik

item.title: Day 15 of #DistributedDilemmas: Distributed logging creates more noise than signal
item.description: Distributed logging creates more noise than signal. Modern distributed systems face two critical logging challenges: 1. Data overload from scattered logs…
item.content:encoded:
Modern distributed systems face two critical logging challenges:

  1. Data overload from scattered logs (noise drowning signal)
  2. Centralized bottlenecks from monolithic log aggregation

The solution lies in hybrid observability combining local, structured logging with distributed tracing.

Why distributed logging fails:

  • Context collapse: 78% of engineers report losing critical request context when logs are fragmented across services.

  • Alert fatigue: Traditional log aggregation increases noise as 1GB of logs typically contains <100KB of actionable data.

  • Query limitations: Cross-service log correlation requires complex joins (avg. 7.2s latency per troubleshooting session)

Best Practices for Modern Logging:

Structured logging essentials:

Deployment checklist:

  1. Embed trace IDs in all log entries.
  2. Implement tiered retention policies:

a. 7 days local storage
b. 24 hours central cache
c. 30 days cold archive

  1. Use edge filtering to discard <2% useful logs before centralization.
  2. Enable log-to-trace bidirectional navigation in monitoring tools.

This approach maintains debugging fidelity while avoiding aggregation chokepoints. The key is making traces your primary investigation tool, with logs as supplemental evidence.

item.title: Day 14 of #DistributedDilemmas: Service discovery often becomes a SPOT (single point of failure)
item.description: Service discovery often becomes a SPOT (single point of failure). Your registry being unavailable shouldn't prevent finding the registry. Design for…
item.content:encoded:
Your registry being unavailable shouldn’t prevent finding the registry. Design for graceful degradation.

Real-World Implementation Examples:

  1. Airbnb’s SmartStack uses ZooKeeper for registration and local HAProxy for failover. https://medium.com/airbnb-engineering/smartstack-service-discovery-in-the-cloud-4b8a080de619#.m0x2ks9ja

  2. Hashicorp Consul combines service discovery with health checking and multi-datacenter support. https://github.com/hashicorp/consul

  3. AWS Cloud Map implements automatic DNS failover when registry components degrade. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_mitigate_interaction_failure_graceful_degradation.html

By layering these techniques, systems maintain >99.95% availability even during registry outages, meeting strict SLOs for critical infrastructure.

The key is designing failure handling as a first-class feature rather than an afterthought.

item.title: Day 11 of #DistributedDilemmas: Queue-based architectures hide scaling issues
item.description: Queue-based architectures hide scaling issues. Kafka topics with long retention become both a blessing and a curse. Backpressure beats unbounded queues!…
item.content:encoded:
Kafka topics with long retention become both a blessing and a curse. Backpressure beats unbounded queues!

Kafka’s Retention Double-Edged Sword:
While queues create an illusion of infinite scalability by buffering load and smoothen temporary spikes, unbounded queues lead to hidden technical debt:

  • Blessing: Long retention enables event replay for recovery/analytics (critical for financial transaction auditing).
  • Curse: Segmentation Trap, Kafka only deletes closed log segments where active segments with expired data remain until rotation.

SlackHQ engineering team found 2-week retention caused 45TB storage bloat, slowing consumer bootstrap from 2s to 1m+. https://slack.engineering/scaling-slacks-job-queue/

Backpressure Patterns Beat Unbounded Queues:

  • Maintain stable throughput under load (94% fewer OOM crashes at voxer : https://engineering.voxer.com/2013/09/16/backpressure-in-nodejs/)
  • Enable native flow control without client-side retry storms (https://www.tedinski.com/2019/03/05/backpressure.html)
  • Prevent consumer lag death spiral.
